confirmed.title: Intermediate pointers (offset +16 and +32) are not NULL-checked before use
confirmed.description: cpp_obj_p (line 59) and conn_ptr (line 62) are taken from ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(...).value, which returns Python None when the read word is 0. Neither is validated. Two concrete reachable failures: (a) If the +16 read yields 0 (cpp_obj_p is None), line 62 evaluates None + 32, raising 'unsupported operand type(s) for +: NoneType and int' — an opaque TypeError, not the documented TypeError('expected duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection...') nor the documented RuntimeError. (b) A closed connection: after conn.close(), the DuckDBPyConnection's unique_ptr<Connection> is reset to null, so the +32 read yields 0 and conn_ptr is None; that None is then passed to ducklib.duckdb_query at line 67 as an intp argument, which either raises a numba typing error or (if coerced to a null address) invokes duckdb_query on a NULL connection (undefined behavior / crash). The sibling numbox bridge explicitly handles this: pysqlite_bridge.py:169-170 does 'if db_ptr is None: raise RuntimeError("extracted null sqlite3* from sqlite3.Connection")'. numbduck has no equivalent check.
confirmed.impact: A closed or otherwise null-backed connection produces a confusing TypeError or a NULL-connection C call instead of a clean, documented RuntimeError; in the coerced-null case it is a potential crash rather than a catchable error.
confirmed.recommendation: After reading cpp_obj_p and conn_ptr, raise RuntimeError with a clear message when either is falsy (None/0), before doing pointer arithmetic on cpp_obj_p or passing conn_ptr into duckdb_query — mirroring the numbox null-pointer guard.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Empirically reproduced on duckdb 1.3.2 / Linux x86-64 (the pinned/validated platform). Reading id(conn)+16 (cpp_obj_p, pybridge.py:59) and then cpp_obj_p+32 (conn_ptr, pybridge.py:62) with ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(...).value: on an open connection both reads are non-null and extract_connection_ptr returns a valid pointer. After conn.close(), the +16 read (cpp_obj_p) stays non-null but the +32 read (conn_ptr) becomes None, confirming the unique_ptr<Connection> reset claim. Calling numbduck.pybridge.extract_connection_ptr(conn) on the closed connection (which passes conn_ptr straight into ducklib.duckdb_query at line 67, before any caller-side use) raised: TypeError: No matching definition for argument type(s) none, int64, int64 -- a numba dispatch typing error, not the documented TypeError('expected duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection...') or RuntimeError('extracted connection pointer failed validation'). This directly confirms scenario (b) in the finding: the function's own docstring promises only TypeError (wrong conn type) or RuntimeError (failed validation query), but a closed connection breaks that contract with an unrelated, confusing numba TypeError instead of a clean guard. (Scenario (a), a null cpp_obj_p causing 'None + 32' TypeError, was not independently reproduced -- the +16 pybind11 instance pointer is set at construction and not realistically nullable via close(); it remains a secondary, more speculative point in the description and does not change the verdict.) numbox's sibling numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py:168-170 has the exact analogous guard ('if db_ptr is None: raise RuntimeError(...)') that pybridge.py lacks, confirming this is a known, deliberate defensive pattern in this codebase that was not carried over. Severity medium is appropriate: the observed failure mode is a confusing/undocumented TypeError (contract violation, poor caller experience for a foreseeable use-after-close call), not a demonstrated memory-safety crash -- numba's strict signature typing rejected the None argument before any native call occurred in this reproduction, so 'UB/crash' in the finding text is speculative/alternative phrasing rather than the observed outcome. Recommendation to add an explicit `if not conn_ptr: raise RuntimeError(...)` (and similarly guard cpp_obj_p) after each ctypes read is sound and directly mirrors the numbox precedent.

confirmed.title: Docstring overstates what the SELECT 1 step validates; no graceful failure path for the layout-drift it warns about
confirmed.description: The docstring promises that the extracted pointer 'is validated by running SELECT 1 via the C API before it is returned' (lines 28-29) and that a RuntimeError is raised 'if the extracted pointer fails the validation query' (lines 49-51). The actual check is `rc = ducklib.duckdb_query(conn_ptr, query_p, result.ctypes.data)` followed by `if rc != DuckDBSuccess` (lines 67-72). This dramatically overstates the guarantee for the one failure mode the same docstring warns about (ABI/offset drift across duckdb 1.4/1.5, lines 31-34): if `+16`/`+32` drift and `conn_ptr` becomes a structurally-wrong (wild) pointer, `duckdb_query` dereferences garbage — undefined behavior / segfault — BEFORE any rc is produced, so the RuntimeError branch never runs. Conversely, when `conn_ptr` is a genuine live `Connection*`, `SELECT 1` essentially always returns DuckDBSuccess, so the RuntimeError branch is effectively dead. The step therefore confirms only 'an already-correct pointer works'; it provides no detection and no graceful failure for a drifted layout. The docstring reads as if the query is a safety net against the offset assumptions, but it is not.
confirmed.impact: A maintainer upgrading duckdb (pin allows >=1.3.2,<1.6) may trust the 'validated before returned' language and the documented RuntimeError as protection against layout change, when in reality the drift scenario is uncatchable UB. Misleads about the actual robustness contract.
confirmed.recommendation: Reword the docstring to state precisely what the query proves: that a *plausibly-correct* pointer resolves to a live connection that can execute a trivial query — it is a liveness smoke-test, not validation of the ABI offsets, and cannot catch a wrong-layout (wild) pointer, which is undefined behavior. Move the offset-drift warning next to this caveat.
confirmed.verdictReasoning:
Verified against numbduck/pybridge.py at HEAD. The docstring text matches exactly: lines 28-29 state the pointer 'is validated by running SELECT 1 via the C API before it is returned', and lines 49-51 document 'RuntimeError: If the extracted pointer fails the validation query.' The actual implementation (lines 64-72) is: `result = create_duckdb_result(); query_p = get_unicode_data_p("SELECT 1"); rc = ducklib.duckdb_query(conn_ptr, query_p, result.ctypes.data); ...; if rc != ducklib.DuckDBSuccess: raise RuntimeError(...)`. This is a single trivial-query round trip through the C API, gated only on the returned duckdb_state rc.

The reviewer's core technical claim holds: duckdb_query (numbduck/ducklib.py:1111-1114, calling _call_lib_func against the C API's `duckdb_state duckdb_query(duckdb_connection connection, const char *query, duckdb_result *out_result)`) receives conn_ptr as a raw pointer value and the C API implementation dereferences it directly (DuckDB's opaque `_duckdb_connection`/`_duckdb_database` handle structs are single-field type-safety fictions; the real implementation reinterpret_casts the bit pattern straight to the C++ object, with no magic-number/tag validation on the handle before dereferencing). If the two hard-coded offsets (id(conn)+16 for the DuckDBPyConnection*, then +32 for the Connection*) drift across a duckdb/pybind11 layout change -- exactly the risk the same docstring flags at lines 31-34 for 1.4/1.5 -- conn_ptr becomes an arbitrary bit pattern read from whatever field now occupies that offset. Dereferencing that inside duckdb_query is undefined behavior: in the overwhelmingly likely case it is an unmapped or non-Connection address, causing a segfault before any duckdb_state is ever produced, so the `if rc != DuckDBSuccess: raise RuntimeError` branch cannot run. Conversely, when the offsets are correct, SELECT 1 against a live connection will essentially always succeed, so that branch is dead in the success path too. Both halves of the reviewer's argument are consistent with the code and with standard C-API/ABI behavior (no runtime layout-tag checking is plausible or evidenced anywhere in ducklib.py/duckdb_utils.py -- confirmed no duckdb.__version__ guard or magic-number check exists in pybridge.py, which is the entirety of the 75-line file).

This is a genuine documentation/robustness-communication defect, not a functional bug on the currently pinned/tested target (duckdb 1.3.2, per the docstring's own 'Validated on' line and PBR-DES.json's notes field, which independently concur the code is correct on that verified target). The mismatch is between the confident wording ('validated', 'raises RuntimeError if... fails') and the actual, much weaker guarantee (a liveness smoke test that cannot catch the wrong-layout/UB case it explicitly warns readers to worry about). Given the project's duckdb pin (>=1.3.2,<1.6) permits installing 1.4/1.5 wheels where this exact drift risk applies, and a maintainer could reasonably read the docstring as license to trust the RuntimeError path as the safety net during an upgrade, medium severity (doc-accuracy/robustness-communication issue with real consequence if relied upon, but no bug in current behavior) is appropriate as claimed.

confirmed.title: No null/validity guard on the extracted pointer before it is dereferenced by the SELECT 1 validation
confirmed.description: conn_ptr is read from `cpp_obj_p + 32` (line 62) and passed straight into ducklib.duckdb_query(conn_ptr, ...) (line 67) with no check that it is non-null or live. The sibling bridge explicitly guards this: `if db_ptr is None: raise RuntimeError('extracted null sqlite3* ...')` (numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py:169-170). Two concrete failure modes follow from the missing guard: (a) if the unique_ptr<Connection> slot at +32 is null (e.g. a closed or not-yet-connected DuckDBPyConnection), ctypes' `c_void_p(...).value` yields Python None, and duckdb_query(None, ...) then fails as an uninformative numba typing TypeError at dispatch — not the RuntimeError the docstring promises (lines 49-50); and worse, if cpp_obj_p itself is null, `cpp_obj_p + 32` on line 62 raises `TypeError: unsupported operand ... NoneType + int`. (b) The SELECT 1 'validation' (lines 64-72) is validation-by-dereference: for a stale/dangling non-null pointer (closed connection, or an ABI/layout drift on a different duckdb build that still passes the isinstance guard at lines 52-55), duckdb_query dereferences the bad Connection* — that is already undefined behavior / a segfault BEFORE any rc can be returned, so the check cannot protect against an invalid pointer, only report a live-but-erroring one.
confirmed.impact: Calling extract_connection_ptr on a closed/uninitialized connection produces a confusing TypeError instead of the documented RuntimeError, and on a dangling (freed-but-non-null) Connection* it is a use-after-free / segfault inside duckdb_query. The docstring claim that the pointer 'is validated ... before it is returned' overstates the guarantee.
confirmed.recommendation: Before the validation query, guard the extracted pointers the way the sibling does: after line 59 check that cpp_obj_p is not None (raise RuntimeError on a null holder), and after line 62 check `if conn_ptr is None: raise RuntimeError('extracted null Connection* from DuckDBPyConnection')`. Optionally document that the SELECT 1 check only distinguishes live-but-failing from success and cannot catch a structurally invalid pointer.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Confirmed by direct code read plus two empirical probes. Code (numbduck/pybridge.py:57-62) reads cpp_obj_p = c_void_p.from_address(id(conn)+16).value and conn_ptr = c_void_p.from_address(cpp_obj_p+32).value with no None-check on either, unlike the sibling numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py:168-170 which explicitly guards `if db_ptr is None: raise RuntimeError(...)`. Installed the real duckdb==1.3.2 wheel in an isolated venv and read the same offsets on a live vs. closed connection: cpp_obj_p is identical and non-null before and after conn.close() (0xc52c8e0 in the probe), but conn_ptr at +32 goes from a valid address to None after close() -- i.e. 'closed connection -> null Connection* at the documented offset' is real and trivially reachable via ordinary usage (duckdb.connect() -> conn.close() -> extract_connection_ptr(conn)), not a contrived edge case. Also confirmed duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection has 'No constructor defined!' from Python, so the cpp_obj_p-is-None half of the claim (a not-yet-connected object) is not independently reachable via the public API, and cpp_obj_p was never observed to go null in the close() probe -- that part of the finding is more theoretical. Separately verified numba dispatch behavior: an eagerly-njit-compiled proxy with an explicit intp(...) signature (matching duckdb_query's `duckdb_state_ty(intp, intp, intp)`), called from Python with None as an argument, raises `TypeError: No matching definition for argument type(s) none, int64, int64` -- confirming that a null conn_ptr produces an uninformative TypeError at dispatch rather than the RuntimeError the docstring promises (pybridge.py:49-50), and confirming this TypeError happens purely in numba's Python-level type-matching layer before any native call is made (so the null-pointer path is NOT itself a segfault -- it's an incorrect/undocumented exception type). The finding's part (b) 'stale/dangling non-null pointer (closed connection...)' is imprecise: the probe shows a closed connection yields a NULL pointer (caught by part a), not a non-null dangling one; the true non-null-dangling scenario is limited to the already-separately-documented ABI/layout-drift risk (also called out in docs/reviews/2026-07-01-numbduck/understanding/bridge.md's own 'Fragile assumptions' section), not something newly demonstrated here. Net: the core claim -- missing null guard vs. the sibling's established pattern, reachable via a realistic closed-connection call, producing a documented-contract violation (wrong exception type instead of RuntimeError) -- is real and correctly identified. The 'segfault' framing in the finding's impact section overstates the concretely-demonstrated closed-connection path (which is safely intercepted by numba's static typing, not a crash), but the recommendation (add `if conn_ptr is None: raise RuntimeError(...)` matching the sibling) is sound and cheap. Medium severity is appropriate: it's a genuine, trivially reachable API-contract violation (not just a doc gap, which is the low-severity PBR-MEM-1 in the same unit), but the reachable failure mode is a confusing exception rather than actual memory corruption.

confirmed.title: No library-coordination guard: a Connection* minted by the duckdb wheel is passed to a possibly-different libduckdb resolved by numbduck's JIT bindings (cross-library type confusion)
confirmed.category: type-confusion / trusting external memory layout across two library instances
confirmed.description: extract_connection_ptr recovers the raw Connection* out of the duckdb Python wheel's C++ DuckDBPyConnection object (id(conn)+16 then +32, lines 59/62) and then hands that pointer straight to ducklib.duckdb_query / ducklib.duckdb_destroy_result (lines 67-68). Those two symbols are NOT resolved from the wheel — they are resolved by numba/LLVM's JIT linker against whatever libduckdb numbduck's loader put into the global symbol namespace via RTLD_GLOBAL (numbduck/utils.py load_duckdb -> load_lib_path). On Linux these coincide (numbduck loads the wheel's own _duckdb.so, so the Connection* and duckdb_query come from the same binary). On macOS, and on any host where the wheel strips the C API, load_duckdb takes a fallback path (loader.md 5a/5b): it loads a *standalone* libduckdb from NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB, from a Homebrew/usr-local path (_MACOS_LIBDUCKDB_SEARCH_PATHS), or a downloaded universal dylib. A brew or env-pointed libduckdb can be a DIFFERENT VERSION/BUILD than the wheel's statically-linked duckdb (brew's copy is whatever brew installed, unrelated to duckdb.__version__). Passing a Connection* created by build A into build B's C-API entry points is undefined behavior: the internal Connection/ClientContext object layout that duckdb_query dereferences is not an ABI-stable contract across builds. The sibling bridge this file is explicitly modeled on refuses exactly this: numbox pysqlite_bridge.libraries_coordinated() (pysqlite_bridge.py:93-107) compares the bindings' linked version against the Python module's linked version and extract_connection_ptr RAISES (pysqlite_bridge.py:159-167) rather than cross a pointer between two mismatched libraries. pybridge.py has no analogous gate; there is no comparison of duckdb.__version__ (the wheel) against duckdb_library_version() (the JIT-linked lib) anywhere before the pointer is used.
confirmed.impact: On the macOS/standalone fallback path, or whenever NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB / a brew libduckdb points at a duckdb whose build differs from the wheel, duckdb_query dereferences a Connection* laid out by a different duckdb build. The SELECT 1 'validation' cannot catch this (a wrong-layout deref is UB, not a returnable rc) so it manifests as an interpreter segfault or silent memory corruption at the first C-API call, not a clean error. Same failure class numbox deliberately guards against.
confirmed.recommendation: Before trusting/returning the pointer, add a coordination check mirroring numbox: compare duckdb.__version__ (the wheel whose object you are walking) against the loaded library's duckdb_library_version() (the lib whose C API you call) and raise RuntimeError with remediation guidance (set NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB to the wheel's own lib) when they disagree. At minimum call it out in the docstring that this bridge is only sound when numbduck's loaded libduckdb is the same build the wheel uses.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current tree. pybridge.py:57-62 (extract_connection_ptr) walks the duckdb wheel's own DuckDBPyConnection C++ object (id(conn)+16, then +32) to obtain a raw Connection*, then at pybridge.py:67-68 passes it to ducklib.duckdb_query / ducklib.duckdb_destroy_result. Confirmed those wrappers (ducklib.py:1111-1114 for duckdb_query) route through numbox's _call_lib_func intrinsic (numbox/core/bindings/call.py), which resolves the C symbol via `ll.address_of_symbol(func_name)` -- i.e. whatever library is currently registered process-wide, not necessarily the wheel's own handle. That process-wide library is whichever one numbduck/utils.py load_duckdb() loaded via load_lib_path (RTLD_GLOBAL). Confirmed load_duckdb (numbduck/utils.py:112-124) has a real fallback chain on the wheel's stripped-C-API path: NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB env override, Homebrew paths (_MACOS_LIBDUCKDB_SEARCH_PATHS), or a downloaded release zip -- none of these are checked against duckdb.__version__ at load time (duckdb.__version__ is used only for cache-directory naming/download-URL construction in utils.py:19-21/51, never compared to the actually-loaded lib's version). Grep across pybridge.py, ducklib.py, and utils.py confirms no duckdb_library_version binding and no version-coordination check exists anywhere in numbduck. This is a real gap distinct from (not fixed by) the prior review's XC-ver-2 finding, which covered the loader's lack of a version check in general -- PBR-SEC-1 is specifically about pybridge.py trusting a pointer minted by the wheel's private, non-ABI-stable pybind11/C++ object layout and handing it to whatever lib got JIT-linked, which is a more fragile contract than the public C API structs XC-ver-2 discussed. The sibling numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py, read directly, confirms the claimed contrast is accurate: libraries_coordinated() (pysqlite_bridge.py:93-107) compares sqlite3_libversion() (bindings) against sqlite3.sqlite_version (Python module) and extract_connection_ptr (pysqlite_bridge.py:159-167) raises RuntimeError on mismatch rather than crossing a pointer between two libraries -- pybridge.py has no analogous check. The failure mode described (UB dereference of a Connection* from one duckdb build inside another build's duckdb_query, unrecoverable via the SELECT-1 validation since a wrong-layout deref is UB not a clean error code) is a correct read of the code. This surface is reachable only via the documented macOS/standalone fallback path (Linux normally loads the wheel's own .so and coincides), which bounds the blast radius -- consistent with rating it medium rather than high, matching the severity precedent set by the related XC-ver-2 finding for the same class of unguarded library-version mismatch.

confirmed.title: macOS is absent from CI, so numbduck's macOS-only library-acquisition subsystem is exercised by no automated job
confirmed.description: The CI arch matrix (numbduck_ci.yml:22) is ["ubuntu-latest", "ubuntu-24.04-arm", "windows-latest"] and no workflow adds a macOS runner. Yet numbduck's most bespoke platform code exists precisely because the duckdb Python wheel strips the C API on macOS: the standalone-dylib discovery (_find_standalone_libduckdb, utils.py:33-47), the network download fallback with consent gate and versioned cache (_download_libduckdb, utils.py:50-91), the legacy-unversioned-cache cleanup (utils.py:37-40), and the Darwin-gated double-load of two duckdb runtimes (load_duckdb, utils.py:113-130). None of this is reached by any test or CI job. This is a pure CI/test coverage gap, not an active defect (the specific defects inside these functions are tracked separately as UTL-* findings); the concern here is that no platform exists to catch a regression in the acquisition path.
confirmed.impact: The platform the project documents as its hardest case (symbol-stripped wheel requiring standalone discovery or download) can regress silently for all macOS users. A change to the download URL scheme, cache layout, version-string-to-release-tag mapping, or the double-load runtime interaction would not be caught by any CI job.
confirmed.recommendation: Add at least one macos-latest (ARM64) matrix entry that exercises load_duckdb end-to-end, ideally with NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB pointing at a brew-installed libduckdb so the standalone path is hit deterministically without the interactive download. A single smoke job materially closes the gap.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Both refutation paths fail; the finding holds on the current tree and is not a duplicate. (1) NOT REAL check: Read all 5 workflows under numbduck/.github/workflows/ (numbduck_ci.yml, release.yml, haversine_bench.yml, doc-codeblock-flake8.yml, link-check.yml) -- none has a macos-latest/darwin runner; numbduck_ci.yml's arch matrix (line 22) is exactly ['ubuntu-latest', 'ubuntu-24.04-arm', 'windows-latest']. Read numbduck/utils.py: the macOS-only acquisition subsystem is present and unchanged in substance from the description -- _MACOS_LIBDUCKDB_SEARCH_PATHS (23-26), _find_standalone_libduckdb (33-47, including the legacy-cache os.remove at 37-40), _download_libduckdb with the interactive consent gate and versioned cache (50-91), and load_duckdb's Darwin-gated double-load fallback (113-130, guarded by platform.system() != 'Darwin' at 124). Grepped test/ for any reference to these functions or to darwin/macos/NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB -- zero hits; no conftest.py exists in the project (only an unrelated numpy vendored one under venv/). So the defect (this subsystem is reached by no automated job) is real and unchanged from the old review to the current tree. (2) DUPLICATE check: read new-index.json and the full text of every candidate current finding that touches this code -- UTL-COR-2, UTL-COR-3, UTL-DES-2, UTL-DES-3, UTL-DES-4, UTL-DES-5, UTL-SEC-1, UTL-SEC-2, XC-ver-1. Each of these asserts a specific in-code correctness/security/design defect inside the macOS path (e.g. UTL-DES-3's EOFError under non-interactive input(), UTL-SEC-1's unverified download, XC-ver-1's version-coordination gap) -- none of them asserts, as its defect, the meta-level claim that no CI job or test exercises this code at all. The only other candidate, TST-cover-10, was REFUTED (verified/TST-cover-10.json) precisely because its Windows-ABI half is false (windows-latest IS in the CI matrix and does exercise _call_lib_func's Windows branches); TST-cover-10's own verifier note explicitly carves out and preserves the macOS sub-claim as a narrower, accurate, but differently-scoped finding that TST-cover-10 as titled/written does not itself carry. So no confirmed current finding covers the CI/test-coverage-gap concern itself. The mapper's audit-adoptions.json justification for BLD-DES-1 correctly reaches this same conclusion. Severity: keeping the reconciler's assigned 'medium' -- this is a coverage-gap/process finding (not an active exploit), consistent with medium rather than the old review's 'high'.

confirmed.title: _download_libduckdb fuses consent, network fetch, unzip, and cache write into one unit with no injectable collaborators (untestable fallback path)
confirmed.description: _download_libduckdb (:50-91) does four unrelated things in one body with no injectable collaborators: (a) decides consent via a blocking builtin input() prompt (:67-77), (b) fetches a URL built inline from duckdb.__version__ (:52-56, :83), (c) unzips an in-memory archive (:85-89), and (d) writes to a path derived from module global _LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_DIR (:86-90). The URL, destination, consent decision, and network opener are all hard-wired rather than parameters, and io/zipfile/urlopen are lazily imported inside the body (:78-80), obscuring the dependency surface. A unit test of the extract-and-cache logic cannot run without monkeypatching builtin input, patching urlopen, and mutating module globals, and can never exercise the happy path without hitting or stubbing GitHub. The name (_download_...) also hides that the call may block on stdin or raise RuntimeError on a declined prompt (:70-77).
confirmed.impact: The fallback download path — the loader logic most likely to break on a duckdb release/layout change — is effectively unit-untestable and can only be validated by an actual network round-trip, so regressions ship undetected.
confirmed.recommendation: Split into (1) a pure-policy _consent_to_download() -> bool (or have the caller decide) and (2) a _fetch_and_cache(url, dest) -> path taking URL and destination as parameters, so tests can drive fetch/cache with a local file:// URL or injected opener and a tmp dest, and consent can be tested in isolation.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Checked both refutation paths; neither holds. (1) NOT REAL: verified every cited line against the CURRENT @proxy tree (numbduck/utils.py, read in full). _download_libduckdb spans exactly :50-91 as claimed. URL built inline from duckdb.__version__ at :52-56 and used at :83. Consent decided via a blocking builtin input() at :67-69, with RuntimeError on decline at :70-77. io/zipfile/urlopen are lazily imported inside the body at :78-80. The in-memory zip is opened and extracted at :85-89, writing to a path derived from module global _LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_DIR (:19-21, :86-90). No parameter of the function is injectable (URL, dest, consent, and opener are all hard-wired), and grep over test/ confirms zero references to _download_libduckdb, _find_standalone_libduckdb, or any split-out consent/fetch helper -- so the described untestability is real on the current tree, not a stale pre-@proxy artifact (this part of utils.py is unrelated to the @proxy/@cres migration the review's staleness warning concerns). (2) DUPLICATE: read the full current UTL-DES.json, UTL-SEC.json, and new-index.json. UTL-DES-2 (current) is a narrower, distinct complaint -- the download branch skips the _has_capi_symbols re-check that every other load path applies -- about a missing runtime validation, not about testability/fused-concerns. UTL-DES-3 addresses the EOFError crash under non-interactive stdin specifically, not the broader lack of injectable collaborators. UTL-DES-6 addresses raw urllib/zipfile errors and a rot-prone version comment. UTL-DES-4 addresses a different function (_find_standalone_libduckdb) and a different defect (its unconditional os.remove side effect), not _download_libduckdb's design. UTL-SEC-1/2 address integrity/timeout risk, not testability. None of these state or imply the core claim here -- that consent decision, network fetch, unzip, and cache write are fused into one non-parameterized unit with no injectable URL/dest/opener, making the fallback path effectively unit-untestable -- so it is not a duplicate of any current finding. Severity kept at medium, consistent with sibling DES findings on this same fallback path (UTL-DES-1/2/3/5 are all medium).

L3075-3176' and line 75 'Source: L3075-3176' for the @cfunc/@njit pattern). In the current test file the Welford callbacks (_welford_state_size_impl/_cb through _welford_destroy_impl/_cb) span L3205-3305. confirmed.impact: Readers following either link land on the array UDAF (which uses inline _incref_meminfo + carray) while the prose describes the structref Welford callbacks (export_meminfo/borrow_structref) -- directly contradicting the surrounding explanation.

confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current test/test_ducklib.md and test/test_ducklib.py (3548 lines). test_ducklib.md:51 and :75 both cite 'test_ducklib.py L3075-3176' as the location of the Welford callbacks. confirmed.title: aux_get_data_vector discards the out_result buffer, making the DuckDB result impossible to destroy
confirmed.description: aux_get_data_vector() (172-182) does duckdb_result = tuple(out_result) at line 174 and returns that tuple plus data_chunk_p, but NOT the out_result numpy array. out_result is the buffer that physically backs the duckdb_result C struct and is the only handle duckdb_destroy_result can be called on (via out_result.ctypes.data). Because it is a local that is not returned, it is refcount-dropped and freed the moment aux_get_data_vector returns, while every consumer (test_duckdb_data_chunk_get_column_count:185, test_duckdb_data_chunk_get_size:192, test_duckdb_destroy_data_chunk:199, test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_data_chunk_get_vector_get_data_vector:222) only receives the value-copied tuple. The tuple carries the internal_data pointer so DuckDB's materialized result stays allocated (never destroyed), but no caller can ever reach duckdb_destroy_result — the result is structurally leaked in all four consumer tests. It also means the numpy buffer backing a C struct is freed while a chunk derived from that result is still in use (safe here only because duckdb_fetch_chunk returns an independently-owned chunk).
confirmed.impact: Four tests unconditionally leak a DuckDB result each; more importantly they can never exercise the duckdb_destroy_result teardown path, so a real result-leak or destroy-time regression in the bindings would not be caught by any of them.
confirmed.recommendation: Return out_result (the numpy buffer) from aux_get_data_vector and have each consumer call duckdb_destroy_result(out_result.ctypes.data) (and duckdb_destroy_data_chunk on data_chunk_p) before aux_close_db, as the other result tests already do.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against test/test_ducklib.py:172-230, numbduck/duckdb_utils.py:36-39, numbduck/ducklib.py:165,172,775-778,943-946, and duckdb.h (duckdb_result struct at line ~452-454; duckdb_query/duckdb_destroy_result docs at lines 923-943). aux_get_data_vector (172-182) computes duckdb_result = tuple(out_result) at line 174 and returns (duckdb_result, data_chunk_p, duckdb_database, duckdb_connection) at line 182 -- out_result itself (the numpy int64[6] buffer from create_duckdb_result(), i.e. allocate_buffer(6) in duckdb_utils.py:37-39) is not returned and becomes unreachable once the function returns. This matters because duckdb_fetch_chunk is bound as intp(duckdb_result_ty) via _call_lib_func_byval (ducklib.py:172,943-946) -- it consumes the struct BY VALUE (a copied tuple works fine for that call) -- whereas duckdb_destroy_result is bound as void(intp) (ducklib.py:165,775-778) and requires an actual pointer (out_result.ctypes.data) to a live buffer holding the struct bytes. The four consumers confirmed by direct read of the file -- test_duckdb_data_chunk_get_column_count (185-189), test_duckdb_data_chunk_get_size (192-196), test_duckdb_destroy_data_chunk (199-209), test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_data_chunk_get_vector_get_data_vector (222-230) -- only receive the tuple and call aux_close_db; none reconstructs a fresh out_result buffer from the tuple values (e.g. numpy.array(duckdb_result, dtype=numpy.int64)) nor calls duckdb_destroy_result, so the duckdb_result from aux_query_1 is never destroyed in any of these four tests. duckdb.h explicitly documents 'duckdb_destroy_result must be called on the result object' (even on query failure) and gives no indication that duckdb_close/duckdb_disconnect (called via aux_close_db) frees outstanding un-destroyed results; the struct is a flat POD (deprecated fields + a void *internal_data) owned independently of the connection, so nothing else reclaims it in this test flow. One nuance in the finding's phrasing: out_result is not literally 'the only handle that can ever exist' in a hypothetical sense -- since duckdb_result is POD, a fresh buffer rebuilt from the tuple's field values (preserving internal_data) would work equally well for destroy_result -- but the code as written performs no such reconstruction anywhere, so in the actual current tree the practical claim holds: no caller of aux_get_data_vector can reach duckdb_destroy_result, and these four tests leak a DuckDB result each. This is a real, correctly localized test-hygiene/resource-leak defect, not a false positive. Severity: this is test-only code (each :memory: database + short-lived pytest process), duckdb_destroy_result itself is otherwise thoroughly exercised elsewhere in the file via the aux_execute_prepared path (18+ call sites), and the four affected tests still validate the bindings they target, so this does not indicate a production bug -- 'medium' (test coverage gap / minor per-test resource leak, not a crash or data-corruption risk) is the right severity; no correction needed.

confirmed.title: Several tests create result/data_chunk handles and never destroy them
confirmed.description: Multiple tests allocate DuckDB handles and never call the matching destroy, unlike the surrounding tests that are careful to do so. Concrete cases: test_query (132-137) leaks out_result; test_duckdb_column_count_and_duckdb_row_count (153-160) leaks out_result; test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_exhausted (212-219) leaks BOTH the first fetched chunk (chunk_p at 215, an independently-owned data chunk that must be duckdb_destroy_data_chunk'd) and the result; the aux_get_data_vector consumers (185, 192, 222) additionally leak the fetched chunk. Only aux_close_db is called, and closing the connection/database does not free outstanding results or fetched chunks in the DuckDB C API.
confirmed.impact: Per-test leaks of DuckDB-owned memory, and — because these tests never touch the destroy path — they cannot detect a leak regression in the bindings they nominally cover (fetch_chunk exhaustion, chunk get_size/column_count, column/row count).
confirmed.recommendation: Destroy every result (duckdb_destroy_result) and every fetched chunk (duckdb_destroy_data_chunk) before aux_close_db in each of these tests; in test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_exhausted, destroy the first chunk before fetching the second.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against test/test_ducklib.py at HEAD and duckdb.h (v1.3.2 doc comments). duckdb.h is unambiguous: duckdb_query's docstring states 'after running duckdb_query, duckdb_destroy_result must be called on the result object even if the query fails' (duckdb.h:928-929), and duckdb_fetch_chunk's docstring states 'The result must be destroyed with duckdb_destroy_data_chunk' (duckdb.h:1093). aux_close_db (test_ducklib.py:67-69) only calls duckdb_disconnect and duckdb_close - no destroy_result/destroy_data_chunk call, and nothing in the C API contract implies disconnect/close frees outstanding results or chunks. Confirmed each cited case: (1) test_query (132-137) obtains out_result via aux_query_1 and calls only aux_close_db - no duckdb_destroy_result. (2) test_duckdb_column_count_and_duckdb_row_count (153-160) same pattern - no destroy_result. (3) test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_exhausted (212-219) calls duckdb_fetch_chunk twice into the same local chunk_p (line 215 then 217), so the first chunk handle is overwritten/lost before any destroy could be issued, and out_result is never destroyed either - both leaked. (4) The three aux_get_data_vector consumers - test_duckdb_data_chunk_get_column_count (185-189), test_duckdb_data_chunk_get_size (192-196), and test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_data_chunk_get_vector_get_data_vector (222-235) - each receive data_chunk_p from aux_get_data_vector and call only aux_close_db, never duckdb_destroy_data_chunk on the chunk (nor destroy_result on the underlying result). This is a real contrast with the surrounding tests that do call the destroy path correctly, e.g. test_query_invalid_sql:149, test_duckdb_destroy_result:168, test_duckdb_destroy_data_chunk:207, test_execute_prepared:333 - confirming the omission in the cited tests is inconsistent with the file's own established pattern, not an intentional/alternate teardown route. Severity of medium is appropriate: these are per-test resource leaks in test code (not a production defect), harmless to correctness since the process exits and OS reclaims memory, but they are real DuckDB-owned C allocations that outlive their scope and - as the reviewer notes - mean these specific tests never exercise the destroy/teardown path, weakening their ability to catch a real leak regression in the bindings.

confirmed.title: No DuckDB C-handle leak accounting anywhere; only NRT (numba) allocations are tracked
confirmed.description: The only leak accounting in the suite is rtsys.get_allocation_stats() asserting alloc==free in the two UDAF end-to-end tests (test_aggregate_function_structref_stddev:3439/3462-3466, test_aggregate_function_array_variance:3521/3544-3548) and the nested-heap dtor test (3344-3389). Those stats count ONLY numba-runtime (NRT/MemInfo) allocations — i.e. the structref/array UDAF state. They are completely blind to DuckDB-side malloc: a leaked duckdb_result, duckdb_data_chunk, duckdb_value, or logical_type would pass alloc==free unchanged. No test wraps DuckDB handle create/destroy in any counting harness, and the handle destroys are verified only by asserting handle[0]==0 in isolated cases (e.g. test_duckdb_destroy_data_chunk:208, test_prepare_and_destroy:287). Consequently the many value/logical_type tests (1173-1918) and the scalar/aggregate registration tests would not catch a binding regression that leaks a DuckDB handle, and the destroy paths are only ever checked for a null-out side effect, never for cumulative balance.
confirmed.impact: Handle-lifetime regressions on the DuckDB side (result/chunk/value/logical_type leaks, or a bind wrapper that fails to copy and drops a handle) are undetectable by the current suite; the leak-clean claims are only proven for the numba-managed UDAF state, not for the C API surface that the file mostly tests.
confirmed.recommendation: Add a C-handle accounting harness (e.g. wrap the DuckDB allocator, or at minimum add per-test create/destroy balance assertions or a loop-N-times-and-watch-RSS/handle-count check) for at least the value and logical_type families, so that missing/extra destroys are caught rather than silently leaking.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified by grep across test/test_ducklib.py: the only cumulative allocation-balance assertions in the suite are `rtsys.get_allocation_stats()` calls at lines 3364-3466 (nested-heap dtor test) and 3439/3462-3466, 3521/3544-3548 (the two UDAF end-to-end tests), all of which read numba's NRT/MemInfo allocator stats (imported from numba.core.runtime.nrt) -- a distinct memory system from DuckDB's own malloc-backed C handles (duckdb_result, duckdb_data_chunk, duckdb_value, duckdb_logical_type). Every other handle-lifetime check in the file (e.g. test_duckdb_destroy_data_chunk:207-208, test_prepare_and_destroy:286-287, test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_exhausted:213-218, and the ~90 duckdb_destroy_result/duckdb_destroy_logical_type/duckdb_free call sites) is a one-off null-out or return-value check after a single destroy, never a before/after cumulative count. There is no conftest.py, no fixture, and no counting harness anywhere in test/ that wraps DuckDB's own allocator or tallies create/destroy calls; the DuckDB C API itself exposes no allocation-stats accessor (checked duckdb.h -- no alloc/memory-usage/allocator-stat function exists), so no such counting is happening implicitly either. This confirms the finding's core claim precisely as stated, with an accurate line citation (3462, inside the first UDAF test's NRT-only assertion block). Severity medium is appropriate: this is a test-coverage gap (undetectable regression risk for DuckDB-side handle leaks across ~750 lines of value/logical_type tests), not an active leak or functional bug, consistent with a 'confidence: medium' self-assessment in the source finding; it does not rise to high/critical because no current test failure or memory corruption results from the gap itself.

confirmed.title: test_struct_size_guard tests pure-Python arithmetic, never the ABI guard it names
confirmed.description: test_struct_size_guard (1706-1724) claims to 'Verify the size computation used by _call_lib_func_struct_in/out.' but its body only computes sum(t.bitwidth for t in <numba tuple type>)/8 and asserts the resulting integers (16, 8, 18, 19, 24). It never imports or calls _call_lib_func_struct_in / _call_lib_func_struct_out, never constructs a ducklib wrapper, and never exercises the <=16-byte vs >16-byte branch that actually decides by-value vs by-pointer lowering. The assertions are tautological restatements of numba's bitwidth attributes; they would still pass verbatim even if ducklib's struct-size threshold logic were deleted or inverted.
confirmed.impact: The one test named as the ABI size guard provides zero protection: a regression flipping the <=16-byte boundary (e.g. a 24-byte decimal struct wrongly lowered by-value) would not be caught here. False sense of coverage over the most delicate part of the binding (struct-by-value ABI).
confirmed.recommendation: Replace the arithmetic assertions with a behavioral test that actually round-trips a 16-byte struct (e.g. hugeint) and a >16-byte struct (24-byte decimal/varint) through the real wrappers and, if feasible, asserts the guard rejects/redirects an oversized struct. If only documenting the threshold, rename it so it isn't mistaken for a guard test.
confirmed.verdictReasoning:
Confirmed against the current tree. test/test_ducklib.py:1706-1724 (test_struct_size_guard) contains only pure-Python arithmetic over numba type metadata: it imports UniTuple/Tuple/int32/int64/uint64/uint8 from numba.core.types and asserts sum(t.bitwidth for t in <tuple type>) / 8 against hand-picked integers (16, 8, 18, 19, 24). It never imports or calls anything from numbduck.ducklib or numbox.core.bindings.call/abi, never constructs a ducklib wrapper, and never invokes @njit/@cfunc compilation that would trigger ABI codegen. Confirmed via grep: 'bitwidth' and 'struct_size' appear nowhere else in the test file or in numbduck/ducklib.py.

The docstring's target itself is dead: grep across numbduck/ducklib.py and numbox/core/bindings/{call,abi}.py shows _call_lib_func_struct_in and _call_lib_func_struct_out do not exist anywhere in either repo (matches the already-confirmed DOC-acc/DCK-wrap-DES findings that CLAUDE.md's 'Struct-by-value helpers' section is stale). The real ABI classification now lives in numbox/core/bindings/abi.py: _classify(ty) calls _struct_bytes -> _basetuple_layout, which computes a natural-alignment C layout with padding (offset = align_up(offset, field_size); total = align_up(offset, max_align)), explicitly documented at abi.py:94-97 as differing from a naive bit-packed sum because padding shifts both the byte count and the eightbyte split. The <=16 vs >16 gate that actually matters is abi.py:80 (_CLASS_STRUCT_SMALL if size <= 16 else _CLASS_STRUCT_LARGE), fed by _basetuple_layout, not by sum(bitwidth)/8.

This also shows the test's numbers are not even a faithful restatement of the real formula for the mixed-width case: Tuple((uint8, uint8, uint64, int64)) is asserted to be 18 bytes (test_ducklib.py:1719) via sum(bitwidth)/8, but running abi.py's actual _basetuple_layout on that same tuple (uint8@0, uint8@1, uint64 aligned up to offset 8, int64 at offset 16, then padded to the 8-byte max alignment) yields 24 bytes, not 18. The homogeneous cases (UniTuple(int64,2), UniTuple(uint64,2), UniTuple(int32,2), UniTuple(int64,3)) coincidentally agree with the real layout because same-width fields never need padding, but the mixed-width assertions at lines 1719-1721 (18, 19, >16) diverge from what the real ABI classifier would compute for the same type. A regression that broke the <=16/>16 gate, or _basetuple_layout's padding logic, would leave this test's assertions completely unaffected since it never calls into abi.py or call.py.

Severity: medium is correct, consistent with the prior review's independently-verified conclusion (docs/reviews/2026-06-29-numbduck/verified/TST-cover-1.json reached the same verdict on an earlier tree state). This is a false-coverage/test-quality defect (the named 'guard' test provides zero protection for the actual ABI classification code, and its own arithmetic model is stale relative to the real padding-aware implementation), not a correctness bug in ducklib.py or numbox itself, so it does not rise to high.

confirmed.title: Multi-chunk (>2048 row) results and the fetch_chunk loop are never exercised
confirmed.description: Every result in the suite comes from aux_query_1 (107-129, 3 rows) or single-value SELECTs. Chunk exhaustion is validated only for a single 3-row chunk: test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_exhausted (212-219) fetches one non-null chunk then asserts the next is null. DuckDB's standard vector size is 2048 (STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE); no test produces a result exceeding one chunk, so the second-and-subsequent duckdb_fetch_chunk return, the multi-chunk iteration loop, and offset handling are never covered. Correspondingly every UDF/UDAF callback (_add_one_impl, _welford_update_impl, _arr_update_impl, etc.) is only ever invoked with a single small chunk, so the finalize 'offset' parameter (offset+count indexing at 2286, 3126, 3278) is always tested with offset==0.
confirmed.impact: A defect in multi-chunk fetch, or in a UDAF finalize that mishandles a non-zero output offset (multiple result chunks), would ship undetected. This is the most likely real-world path (large tables) yet is entirely unexercised.
confirmed.recommendation: Add a test that inserts > 2048 rows (e.g. range(5000)), loops duckdb_fetch_chunk until null accumulating row counts to the expected total, and runs a UDAF/UDF over that many rows so finalize is called with offset != 0 across chunks.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against the current test/test_ducklib.py in full. Every raw-C-API result set used in the suite comes from aux_query_1 (test/test_ducklib.py:107-129, 3 rows) or ad-hoc VALUES lists of 7 rows (t_stddev/t_var at 3403-3404, 3486-3487). test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_exhausted (212-219) fetches exactly one chunk, asserts it's non-null, fetches again, and asserts null -- it never produces or loops through a second real chunk. Every duckdb_fetch_chunk call site in the file (grepped: lines 175, 256, 1093, 1971, 2029, 2173, 2188, 2346, 2411, 2505, 2522, 3446, 3528) is a single call preceded by a query over a small table (<=100 rows via range(10)/range(100), or 3/7-row VALUES); none loop 'while chunk_p != 0' to exhaust a multi-chunk result. The three custom UDAF finalize callbacks that take an offset parameter (_agg_finalize_impl:2281-2296, _arr_finalize_impl:3121-3147, _welford_finalize_impl:3273-3290) are only exercised by test_aggregate_function_structref_stddev (3392-3466) and test_aggregate_function_array_variance (3469-3549), both against 7-row tables (VALUES (1.0)..(7.0)), so finalize is always called with offset==0 -- the offset+count indexing paths at 2286/2290, 3126/3141, 3278/3284 have no test where offset != 0. The only test that runs into the thousands/millions of rows is test_udf_benchmark (2684-2779), which is marked @pytest.mark.benchmark ('slow benchmarks, run only locally (deselected in CI)', pyproject.toml:24-27); even if run, it drives rows through the Python duckdb connection's conn.execute(...).fetchall()/fetchone() path (real duckdb C++ engine, not ducklib.duckdb_fetch_chunk), and registers only a scalar UDF (no finalize/offset parameter), so it would not exercise the fetch_chunk loop or the offset-handling code paths even if de-scoped from the benchmark marker. No counter-evidence found (no hidden loop, no larger fixture, no other test producing a chunk boundary). The finding is accurately characterized: multi-chunk (>2048-row) results, the fetch_chunk exhaustion loop across multiple real chunks, and non-zero UDAF finalize offset are genuinely unexercised in the current tree. Severity of medium is appropriate given this is a coverage gap on the most realistic large-table code path, not a library bug (the library code itself is unmodified and not shown to be wrong).

confirmed.title: High-precision decimal (width>18 / 128-bit value) never bound or created
confirmed.description: test_bind_decimal (891-906) binds DECIMAL(10,2) with value tuple (10, 2, 12345, 0) and reads back an INT64 physical storage; test_create_get_decimal (1319-1327) uses the same (10,2,12345,0). Both are width<=18 (INT64 physical) and always pass the hugeint value's upper 64 bits as 0. The 24-byte decimal struct is passed through the custom >16-byte @intrinsic path (per CLAUDE.md), but the high-precision regime that actually needs the upper 64 bits -- width>18 (INT128 physical) with a non-zero upper word -- is never bound, created, or read back. duckdb_decimal_internal_type is only asserted != 0 (1752), never asserted to be HUGEINT for a wide decimal.
confirmed.impact: A bug that drops or mis-packs the upper 64 bits of the decimal struct (exactly the kind of eightbyte-ABI hazard the custom intrinsics exist to prevent) would pass all decimal tests, since every decimal value tested fits in 64 bits with upper==0.
confirmed.recommendation: Add a DECIMAL(38,0) (or width>18) case binding/creating a value whose magnitude requires the upper 64 bits (e.g. lower!=0, upper!=0), and assert both 64-bit halves of the stored INT128 round-trip.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current tree. test_bind_decimal (test/test_ducklib.py:891-906) uses SELECT $1::DECIMAL(10,2) with duckdb_bind_decimal(stmt[0], 1, (10, 2, 12345, 0)); test_create_get_decimal (1319-1327) uses duckdb_create_decimal((10, 2, 12345, 0)) and only asserts result[0..3] == (10, 2, 12345, 0); test_create_decimal_type (1745-1755) creates a DECIMAL(10,2) type and only asserts duckdb_decimal_internal_type(type_p) != 0. A full grep of the file for DECIMAL(/decimal_type/create_decimal/bind_decimal/get_decimal confirms these are the only three decimal-related tests in the file -- no width>18 case exists anywhere. duckdb_decimal_ty in numbduck/ducklib.py:72 is Tuple((uint8, uint8, uint64, int64)) -- width, scale, hugeint.lower (uint64), hugeint.upper (int64) -- a 24-byte struct matching duckdb.h's `struct duckdb_decimal { uint8_t width; uint8_t scale; duckdb_hugeint value; }` (duckdb_hugeint = {uint64 lower; int64 upper}). For DECIMAL(10,2), width<=18 means DuckDB's internal physical storage is INT64, so the hugeint.upper (int64) field is always 0/unused in the wire value regardless of what's passed -- but the finding's real point is that no test ever exercises a value whose magnitude genuinely needs the upper word (width>18, INT128 physical, e.g. DECIMAL(38,0) with a value > 2^63), so the >16-byte custom intrinsic path's handling of a non-zero upper 64 bits is never verified in either the bind-and-read-back-as-raw-bytes direction (test_bind_decimal style) or the create/get Value round-trip direction (test_create_get_decimal style). This is a real, correctly characterized test-coverage gap, not a false positive. Severity medium is appropriate: it is not a production defect (no evidence the >16B intrinsic path mishandles the upper word), but it is an under-tested path for exactly the byte range (17-24 of the 24-byte struct) that differs from the well-covered INT64-physical case, and per CLAUDE.md this custom intrinsic path already has known ABI subtleties (SysV eightbyte handling), making it the kind of code that most benefits from a round-trip test with a nonzero upper word.

confirmed.title: UDF/UDAF callbacks never read validity; NULL input rows are untested by design
confirmed.description: Every UDF/UDAF update/scalar callback reads duckdb_vector_get_data and iterates all n rows without ever calling duckdb_vector_get_validity (_add_one_impl 1924, _double_it_* 2083/2100, _isqrt_impl 2538, _triple_impl 2602, _welford_update_impl 3229, _arr_update_impl 3064, _agg_update_impl 2226). The NOTE at 3227-3228 makes this explicit: 'skips NULL validity checks -- test data has no NULLs.' All test tables/inputs are dense and NULL-free, so correctness of these callbacks over NULL-containing input is never demonstrated even though the validity bitmap read is tested elsewhere (test_fetch_chunk...get_vector at 227-230).
confirmed.impact: A UDF/UDAF that reads garbage or produces wrong aggregates for NULL rows (the common real case) would pass the entire suite. The callback pattern the tests exist to validate is only shown correct for the no-NULL subset.
confirmed.recommendation: Add at least one scalar-UDF and one UDAF test over a column containing NULLs, with a callback that consults duckdb_vector_get_validity, and assert the result matches a NULL-aware reference (e.g. matches DuckDB's built-in aggregate or a Python computation that ignores NULLs).
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified directly against test/test_ducklib.py at HEAD. Every UDF/UDAF update/scalar callback body reads duckdb_vector_get_data and loops over all n/count rows without ever calling duckdb_vector_get_validity: _add_one_impl (1924-1933), _agg_update_impl (2226-2235), _welford_update_impl (3229-3242), and the finalize callbacks that write output (_welford_finalize_impl 3272-3284) likewise never touch validity on the output vector. The code itself documents this at the explicit NOTE comment at 3227-3228: 'skips NULL validity checks -- test data has no NULLs. Production use must call duckdb_vector_get_validity() and check bits.' Checked every table/data source feeding a scalar-function or aggregate-function test (grep for CREATE TABLE/INSERT INTO/VALUES/range(): lines 112/117, 949/952, 2307, 2434, 2568, 2625, 2741, 3403, 3485) -- all use dense literal VALUES lists or range()-derived integers, none contain NULL. The one place NULLs do appear (j_col = [4, 6, 'NULL'] at line 103, feeding aux_query_1) is only ever used by plain fetch_chunk/vector-data tests (test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_data_chunk_get_vector_get_data_vector at 222-230, which does call duckdb_vector_get_validity), never by any scalar-UDF or aggregate-UDAF test. So the claim is accurate: validity-bit correctness of the UDF/UDAF callback family is completely untested, and the gap is structural (by construction of the test fixtures), not accidental. This is a test-suite coverage gap, not a library bug (the finding itself and the reviewing unit's notes agree it's test-quality only, matching the other TST-cover items rated medium/low). Medium severity is appropriate: it's a real, demonstrable hole in the most operationally common scenario (NULL-containing input), but it is a missing-test issue rather than a proven runtime defect, consistent with how the other missing-coverage items (TST-cover-2, TST-cover-3) in the same batch are also rated medium.

confirmed.title: Downloaded library is returned without the _has_capi_symbols re-check applied to every other path
confirmed.description: Every other load path validates the handle with `_has_capi_symbols` before trusting it: the wheel (:116) and the standalone (:122). The download branch alone returns `load_lib_path(downloaded)` directly (:129-130) with no symbol probe. A stripped, truncated, or wrong-architecture download (the universal zip asset name/layout is assumed correct, see UTL-DES-6) therefore passes the loader silently and only fails much later as an opaque LLVM/JIT 'symbol not found' link error at the first `@njit` call — with no pointer back to the bad download.
confirmed.impact: A corrupt or ABI-mismatched download produces a confusing deferred JIT link failure instead of an immediate, actionable loader error, defeating the whole purpose of the fallback flow.
confirmed.recommendation: Load the download, run `_has_capi_symbols` on it, and raise a numbduck-branded RuntimeError (naming the cached path and suggesting deletion / NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB) if the check fails — mirroring the standalone branch.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against numbduck/utils.py at HEAD. load_duckdb() (lines 113-130) validates the wheel lib with _has_capi_symbols at line 116 and the standalone lib with _has_capi_symbols at line 122, but the download branch at lines 129-130 (`downloaded = _download_libduckdb(); return load_lib_path(downloaded)`) returns unconditionally with no symbol probe. Confirmed numbox's load_lib_path (numbox/core/bindings/utils.py:167-183) performs only a bare ctypes.CDLL(path, mode=RTLD_GLOBAL) call with no symbol validation, so nothing downstream compensates for the missing check. A truncated/corrupted/wrong-layout download would therefore load 'successfully' and only surface as an opaque LLVM/JIT symbol-not-found error at the first @njit call, exactly as described, with no diagnostic tying the failure back to the download. This is a genuine, reproducible inconsistency between the three load paths (wheel/standalone checked, download unchecked), not a misreading of the code or a case where the contract is satisfied elsewhere. Medium severity is appropriate: it doesn't break the common happy path (official DuckDB release assets are normally intact) but it defeats the diagnosability purpose of the fallback exactly at the last-resort step, and the fix (probe + branded RuntimeError) is cheap and mirrors the existing standalone-branch pattern.

confirmed.title: input() consent prompt crashes library import with EOFError under non-interactive stdin
confirmed.description: When the macOS fallback is reached and `NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD != "1"`, the flow calls `input("Download now? [y/N] ")` (:67). Under CI, a piped/closed stdin, a subprocess, or any non-TTY context, `input()` raises `EOFError`, which is uncaught. Because this whole subsystem runs at import time of `ducklib.py` (`load_duckdb()` is called at module top level), a bare `import numbduck.ducklib` turns into an `EOFError` traceback rather than the carefully worded RuntimeError with brew/env instructions that the code clearly intends to surface for the decline case (:70-77).
confirmed.impact: On any headless macOS wheel-without-C-API environment, importing numbduck crashes with an unrelated-looking EOFError instead of the branded 'install via brew / set NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB' guidance, making the failure hard to diagnose.
confirmed.recommendation: Guard the prompt: if stdin is not a TTY (`sys.stdin is None or not sys.stdin.isatty()`) or wrap `input()` in `try/except EOFError`, and in that case raise the same instructional RuntimeError (which also tells the user they can set NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 to auto-download).
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current numbduck/utils.py and ducklib.py. ducklib.py:12 calls duckdb_lib = load_duckdb() unconditionally at module import time. load_duckdb() (utils.py:113-130) falls through to _download_libduckdb() (utils.py:50-91) only when: the bundled duckdb wheel lacks C API symbols, no standalone lib is found via NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB/cache/homebrew paths, and platform.system() == 'Darwin' -- this is exactly the documented macOS 1.4.1-1.5.2 stripped-wheel scenario, which sits inside the current duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6 pin, so it is a live, reachable code path on the current tree, not a stale/removed one. Inside that function, when NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD != '1' (the default), utils.py:67-69 calls input('Download now? [y/N] ') with no try/except and no isatty guard. Standard CPython input() raises EOFError when stdin is closed/redirected from an empty source (e.g. /dev/null, a closed pipe, or any non-TTY invocation), which is common for scripts, cron jobs, notebooks with redirected stdin, or a user's own automation on a real Mac. Because load_duckdb() runs at import time, this EOFError propagates as an unhandled traceback out of 'import numbduck.ducklib' instead of the intended clean RuntimeError (utils.py:71-77) that names the brew-install and NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 remedies. I checked numbduck's own CI (.github/workflows/numbduck_ci.yml) and it currently only runs on ubuntu-latest/ubuntu-24.04-arm/windows-latest, so numbduck's own CI does not trip this; the bug is real for any downstream macOS non-interactive context, which is the scenario the finding describes. Severity medium is appropriate: it's a real defect that degrades error UX in a specific but plausible platform/version/environment combination (import still fails either way -- the only difference is a raw EOFError traceback vs. the intended actionable RuntimeError), not a correctness/data-integrity issue and not universally triggered.

confirmed.title: macOS fallback loads two full DuckDB runtimes RTLD_GLOBAL, enabling cross-runtime handle mismatch
confirmed.description: On the macOS fallback path the symbol-less wheel is first loaded RTLD_GLOBAL (:115) and then the standalone/downloaded dylib is loaded RTLD_GLOBAL as well (:121 / :130). Two complete DuckDB runtimes are now resident in one process with global state (allocator, extension registry, memory manager) duplicated. The Python `duckdb` module continues to operate its own (wheel) runtime; numbduck's JIT code binds to the standalone runtime. Any handle created in Python (`duckdb.connect()`/relation buffers) and then passed into numbduck `@njit` code — or vice versa — is interpreted by a *different* library instance than the one that allocated it, which is undefined behaviour (free-across-allocators, mismatched struct layout across versions), a classic dual-runtime corruption hazard. The loader offers no guard against, or documentation of, this constraint at the seam where both handles become live.
confirmed.impact: Latent under current usage (handles are created and consumed entirely within the standalone runtime via JIT `duckdb_open`), but the design silently permits mixing Python-created and JIT-created handles, which would produce heap corruption or crashes that are extremely hard to trace back to the loader.
confirmed.recommendation: Document the single-runtime invariant at the load site, and consider dlclose-ing / not retaining the symbol-less wheel handle before loading the standalone (it is only kept alive incidentally), or at minimum add a code comment stating that all DuckDB handles used from JIT must originate from the numbduck-loaded runtime, never from the Python `duckdb` module.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Confirmed on the current tree. numbduck/utils.py load_duckdb() (numbduck/utils.py:113-130) loads the wheel's bundled shared lib at line 115 via load_lib_path (numbox/core/bindings/utils.py:167-183, RTLD_GLOBAL on Darwin), and on macOS with a symbol-less wheel (duckdb 1.4.1-1.5.2 per the :118 comment) falls back to a standalone/downloaded dylib at :121, also RTLD_GLOBAL. Because dlopen dedupes by path, the :115 load of the wheel's own file is a no-op refcount bump (same runtime the Python `duckdb` module already uses) -- but the :121 standalone load is a genuinely different file/mapping, so in the fallback branch two independent DuckDB runtimes really are resident with their own statics (macOS two-level namespace keeps each dylib's own copies rather than interposing, so 'duplicated global state' is accurate). This is not theoretical: numbduck/pybridge.py:extract_connection_ptr() reads the raw Connection* out of a `duckdb.connect()` object (created by the wheel's runtime) via pybind11-layout offsets and hands it straight into ducklib.duckdb_query (bound to whatever load_duckdb() returned -- the standalone lib in the fallback case). test/test_ducklib.py:2562-2599 and :2619+ (test_hybrid_jit_udf_on_python_connection, test_jit_udf_vs_python_udf) exercise exactly this: a Python-created connection is bridged into ducklib, a JIT UDF is registered on it, then `conn.execute()` runs back through the Python/wheel side -- a direct cross-runtime handle crossing. numbduck/utils.py itself has no comment, guard, or version check for this seam; the only mitigation is pybridge.py's live 'SELECT 1' smoke test (numbduck/pybridge.py:64-72), which is strictly weaker than numbox's own established precedent for this identical bug class -- numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py's libraries_coordinated() version-checks before ever handing off a raw sqlite3* across a macOS shared-cache/multi-instance boundary (documented in /home/erik/projects/numbox/CLAUDE.md 'LLVM symbol resolution and macOS' / 'detect-and-refuse'). numbduck has no analogous duckdb-version coordination check between the wheel's duckdb.__version__ and whatever load_duckdb() bound to (the homebrew search paths in particular are unversioned, :23-26). Additionally, CI (.github/workflows/numbduck_ci.yml) runs only ubuntu-latest/ubuntu-24.04-arm/windows-latest -- macOS is never exercised, so this exact path (including duckdb-version 1.5.1, which is in CI's matrix and in the affected 1.4.1-1.5.2 range) is untested. Severity: medium is appropriate, not higher -- the defect only manifests on a narrow platform+version combination (macOS, wheel missing C API symbols, and a homebrew/downloaded standalone lib genuinely distinct from the wheel's own file) combined with actual use of the Python-connection bridge; most calls that stay entirely within ducklib's own C API (open/connect/query/destroy all via ducklib) never cross runtimes even in the fallback case.

confirmed.title: Downloaded and cached libduckdb.dylib is dlopen'd RTLD_GLOBAL with no checksum/signature verification (supply-chain + cache poisoning → native code execution)
confirmed.description: _download_libduckdb fetches libduckdb-osx-universal.zip over HTTPS from the DuckDB GitHub release (url built at lines 52-56), reads the whole body (line 84: data = resp.read()), opens the zip in memory (line 85), and writes the extracted member straight to the on-disk cache with NO integrity check whatsoever (lines 88-89: `with zf.open("libduckdb.dylib") as src, open(dest, "wb") as dst: dst.write(src.read())`). load_duckdb then dlopens that file with RTLD_GLOBAL and does not even re-run _has_capi_symbols on it (lines 129-130: `downloaded = _download_libduckdb(); return load_lib_path(downloaded)`). The same unverified file is trusted forever after: on every subsequent import _find_standalone_libduckdb returns the cached path (lines 41-43) and load_duckdb dlopens it RTLD_GLOBAL (lines 119-123). dlopen runs the Mach-O's initializers/constructors immediately and the JIT then resolves extern duckdb_* refs into it, so a swapped binary is arbitrary native code executing in the host process. TLS only guarantees transport integrity against a passive network attacker; it provides ZERO defense against (a) a compromised/replaced GitHub release asset (attacker with push/release access to duckdb, or a stolen signing/CI token), or (b) local cache poisoning — makedirs at line 86 uses default umask perms (typically 0o755 dir / 0o644 file, world-readable), and any same-user process (or a lax-umask multi-user box) can overwrite `~/.numbduck/lib/<version>/libduckdb.dylib` between runs and have it loaded and executed on the next import. There is no pinned SHA-256, no comparison against DuckDB's published checksums, and no env hook to supply an expected digest. The consent gate is not a mitigation: NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 (line 57-58) skips the input() prompt entirely, so an inherited/CI-set env var makes the download+dlopen fully silent and automatic.
confirmed.impact: If the upstream release asset is compromised, or the per-user cache is poisoned by a same-user/lax-umask local actor, numbduck dlopens and executes attacker-controlled native code (dylib constructors run on load; JIT calls dispatch into it) with the full privileges of the importing process. The blast radius is any macOS user on a C-API-stripped wheel who accepts the prompt or runs with NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1.
confirmed.recommendation: Verify integrity before writing/loading: compute SHA-256 of the downloaded bytes and compare against a known-good digest before persisting (ship per-duckdb-version hashes, or fetch and check DuckDB's published SHASUMS for the release), and refuse to dlopen on mismatch. Re-verify the cached file's hash on every load (not just at download time) so a poisoned cache is caught. Create the cache dir/file with restrictive perms (os.makedirs(..., mode=0o700) + explicit 0o600 on the file, or chmod after write) to close the local-poisoning window, and support a NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_SHA256 override for pinning. At minimum, re-run _has_capi_symbols on the freshly downloaded handle before returning it.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current numbduck/utils.py and numbox/core/bindings/utils.py. All cited lines are accurate: URL build at 52-56, consent-prompt bypass via NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1 at 57-58, unauthenticated read+zip-extract+write at 84-89 with zero hash/signature check, unrestricted os.makedirs at 86 (no explicit mode), unconditional trust of the cached path on every later import (41-43), and load_duckdb dlopening both the standalone-search-path lib (119-123, which does re-check _has_capi_symbols) and the freshly downloaded lib (129-130, which does NOT re-check it) via numbox's load_lib_path. Confirmed numbox/core/bindings/utils.py:167-183 load_lib_path is a bare `CDLL(path, mode=RTLD_GLOBAL)` on Darwin/Linux with no integrity verification of any kind -- grepped both numbduck/ and numbox/ for sha256/checksum/hashlib/digest/signature and found no relevant hash-verification logic anywhere in this pipeline (the only hashlib hits in numbox are unrelated JIT-cache-key digests in compile_kernel.py). The finding does not overclaim: zip-slip is correctly excluded (member name and dest are both hardcoded), TLS is correctly scoped to defend only against passive network tampering, and the local cache-poisoning vector is correctly bounded to same-user or lax-umask conditions rather than claimed as a fresh privilege escalation. Exploitability is narrow (macOS only, duckdb 1.4.1-1.5.2 wheel range, requires either a compromised GitHub release asset or pre-existing local write access, and normally requires interactive consent), which is consistent with a medium rather than high/critical rating. Severity of medium is appropriate.

confirmed.title: pybridge Connection* extraction uses hardcoded pybind11/DuckDBPyConnection offsets validated only on duckdb 1.3.2/Linux, guarded only by an rc check that a wrong offset can bypass
confirmed.description: extract_connection_ptr() reads the C++ object pointer at id(conn)+16 (pybind11 instance header) and the Connection* at DuckDBPyConnection+32 (pybridge.py:59-62). The docstring states these offsets were 'Validated on duckdb 1.3.2 / Linux x86-64 / libstdc++' and 'may change with major duckdb releases.' numbduck's supported range is duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6, i.e. these fixed offsets are relied upon across 1.3.2, 1.4.x and 1.5.x wheels (and on Windows/macOS), whose bundled pybind11 version and DuckDBPyConnection C++ layout are not guaranteed to place the Connection at +32 or the holder at +16. The only safety net is the post-extraction `SELECT 1` validation (pybridge.py:64-69): it checks a return code, so it catches a wrong-but-still-valid pointer, but a version where the offset shifted yields an arbitrary/garbage pointer that can segfault inside duckdb_query before any rc is returned — an unrecoverable crash rather than the intended clean RuntimeError.
confirmed.impact: On a duckdb release within the supported <1.6 range (or a platform) where the wheel's C++/pybind11 layout differs from the 1.3.2/Linux baseline, extract_connection_ptr can dereference a garbage pointer and crash the process instead of raising, defeating the validation guard.
confirmed.recommendation: Do not treat the rc check as sufficient portability protection: gate the offsets per validated (duckdb version, platform) or derive the Connection* through a more stable path, and document/enforce which versions are actually validated rather than spanning the entire <1.6 pin on a single 1.3.2/Linux measurement.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Confirmed against current tree. numbduck/pybridge.py:58-62 performs two chained raw pointer-offset reads via ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(py_obj_addr + 16) and .from_address(cpp_obj_p + 32) with zero runtime gating on duckdb version or platform before the walk. Grep of pybridge.py and utils.py confirms no reference to duckdb.__version__, hasattr(), or any hardware/ABI check anywhere in the extraction path — the only downstream check is the SELECT 1 rc validation at pybridge.py:64-69, which architecturally can only catch a wrong-but-still-dereferenceable pointer; it cannot prevent a segfault when the offset walk itself lands on unmapped/garbage memory before duckdb_query is even called, exactly as the finding describes. The docstring (pybridge.py:31-34) self-admits 'Validated on duckdb 1.3.2 / Linux x86-64 / libstdc++ ... may change with major duckdb releases,' while pyproject.toml pins duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6 — a range spanning 1.3.x/1.4.x/1.5.x — so the finding's framing (offsets relied on across a wider range than validated) is accurate. Checked numbduck_ci.yml: CI does exercise duckdb 1.3.2/1.4.0/1.5.1 on ubuntu-latest (x86-64) and ubuntu-24.04-arm (ARM64), and duckdb 1.5.1 on windows-latest — broader than the docstring implies, which somewhat tempers real-world risk for those exact combos — but macOS is completely absent from the CI matrix despite numbduck's own standalone-libduckdb loader existing specifically to support macOS (utils.py), Windows is never tested with 1.3.2/1.4.0, and the locally installed dev venv here (numbduck/venv/bin/python -c 'import duckdb; print(duckdb.__version__)' -> 1.5.4) is itself a version CI has never exercised yet the <1.6 pin silently accepts it — concretely demonstrating the gap between 'pinned/supported' and 'actually validated' that the finding calls out. Severity: medium is appropriate — pybridge is an opt-in bridging feature (only invoked by callers who explicitly import extract_connection_ptr to bridge an existing Python connection), not a default code path, so 'high' would overstate blast radius; but the risk of an unrecoverable process crash on any (duckdb version, platform) combination outside the narrow CI/docstring-validated set is real and understated by relying on an rc check alone, so it is more than a documentation nit.

confirmed.title: flake8 excludes a path that does not exist in the tree

confirmed.impact: None functionally; maintenance noise and a false signal that the exclude is load-bearing.

confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified numbduck_ci.yml:74 contains `flake8 . --count --exclude=test/core/random_image_ref.py --select=E9,F63,F7,F82 --show-source --statistics`.
