confirmed.title: release.yml drifts from other workflows: pinned-action lag, no sdist, inconsistent fallback minor
confirmed.description: release.yml pins checkout@v4 (line 15), setup-python@v5 (line 17), and upload-artifact@v4 (line 40), while every other workflow uses @v6/@v7 (numbduck_ci.yml, doc-codeblock-flake8.yml, link-check.yml). It also builds only a wheel (`python -m build --wheel`, line 37) and never a source distribution, so the published PyPI project will have no sdist (acceptable for a pure-Python `py3-none-any` package but a deliberate gap worth stating). Finally its non-tag version fallback is `0.0.<run_number>` (line 27) whereas numbduck_ci.yml uses `0.1.<run_number>` (line 58) — cosmetic drift in the synthetic scheme. The `else` fallback in release.yml is also effectively dead since `release: published` always targets a tag (release.yml:3-5), so `github.ref_type == 'tag'` is expected always true.
confirmed.impact: Action-version skew accrues silent deprecation warnings and divergent behavior over time; absence of an sdist limits source-based installs; the divergent fallback minor and dead else-branch are minor confusion.
confirmed.recommendation: Sync release.yml action pins to the @v6/@v7 versions used elsewhere; add `python -m build` (both sdist+wheel) or explicitly document wheel-only intent; unify the synthetic-version minor with numbduck_ci.yml.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: All three sub-claims verified against current CURRENT-tree files. (1) Pinned-action lag: release.yml:15 uses actions/checkout@v4, release.yml:17 uses actions/setup-python@v5, release.yml:40 uses actions/upload-artifact@v4, release.yml:60 uses actions/download-artifact@v4 -- while numbduck_ci.yml:46,48 use checkout@v6/setup-python@v6, doc-codeblock-flake8.yml:12,14 use checkout@v6/setup-python@v6, link-check.yml:16,64 use checkout@v6/upload-artifact@v7, and haversine_bench.yml:17,19 use checkout@v6/setup-python@v6. release.yml is the clear outlier, several major versions behind every sibling workflow. (2) No sdist: release.yml:37 runs `python -m build --wheel` only (never `python -m build` for sdist+wheel), so the PyPI-published artifact set has no source distribution; pyproject.toml confirms this is a pure-Python package (setuptools backend, no extension modules), so the gap is real but low-impact (wheel is universally installable). (3) Inconsistent fallback minor: release.yml:27 uses `BUILD_VERSION="0.0.${{ github.run_number }}"` while numbduck_ci.yml:58 uses `BUILD_VERSION="0.1.${{ github.run_number }}"` -- confirmed literal mismatch in the synthetic non-tag version scheme. Bonus detail also checks out: release.yml only triggers on `release: types: [published]` (release.yml:3-5), and GitHub Release-publish events are always tag-backed, so the `else` non-tag branch (release.yml:26-28) is effectively dead code, correctly noted as an ancillary observation rather than the core claim. All findings are cosmetic/maintainability issues in packaging & CI infra with no functional, security, or binding-correctness impact, so severity=low is appropriate and not underrated or overrated.

confirmed.title: CI pulls floating, upper-bound-less numbox (arbitrary latest) via pip install -e .
confirmed.description: numbduck_ci.yml:70 `pip install -e .` resolves numbduck's runtime deps, and pyproject.toml:13 declares `numbox>=0.5.13` with NO upper cap and no lockfile/hash pinning. CI therefore installs whatever the newest numbox on PyPI is at run time and imports concrete internals from it (`numbox.core.proxy.proxy`, `numbox.core.bindings.call`). This is a supply-chain surface: a compromised or malicious future numbox release executes in CI (numbox code is imported/executed at collection/test time), and builds are non-reproducible across time. The test job token is only `contents: read`, so the immediate blast radius is limited, but the unbounded floor-only pin means CI can silently run untrusted new numbox code, and any breaking numbox reshuffle also breaks import with no guard. (numba/duckdb ARE explicitly pinned per matrix at lines 68-69, making numbox the odd one out.)
confirmed.impact: Non-reproducible CI and an unbounded window for a malicious/newer numbox to execute in the CI runner and influence test results or the locally built (unpublished) wheel.
confirmed.recommendation: Add an upper cap to the numbox dependency in pyproject.toml (e.g. `numbox>=0.5.13,<0.6`) matching the internals numbduck relies on, and/or pin numbox explicitly in the CI install step alongside numba and duckdb so the matrix tests a known numbox. Consider a hash-pinned constraints file for the CI environment.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A future numbox 0.6.0 (or a compromised patch release) is published; the next CI run installs it via the uncapped `>=0.5.13`, executing its code during test collection and potentially breaking or subverting the run.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current tree. pyproject.toml:13 declares `numbox>=0.5.13` with no upper bound and no lockfile/constraints file exists anywhere in the repo root (checked for *.lock, constraints*, requirements*.txt - none found). numbduck_ci.yml:70 runs `pip install -e .` in every matrix job, which resolves this uncapped floor and will pull whatever the newest numbox on PyPI satisfies at run time. This is asymmetric with the same step's explicit exact pins for the other two DuckDB-adjacent dependencies: numbduck_ci.yml:68 `pip install "numba==${{ matrix.numba-version }}"` and :69 `pip install "duckdb==${{ matrix.duckdb-version }}"`, both driven by explicit matrix axes (lines 23-24), making numbox the one unpinned dependency in an otherwise carefully version-matrixed CI file. numbduck's ducklib.py imports concrete internals from numbox (`numbox.core.proxy.proxy`, `numbox.core.bindings.call`), so a future numbox release is executed unpinned during test collection/import, and CI runs are not reproducible across time. Severity is correctly low: the build job carries only `contents: read` (numbduck_ci.yml:14, confirmed top-level permission block), the built wheel at this step is never published (only release.yml publishes, and that path is separately flagged as BLD-SEC-1/3), so the blast radius of a malicious/breaking numbox release is confined to CI-runner code execution and flaky/broken test runs, not a supply-chain compromise of a published artifact. No contract elsewhere satisfies this (no pip constraints file, no CI-level numbox pin, no Dependabot/lockfile mechanism found). Recommendation (upper-bound cap or explicit CI pin) is proportionate and correctly targeted.

confirmed.title: Env var injects arbitrary keys into numba jit options without a whitelist
confirmed.description: NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS is parsed and its keys flow unfiltered into njit(**jit_options) for every binding. This is not a code-execution vector (njit only accepts a fixed set of compilation flags, not callables/paths), so the practical security exposure is low and the env var sits inside the same trust boundary as the code. The relevant hardening gap is that flags like boundscheck=false or parallel=true could be injected process-wide via an env var an operator may not realize alters compilation semantics of the numbduck bindings. Worth a whitelist for defense-in-depth and clearer intent, not because it enables an attack.
confirmed.impact: An operator (or an env inherited from a parent process) can silently alter compilation flags (e.g. disable bounds checking) for all bindings; low severity because it requires control of the process environment and cannot execute arbitrary code.
confirmed.recommendation: Restrict get_jit_options() to an explicit allowed-key set (e.g. {'cache','nogil','parallel','boundscheck','fastmath','error_model'}) and reject unknown keys with a clear ValueError; this simultaneously fixes CFG-COR-2's opaque failure.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read numbduck/configurations.py:1-19: get_jit_options() does `as_json = json.loads(as_str); return as_json` with no key or shape filtering (line 13). The resulting dict is assigned to module-level `jit_options` (line 19) and imported by ducklib.py to feed every `@proxy(sig, jit_options=jit_options)` / `@proxy_if_available(...)` call. Confirmed in /home/erik/projects/numbox/numbox/core/proxy/proxy.py:69-75 that `jit_options` is spread directly into `njit(sig, **jit_options)` with no key allowlist on the numbox side either -- so any njit-recognized kwarg (boundscheck, parallel, fastmath, nogil, error_model, etc., not just 'cache') set via NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS silently changes compilation semantics for every wrapper in ducklib.py process-wide. The claim in the finding is technically accurate on the current tree and the reviewer already self-limits the severity correctly: it is not a code-execution vector (njit's kwarg surface is a fixed, non-callable set of compilation flags) and it requires control of the process's own environment, which is inside the same trust boundary as the code that would already need to be compromised to matter -- exactly as the finding itself states. Notably, numbox's own sibling helper (/home/erik/projects/numbox/numbox/core/configurations.py) implements the identical unfiltered NUMBOX_JIT_OPTIONS -> njit(**jit_options) pattern, so this is an established, intentional convention across the numbox/numbduck ecosystem rather than an oversight unique to numbduck -- it does not refute the finding (the property genuinely exists in numbduck/configurations.py:13), but it does confirm 'low' is the right ceiling and not something to escalate. The finding is also substantially the same root cause as CFG-COR-2 (both stem from get_jit_options() not validating keys), so it adds limited independent value beyond CFG-COR-2's fix, but that is a redundancy/value observation, not a correctness refutation. Severity: low is appropriate, matching the finding's own claim.

confirmed.title: get_jit_options accepts valid-but-non-object JSON, silently discarding config and disabling caching for all bindings
confirmed.description: get_jit_options only guards json.JSONDecodeError; it does not assert that the parsed value is a dict. Valid JSON that is not an object (e.g. NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS='true', '5', '[1]', '"x"') passes json.loads and is returned as-is, so the module-level jit_options becomes a bool/int/list/str. Every wrapper in ducklib.py then calls @proxy(sig, jit_options=<non-dict>). numbox's proxy (proxy.py:69) coalesces this via `jit_options = isinstance(jit_options, dict) and jit_options or {}`, so a non-dict is silently replaced with {}. Because the empty dict omits cache, njit(sig)(func) at proxy.py:75 compiles with caching OFF for all 193 bindings, and the user's configuration is discarded with no diagnostic. This defeats the explicit intent of get_jit_options, which was written to reject bad config loudly (it raises ValueError for malformed JSON) but leaks valid-non-object JSON through.
confirmed.impact: A malformed-but-parseable NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS value silently disables the process-stable cached-compile path for every DuckDB binding (default is {"cache": True}) and swallows the misconfiguration instead of raising, making the failure hard to notice or diagnose. No wrong results, but a silent, whole-library performance/behavior regression that the intended ValueError guard was meant to prevent.
confirmed.recommendation: After json.loads, validate the type: `if not isinstance(as_json, dict): raise ValueError("NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS must be a JSON object")` (or equivalent), so both malformed and non-object config raise the same clean ValueError.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Set NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS='true' (or '5'), import numbduck.ducklib: get_jit_options returns True; jit_options=True; every @proxy coalesces to {}; all 193 bindings compile with cache disabled and the config is silently ignored, with no error raised.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current tree. numbduck/configurations.py:12-16 wraps only json.loads in try/except json.JSONDecodeError and returns the parsed value as-is on success (line 14 `return as_json`), with no isinstance(dict) check -- so NUMBDUCK_JIT_OPTIONS='true' (or '5', '[1]', '"x"') parses successfully and jit_options becomes a bool/int/list/str at module scope (configurations.py:19). numbduck/ducklib.py:8 imports this single shared jit_options object and passes it verbatim as jit_options=jit_options to all 193 @proxy/@proxy_if_available call sites (grep confirms 193 occurrences of 'jit_options=jit_options' across ducklib.py). numbox/core/proxy/proxy.py:69 does `jit_options = isinstance(jit_options, dict) and jit_options or {}` -- for any non-dict value (True, 5, [1], 'x') isinstance is False, short-circuiting the 'and' to False, then `False or {}` evaluates to {}, so the non-dict silently becomes an empty dict at every one of the 193 call sites, dropping cache=True and disabling caching library-wide with no exception or diagnostic anywhere in the path. This exactly matches the finding's description and failure_scenario. Impact is silent config loss / caching perf regression only -- no wrong results, no crash, no ABI/correctness issue -- so 'low' severity is appropriate and not overstated.

confirmed.title: idx_t mapped to signed intp instead of uint64 in several count/size/index signatures (inconsistent with duckdb.h and with sibling entries)
confirmed.description: duckdb.h defines idx_t as uint64_t, and CLAUDE.md states the mapping convention 'idx_t -> uint64_t -> uint64'. Most entries follow it: duckdb_nparams (:217), duckdb_get_list_size (:189), duckdb_rows_changed (:227), duckdb_struct_type_child_count (:228), duckdb_union_type_member_count (:231), duckdb_array_type_array_size (:78) all return uint64 for an idx_t; and idx_t index args in duckdb_get_list_child/_map_key/_struct_child (:188,190,193) are uint64. But five entries map the same idx_t to signed intp: return values of duckdb_column_count (:106), duckdb_row_count (:226), duckdb_data_chunk_get_column_count (:156), duckdb_data_chunk_get_size (:157) are all idx_t (uint64_t) in the C API yet declared intp; and the idx_t argument of duckdb_data_chunk_get_vector (2nd arg, :158) and duckdb_validity_row_is_valid (2nd arg 'row', :234) are declared intp instead of uint64. Because intp is signed int64 and idx_t is uint64, and both are 64-bit INTEGER-class in the ABI, the register lowering is byte-identical, so there is NO runtime miscomputation for any realistic count/row value (< 2^63). The defect is purely type fidelity: it deviates from duckdb.h and from the module's own convention, and produces avoidable numba int/uint signature friction (a uint64 result from one binding fed into an intp-typed argument of another, or vice versa, forces an implicit signed/unsigned cast).
confirmed.impact: No runtime corruption on any supported platform (ABI-identical 64-bit integer passing). Cosmetic/convention deviation only; minor numba signed/unsigned interop friction and reduced fidelity to duckdb.h.
confirmed.recommendation: For strict fidelity, change these five entries to use uint64 for the idx_t return/arg positions: duckdb_column_count -> uint64(intp); duckdb_row_count -> uint64(intp); duckdb_data_chunk_get_column_count -> uint64(intp); duckdb_data_chunk_get_size -> uint64(intp); duckdb_data_chunk_get_vector -> intp(intp, uint64); duckdb_validity_row_is_valid -> int8(intp, uint64). This aligns them with the idx_t entries already using uint64 elsewhere in the file. Low priority given zero runtime impact.

confirmed.title: assert_results_match spuriously fails when all variants produce NaN
confirmed.description: assert_results_match compares with `if first != other`. For IEEE-754 NaN, `NaN != NaN` is always True, so if every variant legitimately produces NaN the guard raises AssertionError claiming a mismatch even though the variants agree. This directly contradicts the docstring's promise to let floats 'compare equal at full precision'. The IRR example's finalize explicitly returns NaN for empty/no-root states (irr.py finalize, per examples.md:238), and IRR is a float-returning UDAF whose differential check is exactly the kind of caller this helper serves. Any float result of NaN triggers a false positive.
confirmed.impact: A correct fast/slow variant that both yield NaN (empty group, non-convergent bisection, division-by-zero baseline) is reported as a correctness failure, aborting the example and masking the fact that the variants actually agree. False alarm undermines the differential-test purpose.
confirmed.recommendation: Handle NaN before the inequality, e.g. treat two values equal when both are NaN: `if first != other and not (isinstance(first,float) and isinstance(other,float) and math.isnan(first) and math.isnan(other))`, or use `numpy.array_equal(a, b, equal_nan=True)` for numeric results. Document that NaN==NaN is intentionally treated as a match.
confirmed.verdictReasoning:
The raw code defect is real: examples/_common.py:73 uses `if first != other:` to cross-check variant results, and Python float NaN != NaN evaluates to True (verified interactively: `float('nan') != float('nan')` -> True). So if two variants legitimately both produce NaN, assert_results_match raises a spurious AssertionError, contradicting the docstring's 'compare equal at full precision' promise. That part of the finding is accurate and correctly located.

However the finding's impact narrative and its target ('examples/_common.py + run_irr.py') are not supported by the current tree. Verified via grep that examples/irr.py (the module run_irr.py launches) never calls assert_results_match at all -- it only does explicit NPV-residual assertions with `abs(...) < 1e-6`, so 'IRR is a float-returning UDAF whose differential check is exactly the kind of caller this helper serves' is false on the current code; there is no differential check for IRR to spuriously fail. The same JSON file's own 'notes' field concedes run_irr.py is 'a pure module-identity launcher ... sound as written' and that 'Both findings are in _common.py' -- directly contradicting the target/impact framing that ties this to run_irr.py/IRR.

I also checked all three actual current callers of assert_results_match (examples/fraud_score.py:208/210, examples/online_scoring.py:184, examples/haversine.py:169/171): fraud_score compares integer aggregate sums, online_scoring compares rounded dot-product scores of random linear-model weights against random features (no log/div-by-zero path), and haversine compares great-circle distances -- none of these produce legitimate NaN in normal operation. So today, no code path in the repository actually triggers the false-positive AssertionError; the defect is real but currently dormant/unexercised.

Net: confirmed as a genuine latent logic bug in a shared example/test helper (low blast radius, example-only code, as the finding itself notes), but the medium severity and the described real-world trigger (IRR) are unsupported by the current tree -- downgraded to low.

confirmed.title: format_table does not validate row length; wrong-width rows crash or silently truncate
confirmed.description: format_table validates that headers and alignments are the same length (line 47) but never validates row length. `widths` has exactly len(headers) entries. The loop `for i, cell in enumerate(row): widths[i] = max(...)` (lines 50-52) indexes `widths[i]`, so any row longer than headers raises IndexError. Conversely a row shorter than headers is silently accepted, and fmt_row's `zip(cells, alignments, widths)` (line 55) truncates to the shortest, dropping trailing columns with no error. The focus of this review calls out row-length validation, and it is absent.
confirmed.impact: A caller passing a malformed row gets either an opaque IndexError far from the mistake, or a silently mis-rendered table with dropped columns, rather than a clear ValueError. Low blast radius (example harness only) but a real correctness gap in the stated contract.
confirmed.recommendation: Add an explicit check, e.g. `for row in rows: if len(row) != len(headers): raise ValueError('each row must match headers length')`, before computing widths.
confirmed.verdictReasoning:
The code defect is real and accurately described. examples/_common.py:45-60 defines format_table(headers, rows, alignments). It validates headers vs alignments length (line 47-48) but never validates row length against headers. `widths = [len(h) for h in headers]` (line 49) has exactly len(headers) entries; the loop at lines 50-52 (`for row in rows: for i, cell in enumerate(row): widths[i] = max(widths[i], len(cell))`) will raise IndexError on `widths[i]` if any row has more elements than headers. Conversely, if a row has fewer elements than headers, no IndexError occurs there, but `fmt_row`'s `zip(cells, alignments, widths)` (line 55) silently stops at the shortest iterable (len(cells)), so fmt_row for that row emits fewer columns than the header row with no error -- exactly the 'crash on over-width, silently truncate on under-width' behavior claimed. Verified interactively that this is standard Python zip/list-index semantics, no subtlety missed.

However, checked all three real current call sites (grep for format_table usage): examples/online_scoring.py:250-259 and 297-301, examples/fraud_score.py:252-256, examples/haversine.py:205-209. In every case the constructed row lists have exactly as many elements as headers/alignments (hand-verified element counts at each call site), so the defect is not exercised anywhere in the current codebase -- it is a latent robustness/validation gap in an internal, non-shared, example-only helper (the module's own docstring caps it at ~80 lines and says to keep it 'DuckDB-agnostic'), not an active bug. The line citation (50) points at the `for row in rows:` loop header rather than the exact indexing line (52), a minor imprecision but the mechanism described is correct.

Given: (1) example-harness-only code with no production/library callers, (2) zero current call sites trigger it, (3) the fix is a trivial one-line guard as the finding itself proposes -- this is a genuine but low-impact validation gap, not a medium-severity defect. Downgraded from medium to low, consistent with the sibling finding EX-common-1's calibration in this same file (also downgraded medium->low for the same 'real but currently dormant, example-only' reasoning).

confirmed.title: func_p scalar-function handle leaked on the register-failure path
confirmed.description: In register_jit_udf, the scalar-function builder handle func_p (created at line 154 by duckdb_create_scalar_function) is only destroyed at lines 172-173 (duckdb_destroy_scalar_function), which run AFTER the 'assert rc == ducklib.DuckDBSuccess' at line 171. If duckdb_register_scalar_function returns DuckDBError, the assert raises before the destroy call, so func_p is never freed. Per CLAUDE.md 'Error Handling' the C API uses return-code checks and, per the create/destroy contract (understanding/examples.md cross-cutting invariant 3), every handle created must be destroyed. The logical types (dbl_p/tin_p/int_p) are already destroyed at lines 166-168 before the assert, so only func_p is orphaned.
confirmed.impact: A single duckdb_scalar_function allocation is leaked on the registration-failure branch. Because this is a standalone benchmark whose only failure mode here is the AssertionError terminating the interpreter (which reclaims all memory on teardown), the practical impact is negligible; it matters mainly as a copied usage pattern for real applications that catch the error and continue.
confirmed.recommendation: Destroy func_p before asserting, e.g. capture rc, run the numpy-buffer destroy idiom on func_p, then 'assert rc == ducklib.DuckDBSuccess'; or wrap registration in try/finally so the handle is freed on both paths.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified directly against examples/fraud_score.py:152-173 (register_jit_udf). func_p is created at line 154 via ducklib.duckdb_create_scalar_function(); the three logical-type handles are destroyed at lines 166-168 (correct, since duckdb_scalar_function_add_parameter/set_return_type copy the type per DuckDB's create/destroy contract, so those destroys before the assert are safe). At line 170, rc = duckdb_register_scalar_function(conn_ptr, func_p); line 171 is a bare 'assert rc == ducklib.DuckDBSuccess' with no try/finally; only after that (lines 172-173) is func_p destroyed via duckdb_destroy_scalar_function. duckdb.h's doc comment for duckdb_register_scalar_function ('If the function is incomplete or a function with this name already exists DuckDBError is returned') confirms failure is a normal, expected return path, not a fatal-only condition, and nothing in the C API contract states registration takes ownership of or frees scalar_function on failure -- create/destroy is symmetric and caller-owned regardless of registration outcome (consistent with duckdb_register_scalar_function_set/duckdb_register_aggregate_function siblings in ducklib.py, all following the same create->configure->register->destroy shape). So on the DuckDBError branch, the AssertionError at line 171 fires before line 172-173 ever runs, and func_p (the scalar_function handle allocated by duckdb_create_scalar_function) is never freed -- a genuine handle leak, exactly as described. Severity is correctly low: this is a stdalone benchmark example (not library code), the only way to reach the leak is a registration failure (e.g. duplicate name or incomplete function spec) which does not occur in the script's actual call sequence, and the AssertionError, if it did fire, would propagate to interpreter exit, at which point OS process teardown reclaims the leaked native allocation anyway. The bug is real as a copy-paste-able anti-pattern, but has no runtime consequence in this script as currently written and exercised.

confirmed.title: Fixed bisection bracket [-0.99, 10.0]; roots outside the bracket silently return NaN
confirmed.description: irr_bisect hard-codes r_lo = -0.99 and r_hi = 10.0 (lines 80-81). Bisection can only locate a root inside this bracket. Because the only successful-exit path is the absolute-tolerance test at line 88, a true monthly IRR above 10.0 (1000%/month) or a loss scenario with IRR below -0.99 leaves npv the same sign at both ends, the tolerance is never met, and the function returns NaN (line 94) rather than signalling out-of-range. The routine also implicitly assumes NPV is monotonically decreasing in r (true only when all cashflows are positive, which the docstring formula at lines 9-11 does not require); a group mixing positive and negative cashflows can have multiple sign changes and the sign-driven bracket update (lines 90-93) may converge to the wrong root.
confirmed.impact: Edge-case correctness: legitimate high-return or mixed-sign groups return NaN or a wrong root. Lower severity than EX-irr-COR-1 because typical monthly IRRs fall inside the bracket and the documented per-group contract uses positive cashflows, but it is an undocumented silent-failure boundary of the example.
confirmed.recommendation: Document the [-0.99, 10.0] monthly-rate bracket and the all-positive-cashflow (single sign change) assumption in the irr_bisect docstring, and/or widen the bracket. At minimum this limitation should be stated so users porting the example understand when it silently yields NaN.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against /home/erik/projects/numbduck/examples/irr.py:78-94. irr_bisect hard-codes r_lo = -0.99 (line 80) and r_hi = 10.0 (line 81), runs 100 bisection iterations (line 82), and the only successful-exit path is the abs(npv) < 1e-9 tolerance check (line 88); the sign-driven bracket update is `if npv > 0.0: r_lo = r_mid else: r_hi = r_mid` (lines 90-93), and if the loop completes without meeting tolerance it falls through to `return math.nan` (line 94) with no error, warning, or side channel signaling out-of-range. If the true monthly IRR lies above 10.0 or below -0.99, npv keeps the same sign at both bracket endpoints throughout every iteration (since the algorithm assumes a single sign change inside [-0.99, 10.0]), r_lo/r_hi converge toward one bracket edge without ever driving npv near zero, and the loop exhausts its 100 iterations returning NaN silently -- exactly as claimed. The module docstring (irr.py:9-11) states the NPV formula with no restriction to positive cashflows or single sign change, so the bisection's implicit monotonicity assumption (needed for the sign-based bracket update to correctly converge) is indeed undocumented; a mixed-sign cashflow group could converge to a spurious root rather than NaN, which the finding also notes correctly. This is a real, accurately characterized limitation of the bisection routine. Severity 'low' is appropriate: it only affects examples/irr.py, an illustrative demo script (not numbduck's DuckDB C API bindings or core library correctness), and the finding's own text acknowledges typical monthly IRRs and the documented per-group usage pattern (positive cashflows) fall inside the bracket in ordinary use, so this is an edge-case/undocumented-boundary issue rather than a functional defect in common paths. No mitigating factor was found that would refute or elevate the finding -- confirmed as stated with severity unchanged at low.

confirmed.title: Borrowed structref ref leaks (and result is silently wrong) if an impl raises inside a @cfunc-wrapped callback
confirmed.category: NRT refcount leak across a raising call / swallowed exception
confirmed.description: None of the five @cfunc-wrapped @njit impls (_irr_update_impl/_combine_impl/_finalize_impl, plus init/destroy) wraps its body in a try/except. Per the documented numba @cfunc contract (MEMORY 'numba @cfunc swallows exceptions'), a raise inside an impl called from a @cfunc returns the zero/void default with no unwind to DuckDB (silent wrong result) AND leaks any NRT ref held across the raising call. update/combine/finalize each hold a live borrowed structref (borrow_structref, lines 156, 178-179, 201) at the moment they call vector_push (157-158) / vector_extend (180-181) / irr_bisect (206). vector_push/vector_extend call numpy.empty (numbox vector.py), which raises MemoryError on allocation failure; on that raise the borrowed structref's scope-exit decref is skipped, so the +1 from borrow_structref leaks, and DuckDB continues as though the row/group succeeded. The only realistic trigger is OOM during vector growth, so this is a latent hazard rather than a happy-path bug; but it is the exact failure mode called out in the review focus.
confirmed.impact: On an allocation failure during vector growth, a borrowed structref meminfo is leaked (NRT alloc!=free) and DuckDB silently proceeds with a partial/incorrect aggregate; the exception never reaches SQL. Undetectable except by the end-of-run leak assertion, which itself only runs after a successful query.
confirmed.recommendation: Wrap each impl body in a bare try/except that swallows-and-signals (or at minimum releases the borrowed ref) so a raise cannot both leak the ref and be silently discarded; e.g. compute results under try/except and, on failure, write NaN / set an error flag. Bare try/except (not try/finally, which re-raises on 0.65.1) both prevents the leak and makes the failure observable.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Structurally verified against the current tree. examples/irr.py has no try/except anywhere (grep confirms none). _irr_update_impl (examples/irr.py:154-162) does `s = borrow_structref(irr_state_type, slot[0])` at line 156, then calls `vector_push(s.cashflows, cf_data[iu])` (157) and `vector_push(s.periods, pd_data[iu])` (158), with `s` still read afterward at line 159 (`if s.initialized == 0`) -- so `s` is a live NRT reference held across two separate @njit calls. The same pattern recurs in _irr_combine_impl: `src`/`tgt` borrowed at lines 178-179, held live across `vector_extend(tgt.cashflows, src.cashflows)` / `vector_extend(tgt.periods, src.periods)` (180-181) and read again at 183-185. _irr_finalize_impl borrows `s` at line 201, held live across `irr_bisect(...)` at line 206. Read numbox/core/vector/vector.py:120-141: vector_push and vector_extend both call `numpy.empty(...)` for geometric buffer growth, which is the realistic MemoryError trigger the finding cites. Read numbox/utils/meminfo.py:131-140: borrow_structref does `_incref_meminfo(p)` then reconstructs the structref -- 'net-zero for the external owner if the caller's scope exits without additional actions' per its own docstring, i.e. it relies on the njit function's normal scope-exit decref of the local variable to balance the +1. If vector_push/vector_extend raises (e.g. OOM) while `s`/`src`/`tgt` is still live, the scope-exit decref is skipped by the exception unwind, so the borrow's +1 is never balanced -- a leaked reference on the IRRState meminfo, and the mutation from that row/group never completes. Because these impls are called from @cfunc wrappers (_irr_update_cb/_irr_combine_cb/_irr_finalize_cb, examples/irr.py:165-167, 188-190, 209-211) with no try/except anywhere in the module, numba's cfunc boundary catches the exception, prints to stderr, and returns the type's zero/void default with no unwind into DuckDB -- so DuckDB is never told an error occurred (silent wrong result), consistent with documented numba @cfunc behavior (exception caught only at the C-ABI boundary, swallowed with a zero-default return). This matches known numba internals: NRT refcounts are balanced via scope-exit decrefs inserted according to liveness, and a raise that unwinds past a call boundary while a reference is still live-but-not-yet-decremented skips that decref. I could not execute code to reproduce the OOM trigger (task forbids running the app/tests), so this remains verified by static/structural analysis plus known numba semantics rather than a fresh empirical repro, but the code pattern the finding describes is real and precisely as cited (file:line matches examples/irr.py:156, 178-181, 201 exactly, and no mitigating try/except exists anywhere in the file). The trigger (allocation failure during a 64-double vector's geometric growth) is genuinely rare/OOM-only, matching the finding's own 'low severity / low confidence / latent hazard, not happy-path bug' framing -- so both the defect's existence and its 'low' severity rating are appropriate; nothing in the current tree (no guard, no try/except, no alternate cleanup path) refutes it.

confirmed.title: Prepared statement leaked when duckdb_prepare fails (cleanup missing on error path)
confirmed.description: score_jit() calls `rc = ducklib.duckdb_prepare(...)` then `assert rc == ducklib.DuckDBSuccess` (lines 155-156), and only reaches `duckdb_destroy_prepare(stmt.ctypes.data)` at line 161 if the assert passes. duckdb.h documents that a prepared statement must be destroyed with duckdb_destroy_prepare even when duckdb_prepare fails (a statement object is allocated to carry the error message). On a failed prepare the AssertionError unwinds out of score_jit before line 161, so the failed statement handle in stmt[0] is never freed.
confirmed.impact: One prepared-statement handle (and its attached error message) is leaked whenever prepare fails. Impact is minor: it is an error path in a benchmark/demo that aborts the process anyway, and cannot occur for the example's own fixed SQL. But as a canonical usage contract that users copy, it teaches an incomplete cleanup pattern that violates the documented duckdb_destroy_prepare-even-on-failure rule.
confirmed.recommendation: Destroy the statement before asserting, e.g. capture rc, and on failure call duckdb_destroy_prepare(stmt.ctypes.data) before raising (or wrap the loop + destroy in try/finally). This mirrors the numpy-buffer destroy idiom already used at line 161.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against the current tree. examples/online_scoring.py:150-162 (score_jit) reads: line 155 `rc = ducklib.duckdb_prepare(conn_ptr, get_unicode_data_p(sql), stmt.ctypes.data)`, line 156 `assert rc == ducklib.DuckDBSuccess`, and only line 161 `ducklib.duckdb_destroy_prepare(stmt.ctypes.data)` frees the handle -- reached only after the njit loop runs, i.e. only on the success path. If duckdb_prepare fails, the AssertionError at line 156 unwinds out of score_jit before line 161 is ever reached, so the prepared-statement object allocated by duckdb_prepare (which DuckDB uses to carry the error message on failure) is never destroyed. Confirmed the documented contract directly from duckdb.h: the comment immediately preceding the duckdb_prepare declaration states verbatim 'Note that after calling `duckdb_prepare`, the prepared statement should always be destroyed using `duckdb_destroy_prepare`, even if the prepare fails.' This is the exact rule the finding cites, and the code path genuinely violates it -- there is no try/finally, no early destroy-on-failure branch, and no other cleanup of stmt on the error path. Checked numbduck/duckdb_utils.py:25-27 (create_duckdb_prepared_statement just allocates a 1-slot int64 buffer) and numbduck/ducklib.py:769-772 (duckdb_destroy_prepare is a straightforward _call_lib_func wrapper matching the C signature `void(intp)`) -- nothing here mitigates the gap; on failure stmt[0] would hold whatever duckdb_prepare wrote (a valid statement-with-error object per the C API contract), and it is simply never passed to duckdb_destroy_prepare. The reviewer's own impact assessment is accurate and not overstated: this cannot fire for the example's own fixed, valid SQL (so no live bug in this file as shipped), the assert typically aborts the whole script anyway so the leaked handle's practical lifetime is near-zero, and the finding is framed correctly as a 'canonical usage pattern that copiers would replicate' issue rather than a functional defect in this example run. Severity 'low' is appropriate -- real contract violation, correctly characterized, but genuinely inert in the shipped file and confined to an example/demo (not library) error path.

confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read examples/online_scoring.py:106-148 directly. Confirmed chunk_p = ducklib.duckdb_fetch_chunk(result_tup) at line 123 is used unguarded at lines 125-128 (duckdb_data_chunk_get_vector calls) and the resulting vectors are read via carray(..., (1,), float64)[0] at lines 133-140 assuming exactly one row, with no duckdb_data_chunk_get_size check. Checked duckdb.h (scratchpad copy matching the v1.3.2-1.6 pinned range): duckdb_fetch_chunk's docstring states it returns NULL on error and must be called repeatedly 'until the result is exhausted' -- the established DuckDB C API contract is that NULL also signals exhaustion/empty result, not only error. Checked ducklib.py:732-735 (duckdb_data_chunk_get_vector) and :943-946 (duckdb_fetch_chunk): both are thin pass-through wrappers (_call_lib_func / _call_lib_func_byval) with no null-check injected by the binding layer, so any NULL-safety is entirely the caller's responsibility and none exists here. Verified the 'no live bug' claim: setup_events draws ids via rng.integers(0, k_features) and setup_features creates the table via range(k_features), so every WHERE id = $1 lookup is guaranteed to match exactly one row for this example's own fixed inputs -- the defect is real but latent, not an active crash when run as shipped. This matches the finding's own characterization. The defect is real, correctly cited at file:line, and correctly scoped as a latent/teaching-pattern gap (not a live bug in the example as run) -- so 'low' severity is appropriate, not inflated and not dismissible.

confirmed.title: No NULL/size guard on fetched chunk before dereferencing it
confirmed.description: Inside _score_jit_loop, duckdb_fetch_chunk (line 123) is called once per execute and its return (chunk_p) is immediately passed to duckdb_data_chunk_get_vector (lines 125-128) and the vector data is read as carray(..., (1,), float64) (lines 133-140) assuming exactly one chunk with exactly one row. Per duckdb.h, duckdb_fetch_chunk returns NULL once the result is exhausted (i.e. a query that matched zero rows yields a NULL chunk on the first fetch). If the point lookup returns no row, chunk_p == 0 and duckdb_data_chunk_get_vector(0, 0) dereferences a NULL handle inside a nogil njit region — an unrecoverable segfault, not a Python exception. There is also no duckdb_data_chunk_get_size check, so even a non-NULL empty chunk would read row 0 of a zero-length vector (out-of-bounds read). In this example the ids are drawn from range(0, N_FEATURES) and the features table has exactly ids range(N_FEATURES), so every lookup matches and the path is never hit, which is why it is low severity — but the kernel is presented as the canonical prepared-execute reading pattern and carries no guard.
confirmed.impact: Latent: any adaptation with a non-matching key (or a genuinely empty result) segfaults the process from inside the GIL-free loop with no traceback. Not triggered by the example's own data.
confirmed.recommendation: After duckdb_fetch_chunk, guard on chunk_p != 0 and on duckdb_data_chunk_get_size(chunk_p) >= 1 before reading vectors; skip/emit NaN and still destroy the (empty or NULL-safe) result when no row is present. At minimum document the one-row precondition at the fetch site.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Empirically verified against the pinned duckdb runtime (1.5.4, within the numbduck pin duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6) by calling the actual C API via ctypes (same shared lib numbduck/utils.py:find_duckdb_shared_lib locates): a zero-row query's FIRST call to duckdb_fetch_chunk returns NULL, not merely on a later exhausted call. This matches the project's own test/test_ducklib.py:212-219 (test_duckdb_fetch_chunk_exhausted), which only exercises the second-call-after-exhaustion case for a non-empty (3-row) result, so it does not cover the zero-row-on-first-call path that is at issue here. examples/online_scoring.py:123 assigns chunk_p = ducklib.duckdb_fetch_chunk(result_tup) with no check, and lines 125-128 immediately call ducklib.duckdb_data_chunk_get_vector(chunk_p, 0..3). ducklib.py's binding (ducklib.py:732-735, duckdb_data_chunk_get_vector) is a raw _call_lib_func wrapper with no null/validity check, consistent with numbduck's documented policy (CLAUDE.md 'Error Handling': bindings mirror the C API exactly, never inject checks) -- so no guard exists anywhere in the path, and a NULL chunk_p would be dereferenced inside the nogil njit region. Severity is correctly 'low': setup_features (online_scoring.py:72-79) populates the features table with id = range(N_FEATURES) (0..k-1) and setup_events (line 84) draws ids via rng.integers(0, k_features, ...), so every generated id is guaranteed to match a row and the path is provably unreachable with this example's own data -- it is a latent defect in the canonical pattern being taught, not a live bug in the shipped example. No mitigating contract, prior guard, or version-specific behavior refutes it; verdict CONFIRMED at the claimed low severity.

confirmed.recommendation: Repin the URL to the supported numbox version (e.g. /blob/0.5.13/... or a tag matching the pin), consistent with the other numbox links.

Severity is correctly low: clock.py's monotonic_ns API and docstring (verified in the current numbox source at numbox/utils/clock.py:1-40) is stable/self-contained, so a reader following the stale link still lands on materially the same function; this is a doc-hygiene inconsistency, not a functional or misleading-content defect.

confirmed.category: cfunc exception-swallow / silent output corruption at the C boundary
confirmed.title: Scalar-UDF @cfunc callbacks have no exception guard; a raise inside the impl is swallowed at numba's cfunc boundary, handing DuckDB a silent 'success' with a partially-written/garbage output vector and no error signalled
confirmed.description: Both scalar chunk callbacks are thin @cfunc wrappers over a module-level @njit impl with no try/except: _haversine_chunk_cb (haversine.py:116-118) -> _haversine_chunk_impl (haversine.py:87-113), and _fraud_chunk_cb (fraud_score.py:147-149) -> _fraud_chunk_impl (fraud_score.py:102-144). Per the codebase's verified numba contract (MEMORY reference_numba_cfunc_swallows_exceptions; confirmed against numba's np_cfarray) a Python exception escaping an impl called from a @cfunc is caught at the boundary, printed to stderr, and the void zero-default is returned WITHOUT unwinding into DuckDB. DuckDB therefore treats the scalar callback as successful and consumes whatever values were already written into the output vector (a_out, written in place at haversine.py:113 / fraud_score.py:144) up to the raise point -- a silent wrong result for the whole chunk with no SQL-level error. IMPORTANT DISTINCTION FROM THE UDAF FINDING (XC-numbox-MEM-1 / EX-irr-MEM-1): the scalar impls hold NO NRT reference across any call, so the swallow's leak component does NOT apply here. Every carray view is created unmanaged -- numba's np_cfarray calls populate_array(..., meminfo=None, '# Array is not memory-managed') (arrayobj.py:5574-5581) -- and _cast_int_to_void_p is a pure inttoptr with no incref (numbox lowlevel.py:49-53); the impls never take a borrow_structref/export_meminfo +1 (contrast irr.py). So there is nothing to leak: the sole consequence is the silent corrupt/partial output. Reachability is latent: for the examples' own dense non-NULL numeric inputs no impl actually raises (numba's math.sqrt/asin return NaN on domain errors rather than raising; the loops use only float/int comparisons, adds, and in-bounds carray writes; n comes from duckdb_data_chunk_get_size and carray does not validate the backing buffer), so a raise is reachable only via a future edit that introduces a raising call, or a port to nullable/validity-checked inputs.
confirmed.impact: If either impl ever raises (future edit adds a raising call, or the pattern is copied to nullable inputs), DuckDB silently returns a wrong scalar result for the entire chunk -- the output vector holds whatever was computed before the raise (garbage for the un-reached rows) and no error reaches SQL. No memory is leaked (carray views are unmanaged, meminfo=None). As the two canonical scalar-UDF usage examples, they teach an idiom with no swallow guard, so the corruption becomes live the moment a raising operation is added.
confirmed.recommendation: For parity with the numbox phase-3 UDAF guard and XC-numbox-MEM-1, either wrap each impl body in a bare try/except (NOT try/finally -- it re-raises on numba 0.65.1) that writes a defined sentinel to the output on failure, or, since the current binding set exposes no per-row error-signalling channel for a chunk scalar callback, at minimum add a comment at each @cfunc wrapper documenting the swallow-on-raise contract and the invariant that the impl must stay raise-free, so a future edit does not silently introduce an uncaught raising call.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against the CURRENT tree, not the stale 2026-06-29 review. examples/haversine.py:87-118 and examples/fraud_score.py:102-149 read exactly as cited: _haversine_chunk_impl/_fraud_chunk_impl are module-level @njit functions with no try/except, called from thin @cfunc(void(intp,intp,intp)) wrappers _haversine_chunk_cb (haversine.py:116-118) and _fraud_chunk_cb (fraud_score.py:147-149) with no guard of their own. Confirmed numba's cfunc-boundary swallow behavior directly against the installed numba 0.65.1 in numbduck/venv: numba/core/cpu.py CPUContext.create_cfunc_wrapper (lines ~230-259) builds the cfunc trampoline so that on `status.is_error` it merely GIL-acquires and calls `pyapi.err_write_unraisable(strobj)` (prints 'Exception ignored in: ...' + traceback to stderr) and then unconditionally falls through to `builder.ret(out)` -- there is no path that unwinds an exception into the C caller; numba's own test suite (numba/tests/test_cfunc.py TestCFunc.test_errors) exercises exactly this and asserts the returned value is the zero default while stderr contains 'Exception ignored'. This confirms: if either impl raised, DuckDB would receive a normal (non-error) void return with whatever was already written into a_out up to the raise point -- a silent, uncaught corruption, exactly as the finding describes. Verified the 'no leak' sub-claim too: numba/np/arrayobj.py np_cfarray (source line ~5574, matching the finding's cited 5574-5581) calls populate_array(..., meminfo=None, # Array is not memory-managed), and numbox/utils/lowlevel.py:49-53 _cast_int_to_void_p is a bare `builder.inttoptr` with no incref -- so carray views in both impls are genuinely unmanaged and nothing leaks on a swallowed raise, matching the finding's explicit distinction from the UDAF/XC-numbox-MEM-1 leak finding. Reachability check on current example code also holds: setup_data (haversine.py:140-145, fraud_score.py:176-188) generates dense non-NULL numeric columns, n = duckdb_data_chunk_get_size(chunk) matches the carray shape used for every view, and the loop bodies use only math.radians/sin/cos/asin/sqrt (NaN on domain error, never raises) and plain int/float comparisons and in-bounds carray writes -- no raise is reachable today; the defect is latent, contingent on a future edit that introduces a raising call or nullable/validity-checked inputs. This latency is exactly what caps the severity at 'low': a real, correctly characterized swallow-and-corrupt pattern with a verified mechanism, but not a currently live wrong-result bug in the examples as shipped. No basis found to raise or lower the reviewer's severity.

confirmed.title: Docstring claims the pointer is 'validated' but the SELECT 1 check cannot detect a structurally-wrong pointer
confirmed.description: The docstring (lines 28-29, 49-50) states the extracted pointer 'is validated by running SELECT 1 via the C API before it is returned' and documents RuntimeError 'If the extracted pointer fails the validation query'. The validation (lines 65-72) can only distinguish 'live connection whose query failed' (rc != DuckDBSuccess) from success. A structurally-wrong conn_ptr arising from any offset/layout drift is undefined behavior inside duckdb_query (likely a segfault), which is not a value rc can report — so the check cannot actually catch the failure mode it most needs to. The rc-check-after-unconditional-destroy ordering itself is correct (duckdb_query populates the result even on error, so destroying on both paths at line 68 is right), but the guarantee the docstring advertises is stronger than what the code can deliver.
confirmed.impact: Callers may trust the 'validated' guarantee and assume a returned pointer is safe on any in-pin duckdb, when in reality a wrong-layout pointer would have crashed rather than raised. Documentation overstates the safety net.
confirmed.recommendation: Soften the docstring to state the validation only confirms a live connection responds to a trivial query and cannot detect a wrong pointer from ABI/layout drift; pair it with the version guard from PBR-COR-1 so the trusted-offset precondition is enforced up front.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against numbduck/pybridge.py:28-29,49-50 (docstring) and :64-72 (implementation), plus numbduck/ducklib.py:221,1111-1114 (duckdb_query proxy) and :17,19 (duckdb_state_ty/DuckDBSuccess). The docstring literally claims the pointer 'is validated by running SELECT 1' and documents RuntimeError only for the case the query fails. The implementation's sole check is `rc != ducklib.DuckDBSuccess` (pybridge.py:69) after calling duckdb_query(conn_ptr, query_p, result.ctypes.data). duckdb_query is a thin proxy (ducklib.py:1111-1114) with signature duckdb_state_ty(intp, intp, intp) that passes conn_ptr straight into the C library with no pointer sanity check of its own -- confirmed by reading the wrapper body, which is a direct _call_lib_func passthrough. If conn_ptr is structurally wrong (e.g. due to an ABI/offset-layout drift the docstring itself flags as a risk in lines 31-34), the C API will dereference an invalid Connection* inside duckdb_query; this is undefined behavior in C (most likely a segfault) that occurs before any duckdb_state return code can be produced or inspected by Python. So the rc check can only ever distinguish 'live, correctly-typed connection whose SQL failed' from success -- it structurally cannot catch a wrong-pointer/layout-drift failure, which is exactly the risk the surrounding docstring text (lines 31-34) warns about. This matches the finding's description precisely, including its acknowledgment that the destroy/rc ordering itself is correct (duckdb_destroy_result at line 68 runs unconditionally, matching the C API's populate-on-both-paths contract) -- the defect is purely that the docstring's use of the word 'validated' plus the documented RuntimeError contract overstate what the check can actually catch. This is a real, verifiable documentation-accuracy gap, not a functional bug (no incorrect behavior results from it beyond the crash risk that PBR-COR-1 already covers at higher severity), so 'low' is the appropriate severity: it does not change program behavior, only the truthfulness/precision of the docstring's safety claim.

confirmed.title: Hard-coded ABI offsets with no named constants, no duckdb version guard, and no programmatic re-verify mechanism
confirmed.description: The two load-bearing ABI offsets are inline magic numbers: `ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(py_obj_addr + 16)` (line 59) and `ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(cpp_obj_p + 32)` (line 62). The docstring validates them only against 'duckdb 1.3.2 / Linux x86-64 / libstdc++' and instructs a human to 'Re-verify offsets when upgrading duckdb' (lines 31-34), but (a) the package pins `duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6`, so a 1.4 or 1.5 wheel installs and runs the identical hard-coded offsets with zero runtime check; (b) there are no named module-level constants (e.g. CPYTHON_OBJ_HEADER = 16, DUCKDBPY_CONNECTION_OFFSET = 32) tying the numbers to their meaning — the `+16` in particular has no explanation in the code (the CPython 16-byte object header rationale exists only in the review note, not the source); and (c) 'Re-verify offsets when upgrading duckdb' is a manual instruction with no supporting mechanism — no `duckdb.__version__` guard that fails fast or warns on an untested version, and no test that would flag drift. This is precisely the fragility-management gap the review focus asks about: no version guard, no named offset constants, no automated re-verify, and (per PBR-DES-1) no graceful failure path.
confirmed.impact: On any in-pin-range duckdb release whose pybind11 holder layout or DuckDBPyConnection field order differs, the code silently reads a wrong pointer and (best case) fails an opaque RuntimeError or (worst case) segfaults, with nothing directing the maintainer to the offsets. The bare integers also make the code hard to audit and to correct.
confirmed.recommendation: Promote the offsets to named module-level constants with a one-line rationale each (CPython object header = 16; unique_ptr<Connection> at +32). Add a fail-fast/warn guard that checks `duckdb.__version__` against a known-verified set (or at least the pinned range) and raises a clear, actionable error naming the offsets to re-verify when an untested version is detected — turning silent UB into a diagnosable failure and giving the 're-verify' instruction teeth.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Confirmed on current tree: numbduck/pybridge.py:59 (`ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(py_obj_addr + 16)`) and :62 (`ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(cpp_obj_p + 32)`) are bare inline integers with no module-level named constants anywhere in the file, and there is no `duckdb.__version__` guard in pybridge.py or elsewhere in numbduck/*.py (grep confirms `duckdb.__version__` is used only in numbduck/utils.py for a lib-cache directory path, unrelated to ABI validation). The docstring's 'Re-verify offsets when upgrading duckdb' (lines 31-34) is indeed a manual-only instruction. The `duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6` pin (pyproject.toml:12) does admit 1.4.x/1.5.x with these same hard-coded offsets and no runtime check, so parts (a) and (b) of the finding are accurate. However, part (c) -- 'no programmatic re-verify mechanism' / 'no test that would flag drift' -- is materially overstated: .github/workflows/numbduck_ci.yml runs a full `pytest` matrix across duckdb-version in ["1.3.2", "1.4.0", "1.5.1"] (line 24, 69), and test/test_ducklib.py has at least two tests (test_hybrid_jit_udf_on_python_connection L2562, test_jit_udf_vs_python_udf L2619) that call extract_connection_ptr and would fail (via the existing SELECT-1 validation, a wrong query result, or a crash) if the +16/+32 offsets drifted on 1.4.0 or 1.5.1. This is precisely a 'programmatic re-verify mechanism' and 'a test that would flag drift' across almost the entire pinned range -- contradicting the finding's claim that none exists. The residual real gap is narrower than described: only patch releases inside the pin that CI does not explicitly test (e.g. 1.4.1-1.4.x, 1.5.2+) plus lack of an in-source runtime guard for end users running an untested patch version outside CI. Given the magic-numbers/no-named-constants observation is valid but purely stylistic (readability, not correctness), and the claimed absence of any automated drift-detection is factually wrong given the CI matrix already covering the practically-relevant minor versions, severity should be downgraded from medium to low.

confirmed.title: Returned Connection* is a borrowed pointer with an undocumented keep-alive / use-after-close contract
confirmed.description: extract_connection_ptr returns conn_ptr (line 74) as a bare Python int read from offset +32 inside the C++ DuckDBPyConnection (line 62). This int is a *borrowed* raw pointer: the underlying Connection is owned by the Python `conn` object (the unique_ptr<Connection> living inside the pybind11 instance). A Python int cannot hold `conn` referenced, so the pointer is only valid while `conn` is alive AND open. The docstring's Returns section (lines 41-43) documents only 'The Connection* as a Python int (intp-compatible)' and says nothing about this borrow. This is the exact invariant the sibling numbox bridge — which this file is explicitly modeled on — spells out in dedicated Returns + Warning sections (numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py:129-144: 'borrowed from conn ... stays valid only while conn is alive and open ... must not use the pointer after conn.close() or after conn is garbage-collected — doing so is a use-after-free'). The omission is a real memory-safety documentation gap, not a behavioral bug: the borrow design itself is correct.
confirmed.impact: A downstream caller who writes `ptr = extract_connection_ptr(duckdb.connect())` (not retaining the connection), or who uses the pointer after `conn.close()` / after `conn` is GC'd, dereferences a dangling `Connection*` inside @njit duckdb_* calls — a silent use-after-free / segfault. In-repo callers (examples/*.py, test/test_ducklib.py) all keep `conn` in a live local, so no current crash; the risk is for external API consumers who lack the warning.
confirmed.recommendation: Add to the docstring the same borrowed-pointer contract the sibling documents: state in Returns that the pointer is borrowed from and owned by `conn`, and add a Warning that the caller must retain `conn` (alive and open) for the entire lifetime of any @njit use of the returned pointer, and must not use it after conn.close() or GC.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current tree. numbduck/pybridge.py:10-51 (extract_connection_ptr) returns conn_ptr (line 74) read via ctypes from offset +32 inside the DuckDBPyConnection C++ object; the docstring's Returns section (lines 41-43) states only 'The Connection* as a Python int (intp-compatible)' with no lifetime/borrow contract. The underlying Connection is owned by conn's internal unique_ptr, so the returned int is a borrowed pointer valid only while conn is alive and open; a bare Python int cannot keep conn referenced. This is exactly the pattern the file is explicitly modeled on: numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py:129-144 documents the identical borrow ('is owned by the Python Connection and stays valid only while conn is alive and open... An int cannot keep conn referenced, so the keep-alive is the caller's responsibility') plus a dedicated Warning section about use-after-close/GC. pybridge.py has no equivalent language anywhere in its docstring. All current in-repo call sites (examples/fraud_score.py:153, examples/haversine.py:124, examples/online_scoring.py:152, examples/irr.py:231, test/test_ducklib.py:2569/2626/2724) keep conn in a live local for the call's duration, so there is no observable current-tree bug -- this is purely a missing-documentation gap for external API consumers, matching the finding's own characterization ('not a behavioral bug: the borrow design itself is correct'). Severity of low is appropriate for a documentation-only gap with no reproducible in-repo failure.

confirmed.title: isinstance guard is not an ABI-layout proof: a spoofed/subclassed object turns the two chained from_address reads into attacker-influenced pointer dereferences
confirmed.category: type-confusion / arbitrary memory read via pointer arithmetic
confirmed.description: The only gate before the raw pointer walk is isinstance(conn, duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection) (line 52). isinstance is not a proof of memory layout: it is satisfied by (a) a subclass of DuckDBPyConnection, (b) any object whose metaclass overrides __instancecheck__, or (c) an object with a spoofed __class__, none of which guarantee the pybind11 simple-holder header at +16 or the unique_ptr<Connection> at +32. For any such object, id(conn)+16 reads a word from within/after that object's header and treats it as a C++ object pointer (cpp_obj_p, line 59); cpp_obj_p+32 then dereferences THAT value as an address (line 62) — an attacker-influenced, essentially arbitrary pointer read. The resulting conn_ptr is then passed to duckdb_query (line 67). So a caller that passes a crafted object that merely answers True to isinstance drives two chained wild-pointer dereferences plus a C-API call on a bogus Connection*. bridge.md 3.1 notes the same: the guard 'guards the Python type only; it does not guarantee the pybind11/ABI layout matches'. This is a hardening gap rather than a boundary bypass (numbduck is a library, and a caller that wants to crash the process can do so directly), which is why it is low severity — but the isinstance check materially overstates the safety it provides, and the second read (line 62) in particular dereferences a value read out of the object, so it is a genuine attacker-influenced pointer deref, not merely a wrong-but-bounded offset.
confirmed.impact: A caller passing an isinstance-satisfying but layout-mismatched object (subclass, __instancecheck__/__class__ spoof) causes two chained arbitrary pointer dereferences and a duckdb_query on a garbage pointer -> segfault / undefined behavior, with no error path that can distinguish this from a legitimate connection until it crashes.
confirmed.recommendation: Treat the isinstance check as a convenience type-hint, not a safety guarantee, and document it as such. Where feasible tighten to an exact-type check (type(conn) is duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection) to reject subclasses, and pair the walk with the version/coordination guard (PBR-SEC-1) so the offsets are only trusted for the exact known-good build. Note in the docstring that a non-canonical DuckDBPyConnection is undefined behavior.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read numbduck/pybridge.py in full (current tree). Line 52 is the only gate: `if not isinstance(conn, duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection): raise TypeError(...)`. No other check (type identity, version/coordination guard, sentinel, etc.) precedes the raw walk anywhere in the function or in any caller (grepped all call sites: examples/fraud_score.py:153, examples/irr.py:231, examples/haversine.py:124, examples/online_scoring.py:152, test/test_ducklib.py:2569/2626/2724 -- none add extra validation before calling extract_connection_ptr). Lines 58-59 (`py_obj_addr = id(conn); cpp_obj_p = ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(py_obj_addr + 16).value`), 61-62 (`conn_ptr = ctypes.c_void_p.from_address(cpp_obj_p + 32).value`), and 67 (`ducklib.duckdb_query(conn_ptr, ...)`) match the finding's line citations exactly. isinstance() is a nominal-type check, not a layout proof, and this is not exploit folklore -- it is standard, well-documented Python semantics: (1) a metaclass overriding `__instancecheck__` on the class object referenced by `duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection` (achievable by monkeypatching the module attribute in-process) makes isinstance() return True for an arbitrary object with no C++ backing at all; (2) a Python subclass of DuckDBPyConnection also satisfies isinstance trivially. Either bypass drives id(conn)+16 and cpp_obj_p+32 to read whatever bytes happen to sit at those relative offsets in the attacker-supplied object, which are then fed to duckdb_query as a connection pointer -- a real, attacker-influenced pointer walk, not a hypothetical. The project's own understanding note (docs/reviews/2026-07-01-numbduck/understanding/bridge.md section 3.1 and section 5) independently reaches the identical conclusion ('This guards the Python type only; it does not guarantee the pybind11/ABI layout matches the offsets below') before this finding was authored, corroborating rather than being copied verbatim into the finding. The 'low' severity is well-calibrated, not overstated: exploiting this requires the caller to already be executing arbitrary Python in the same process (to monkeypatch the class or metaclass), at which point that caller already has unrestricted memory access via ctypes directly, so the finding correctly frames this as a hardening/documentation gap rather than a boundary-crossing vulnerability -- exactly the caveat baked into the finding's own severity justification. No contract-satisfied-elsewhere, no version/platform mitigation, and no evidence the finding mischaracterizes the code was found.

confirmed.title: Borrowed / use-after-free ownership contract of the returned pointer is undocumented (sibling documents it explicitly)
confirmed.description: extract_connection_ptr returns a bare int (line 74) that is a pointer BORROWED from conn: it stays valid only while conn is alive and open, and it cannot keep conn referenced. The docstring (lines 41-51) documents only the int return and the TypeError/RuntimeError, and says nothing about lifetime. A caller that stashes the returned int and uses it inside @njit after conn.close() or after conn is garbage-collected is dereferencing a freed/reset Connection* — a use-after-free. The sibling numbox bridge documents this contract prominently: pysqlite_bridge.extract_connection_ptr has a dedicated Returns note ('borrowed ... stays valid only while conn is alive and open') and a Warning section (pysqlite_bridge.py:132-144) spelling out that using the pointer after close()/GC is a use-after-free. numbduck's version drops that guidance entirely, so the most dangerous misuse of this API is silently undocumented. (This is the after-return UAF; the at-extraction null-after-close case is a separate correctness gap already noted for the COR unit.)
confirmed.impact: Callers unaware of the borrow semantics can build @njit code that dereferences a dangling duckdb_connection after close()/GC, a use-after-free that crashes or corrupts memory with no diagnostic. The omission is purely documentary but on a raw-pointer API the contract is the safety mechanism.
confirmed.recommendation: Add a Returns/Warning note mirroring numbox pysqlite_bridge: the returned int is a borrowed duckdb_connection owned by conn, valid only while conn is alive and open; the caller must retain conn for the full lifetime of any @njit use and must not use the pointer after conn.close() or GC.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current numbduck/pybridge.py:36-74 and numbox/utils/pysqlite_bridge.py:110-176. extract_connection_ptr's docstring (pybridge.py:36-51) documents only the `int` return type and the TypeError/RuntimeError exceptions; it says nothing about the returned pointer's lifetime, ownership, or borrow semantics. The returned conn_ptr (line 62, returned line 74) is read straight out of the live DuckDBPyConnection's internal unique_ptr<Connection> slot -- it is unmistakably a borrowed pointer that becomes dangling once conn.close() runs or conn is GC'd, and a bare Python int cannot keep conn alive. The sibling numbox.utils.pysqlite_bridge.extract_connection_ptr (pysqlite_bridge.py:110-176) documents exactly this contract explicitly: a 'Returns' note stating the pointer is 'borrowed ... owned by the Python Connection and stays valid only while conn is alive and open... the keep-alive is the caller's responsibility' plus a dedicated 'Warning' section (pysqlite_bridge.py:137-144) spelling out the use-after-free risk on close()/GC. numbduck's pybridge.py has no equivalent language anywhere in the file. This is a real, verifiable asymmetry between the two sibling bridges and a genuine documentation gap on a raw-pointer API where the docstring is the only safety mechanism a caller has. Severity: the gap is purely documentary (it doesn't change extract_connection_ptr's own behavior, which still validates the pointer via SELECT 1 at extraction time), so 'low' is the right rating -- consistent with the reviewer's own low severity assignment.

confirmed.title: Chunk callback reads inputs and writes output with no validity/NULL handling

confirmed.title: Chunk callback reads input vectors without validity (NULL) guard
confirmed.description: The @njit callback _fraud_chunk_impl (examples/fraud_score.py:102-144) indexes a_amt/a_co/a_hco/a_hr/a_rt/a_rx[i] for every row 0..n-1 (loop at 125-144) without ever fetching the DuckDB validity mask (no duckdb_vector_get_validity). For a NULL input cell DuckDB does not guarantee the data-slot value is initialized, so the loop folds an undefined value into the fraud score. This is the value-domain inverse of a bounds bug: the data buffers are allocated full-width, so every read is in-bounds (no OOB/use-after-free), but the byte content for a NULL row is garbage, yielding a silently wrong score. examples/irr.py is the in-repo reference that does this correctly (duckdb_vector_get_validity + duckdb_validity_row_is_valid per row); both APIs are bound in ducklib.py, so the fix is available in-repo.

confirmed.title: Chunk callback reads no validity mask; the reference scalar-UDF pattern is silently wrong on NULL input
confirmed.description: _haversine_chunk_impl (examples/haversine.py:87-113) unconditionally carrays each input vector's data buffer (lines 94-102) and reads a_lat1[i]/a_lon1[i]/a_lat2[i]/a_lon2[i] for every i in range(n) (lines 105-113) with no call to duckdb_vector_get_validity and no write to the output vector's validity. DuckDB leaves the data slot of a NULL row uninitialized/stale, so a NULL input is read as a garbage double, pushed through math.asin(math.sqrt(...)), and written to the output as a non-NULL value. In this example it is safe by construction: setup_data (lines 140-145) fills lat/lon via random()*180-90 / random()*360-180 over range(n), which never yields NULL, and the store coordinates are non-NULL literals, so no NULL reaches the UDF and the count(*) cross-check passes. The 'assumes non-NULL inputs' invariant is documented in understanding/examples.md:110-111, but the callback itself carries no comment or guard, so a downstream caller copying it for a nullable column gets silently wrong results.
confirmed.impact: No behavioral defect in the running example (dense generated data). The risk is pattern propagation: a caller reusing this callback on a nullable column reads garbage doubles for NULL rows and emits them as non-NULL output with no error.
confirmed.recommendation: Either add a one-line precondition comment at the loop asserting inputs are non-NULL, or (better for a reference example) fetch each input's validity via duckdb_vector_get_validity and gate each row with duckdb_validity_row_is_valid (guarded by validity_ptr != 0), mirroring irr.py:140-153, so the pattern is safe to copy for nullable columns.

Not NOT-REAL: the defect holds exactly as described on the current @proxy tree (line numbers 87-113/94-102/105-113 all verified to match). Not a DUPLICATE: current findings touching haversine.py are EX-hav-1 (severity high, constant-vector out-of-bounds read on literal args 3/4), EX-hav-2 (severity low, scalar-function handle leak on register failure), and EX-scalar-MEM-1 (severity low, @cfunc swallows exceptions from the same impl) -- none of these addresses validity/NULL handling; the root cause here (no validity mask read/write) is distinct from all three. confirmed.title: Combine refcount/borrow-balance path is never exercised by the in-file NRT leak guard
confirmed.description: The module ends with an NRT alloc/free balance guard (examples/irr.py:372-377: `if alloc_delta != free_delta` -> WARNING + sys.exit(1)), the file's only runtime check that the meminfo lifecycle (export_meminfo / borrow_structref / release_meminfo) is balanced. That guard only validates the callback paths the three queries actually drive: state_size, init, update, finalize, destroy. DuckDB invokes `_irr_combine_impl` (170-186) only when it merges thread-local / partitioned partial aggregate states. All three test datasets are tiny (Test 1: 12 rows ungrouped at 275-285; Test 2: 18 rows / 2 groups at 302-331; Test 3: 1 row at 352-363), so DuckDB's hash aggregate runs single-partition and almost certainly never calls combine. The combine path — where the borrow/release balance across `borrow_structref` (178-179) and the no-aliasing property of `vector_extend` (180-181) matter — carries no coverage from the guard. Per the documented removerefctpass fragility (test_ducklib.md, udaf.md risk #1/#2): the borrow net-zero property in combine depends on an NRT-alloc symbol (via vector_extend -> numpy.empty) landing in the `_irr_combine_impl` LLVM module to disable removerefctpass; if a numba build inlines/lowers vector_extend such that no NRT_MemInfo_alloc symbol remains in `_irr_combine_impl`, the surviving borrow incref (from borrow_structref, a separate NRT-typed unit) would be paired with a stripped scope-exit decref, leaking +1 per merged source and target — silently, only under parallel aggregation, with no guard coverage.
confirmed.impact: A combine-specific refcount imbalance (a leak, or in the mirror case an early free / use-after-free of a partial state) would ship undetected: the example asserts correctness only for paths DuckDB exercises on small single-threaded inputs, and combine is not among them. The risk is dormant until a large/parallel aggregation triggers combine in a downstream consumer.
confirmed.recommendation: Force the combine path to run inside the guarded region: run at least one query against a table large enough (or with `PRAGMA threads` raised / forced parallelism) to produce multiple partial states per group, keeping the existing alloc==free assertion at 375. This turns the combine borrow/release balance and the no-aliasing property of vector_extend into a checked invariant rather than dead, unvalidated code.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against the CURRENT tree (examples/irr.py). Read the full file: the NRT alloc/free balance guard is exactly at lines 372-377 (`if alloc_delta != free_delta: ... sys.exit(1)`), the combine callback is exactly at lines 170-186 (`_irr_combine_impl`, with `borrow_structref` at 178-179 and `vector_extend` at 180-181), and the three test datasets are exactly as described: Test 1 = 12 ungrouped rows (275-285), Test 2 = 18 rows / 2 groups (302-331), Test 3 = 1 row (352-363). No PRAGMA/SET threads or forced-parallelism call appears anywhere in the file, so DuckDB's default single-partition hash-aggregate execution on these tiny inputs will not invoke the combine callback, meaning the module's only runtime check (the NRT alloc==free guard) never exercises the borrow/release balance inside combine. This is corroborated by the project's own test suite: test/test_ducklib.py's Welford UDAF tests separately unit-test the combine merge logic via a direct Python call (`_compute_combined` at line 3319, calling `welford_combine` at 3176/3251 directly) rather than relying on the DB-driven end-to-end query to exercise DuckDB-invoked combine -- an implicit acknowledgment that a small single-threaded E2E query does not reliably drive the C-API combine callback. The removerefctpass fragility premise is also grounded in real code: numbox's vector_extend (numbox/core/vector/vector.py:131-141) conditionally calls numpy.empty (an NRT_MemInfo_alloc-emitting call) only when the destination vector must grow, so whether removerefctpass is disabled for _irr_combine_impl's LLVM module is data-dependent, exactly as described. NOT A DUPLICATE: grepped docs/reviews/2026-07-01-numbduck/reconcile/new-index.json for 'combine' -- the only two hits (EX-irr-MEM-1 current, XC-numbox-MEM-1) both concern a different root cause (missing try/except exception guards around the @cfunc callbacks, i.e. exception-swallowing at the ABI boundary), not the test-coverage gap that the combine path is never DB-invoked at all. No TST-cover-* finding covers this gap either (TST-cover-4 is about NULL/validity coverage, TST-MEM-3 is about NRT stats scope, neither about combine invocation coverage). The finding survives both refutation routes (still real on current tree; not a duplicate of any current finding) and is a legitimate, narrowly-scoped, low-severity test-coverage observation, matching the mapper's proposed severity/confidence.

confirmed.title: welford_combine's merged-mean arithmetic is never asserted (too loose)
confirmed.description: welford_combine computes the pooled mean at line 3187 (`new_mean = tgt.mean + delta * src.count / new_count`) and writes it to tgt.mean at 3190, but no test ever reads `.mean` after a combine. test_welford_numba_only._compute_combined (3319-3327) calls welford_combine(sa, sb) then returns only welford_finalize(sb), and welford_finalize (3195-3199) returns sqrt(m2/(count-1)) which depends solely on m2 and count. The m2 merge term (3188-3189) uses delta = src.mean - tgt.mean captured at 3186 BEFORE new_mean overwrites tgt.mean at 3190, so m2 is correct independent of new_mean. The UDAF combine callback path (_welford_combine_impl 3251-3263) likewise has no downstream mean assertion. Consequently a sign or operator-precedence regression on line 3187 would pass the entire suite silently.

A grep for 'invalid_param_index' and the literal '999' across the whole file confirms only 5 wrappers have that negative test: duckdb_bind_int32 (:388-396), duckdb_bind_boolean (:507-517), duckdb_bind_float (:541-551), duckdb_bind_date (:577-587), duckdb_bind_timestamp (:613-623). test_bind_int8_negative/test_bind_int16_negative exercise negative VALUES, not out-of-range indices, as the candidate states. confirmed.title: test_create_get_bit asserts only the byte length, not the bit payload

confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current tree test/test_ducklib.py:1359-1367 (test_create_get_bit): the test creates a BIT value from b"\x05\xA0", calls duckdb_get_bit, asserts only result[1] == 2 (size), and passes result[0] straight to duckdb_free at line 1366 without ever reading/comparing the payload bytes.
