confirmed.title: Non-Darwin error message gives circular NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB guidance and hides the macOS-only download asymmetry
confirmed.description: _find_standalone_libduckdb consults NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB (:34-36) and silently returns None if the path is missing/invalid. load_duckdb then reaches the non-Darwin branch (:124-128) and raises with only 'Set NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB=/path/to/libduckdb.so' — so a user who set the var to a non-existent path is told to do exactly what they just did, with no hint the path was rejected. Meanwhile the Darwin path (:129) silently proceeds to an interactive network download. The two terminal branches give materially different experiences for the same root cause (stripped wheel) with no shared explanatory message, and the non-Darwin message offers no diagnostic about why the env var did not take effect.
confirmed.impact: A user who set NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB to a bad path on Linux gets unhelpful, circular guidance; the platform behavior asymmetry (download is macOS-only) is undocumented at the call site.
confirmed.recommendation: Distinguish 'env var unset' from 'env var set but file missing' in the message (echo the offending path), and state the platform asymmetry (download is macOS-only) so a non-Darwin user understands the env var is their only recourse.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against the CURRENT tree (numbduck/utils.py, HEAD of review/numbduck-2026-06-29). _find_standalone_libduckdb (:33-36) reads NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB and, if os.path.isfile() is False, silently falls through to return None with no diagnostic distinguishing 'unset' from 'set but invalid'. load_duckdb's non-Darwin branch (:124-128) then raises RuntimeError('DuckDB C API symbols not found in the Python wheel. Set NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB=/path/to/libduckdb.so') without echoing the rejected path and without noting that the Darwin branch (:129, _download_libduckdb) offers an interactive-download fallback unavailable on non-Darwin. Both the message-content defect and the platform-asymmetry omission described in the candidate hold verbatim on current line numbers 124-128 / 34-36 / 129. Checked for duplication against docs/reviews/2026-07-01-numbduck/reconcile/new-index.json: the current UTL-DES set (DES-1 dedup constants, DES-2 missing symbol re-check on download path, DES-3 input() EOFError, DES-5 dual RTLD_GLOBAL runtimes, DES-6 raw urllib/zipfile errors) and UTL-COR set (COR-1 regex anchoring, COR-2 os.remove crash-on-import, COR-3 dual-runtime shadowing) all target different root causes on utils.py; none discuss the non-Darwin RuntimeError message's content, the missing path echo, or the macOS-only download asymmetry. UTL-COR-2 is adjacent (same os.remove/discovery-function critique) but is about a crash side effect, not the terminal error message's wording. No existing current finding covers this specific ergonomics defect, so it is neither refuted-as-unreal nor a duplicate. Severity 'low' matches the candidate: it's a message-quality/UX issue on an already-terminal failure path, not a functional bug.

confirmed.title: Version-gated bindings surface a numba TypingError, not NotImplementedError, for JIT callers on a libduckdb missing the symbol
confirmed.description: Three bindings are gated with @proxy_if_available(duckdb_lib, ...) so they degrade when the loaded libduckdb lacks the symbol: duckdb_create_varint (ducklib.py:726), duckdb_get_varint (ducklib.py:1051), duckdb_scalar_function_set_init (ducklib.py:1285). numbox's proxy_if_available (numbox/numbox/core/proxy/proxy.py) returns a plain Python `stub(*args, **_kwargs)` that raises NotImplementedError when the symbol is absent, and its docstring promises callers 'get a stub that raises NotImplementedError instead of a confusing LLVM link error at call time'. That promise only holds for pure-Python callers. These are JIT bindings whose intended call site is inside @njit code; from @njit the stub is an untyped Python global and numba raises an opaque TypingError at compile time, not the documented NotImplementedError. When the symbol IS present, proxy_if_available returns an @njit dispatcher, so the same name is two different object types depending on the runtime library — only the present case is @njit-callable. This is the same defect the pre-@proxy review flagged against numbox cres_if_available; it carried over unchanged in the @cres->@proxy migration.
confirmed.impact: On a DuckDB in the supported range (>=1.3.2,<1.6) that lacks a gated symbol, JIT code calling the gated wrapper fails to compile with a generic numba typing error instead of a clear 'X is not available' message. No exception leaks across the JIT/C boundary at runtime (compile-time failure, the safe direction), so the binding-level error-handling contract is not violated; the defect is the unmet diagnostic promise. Root cause lives in numbox proxy.py, but numbduck relies on this stub for cross-version portability.
confirmed.recommendation: Make the unavailable-symbol stub @njit-introspectable so JIT callers get a clear NotImplementedError-equivalent — e.g. have proxy_if_available register an @intrinsic/overload that raises a numba error naming the function at typing time — or, in numbduck, document that gated functions are unavailable in @njit on older libduckdb and guard dependent JIT code with a Python-level hasattr(duckdb_lib, name) capability check before compiling. Fix is in numbox; track as an upstream numbox follow-up.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against the CURRENT @proxy tree, not the stale 2026-06-29 review. Read numbox/numbox/core/proxy/proxy.py proxy_if_available (lines 136-164) directly: when hasattr(lib, func.__name__) is False, it returns `stub`, a plain, undecorated Python closure (`def stub(*args, **_kwargs): raise NotImplementedError(...)`) with only cosmetic __name__/__qualname__/__doc__ reassignment -- no @njit, @overload, or @intrinsic registration of any kind. Numba cannot type-check or call an arbitrary untyped Python function object referenced as a global from inside @njit code; such a reference fails at compile time with a numba TypingError, not the documented runtime NotImplementedError. The docstring's own phrasing ('a stub that raises NotImplementedError instead of a confusing LLVM link error at call time') only holds for the plain-Python call path; a JIT caller referencing the stub as a global never reaches the `raise` line at all before numba's typing phase rejects it. Read the current ducklib.py and confirmed all three cited sites are unchanged and exact: duckdb_create_varint at ducklib.py:726 (`@proxy_if_available(duckdb_lib, signatures.get("duckdb_create_varint"), jit_options=jit_options)`), duckdb_get_varint at ducklib.py:1051, and duckdb_scalar_function_set_init at ducklib.py:1285 -- all three still gated with proxy_if_available, so file:line refs are not stale. Checked test/test_ducklib.py:1342-1350 and 2373-2396: the only current exercises of these three gated wrappers are hasattr-skipped, Python-level (non-JIT) calls, so the JIT-typing failure mode is real but currently untested/undetected -- consistent with the finding's claim. Checked docs/reviews/2026-07-01-numbduck/reconcile/new-index.json (91 current findings) for duplication: grepped for proxy_if_available/NotImplementedError/TypingError/varint/scalar_function_set_init. The only current findings touching these three wrappers are DCK-sig-DES-3 and DCK-wrap-COR-2 (divergent docstring URL format) and DOC-acc-2 (CLAUDE.md documents removed @cres pattern) -- all a distinct defect class (documentation/style), not the JIT-typing error-contract gap. No current finding covers the NotImplementedError-vs-TypingError diagnostic-contract defect. Both refutation paths (NOT REAL, DUPLICATE) fail: the defect is real on the current tree and is not covered by any existing current finding. Severity 'low' and confidence 'medium' from the candidate are appropriate: root cause is upstream in numbox, the failure direction is safe (compile-time rejection, no runtime exception leak across the JIT/C boundary), and impact is a degraded diagnostic message rather than incorrect behavior.

confirmed.title: test_get_value_type asserts only non-null, never verifies the returned type id
confirmed.description: test_get_value_type (lines 1687-1694) creates an INT32 value, calls duckdb_get_value_type(val_p), and asserts only `type_p != 0`. It never confirms the returned logical type is actually DUCKDB_TYPE_INTEGER (e.g. via duckdb_get_type_id). Any binding that returned a non-zero-but-wrong handle -- or a wrong type id -- would still pass. Contrast with the sibling logical-type tests (e.g. test_create_logical_type_integer line 1730) which do assert duckdb_get_type_id == DUCKDB_TYPE_INTEGER.
confirmed.impact: The test cannot distinguish a correct duckdb_get_value_type binding from one returning the wrong (but non-null) type handle; a real signature/return-value regression in this wrapper would go undetected.
confirmed.recommendation: Add `assert ducklib.duckdb_get_type_id(type_p) == ducklib.DUCKDB_TYPE_INTEGER` after the non-null check (do not destroy type_p separately -- the existing comment correctly notes it aliases the value for scalar types).
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current tree. test_get_value_type at test/test_ducklib.py:1687-1694 only asserts `type_p != 0` (line 1691) after calling duckdb_get_value_type, and never calls duckdb_get_type_id to check the returned logical-type id. numbduck/ducklib.py:208 declares duckdb_get_value_type's signature as intp(intp) (returns a logical-type handle), and numbduck/ducklib.py:201/1033-1036 shows duckdb_get_type_id (int32(intp)) is the standard way to inspect that handle's type id -- exactly the pattern used by every sibling logical-type test in the same file (e.g. test_create_logical_type_integer at test/test_ducklib.py:1727-1733, and the list/array/map/struct/union tests at lines ~1780-1881), all of which assert `duckdb_get_type_id(...) == ducklib.DUCKDB_TYPE_INTEGER` or similar. test_get_value_type is the outlier: it stops at a non-null check, so a wrapper bug that returns a wrong-but-nonzero type handle (e.g. wrong offset/sig, or accidentally returning val_p type-punned) would still pass. This is a real too-loose-assertion gap, correctly characterized and correctly scoped to a single test; severity 'low' is appropriate since it doesn't affect production code, only reduces this one test's discriminating power, and the fix is a one-line addition consistent with the existing test suite's own pattern.

confirmed.title: test_create_array_value never reads back element contents
confirmed.description: test_create_array_value (lines 1634-1647) builds a 3-element ARRAY value from three int32 values and asserts only `av != 0` before destroying it. Unlike test_create_get_list_value (line 1531), test_create_get_map_value (line 1563), and test_create_get_struct_value (line 1602) -- which read children back and assert their integer values -- the array test verifies nothing about size or element contents.
confirmed.impact: A duckdb_create_array_value binding that produced an empty/garbage-but-non-null value would pass; the array-value path is effectively only smoke-tested.
confirmed.recommendation: Read back and assert at least the array size and one element (e.g. via duckdb_array_type / list-child accessors on the value or its type), matching the depth of the list/map/struct value tests.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read test/test_ducklib.py:1634-1647 (test_create_array_value): it creates a 3-element ARRAY value via duckdb_create_array_value, asserts only `av != 0` (line 1641), then destroys it. No size or element-content check is performed. This is directly comparable to the sibling container tests in the same file -- test_create_get_list_value (1531-1548), test_create_get_map_value (1563-1596), and test_create_get_struct_value (1600-1633) -- all of which read children back via duckdb_get_list_child/duckdb_get_map_key/duckdb_get_map_value/duckdb_get_struct_child and assert the underlying int32 values. The array test has no analogous readback, so a duckdb_create_array_value binding that produced an empty or garbage-but-non-null value would still pass. Verified against numbduck/ducklib.py:450-453 (duckdb_create_array_value wrapper) and confirmed via DuckDB's actual C API source (src/main/capi/duckdb_value-c.cpp) that duckdb_get_list_child/duckdb_get_list_size explicitly check `val.type().id() != LogicalTypeId::LIST` and reject ARRAY-typed values (return nullptr/0) -- so the finding's suggested fix wording ('list-child accessors on the value') is technically imprecise (list-child does NOT work on ARRAY values), but this only affects the recommendation, not the core defect: the test genuinely never reads back size or contents, and no other test in the suite exercises an ARRAY value's contents (grep for 'array'/'ARRAY' across test/ shows only this one test plus unrelated logical-type-metadata tests at lines 1797-1800). A viable fix does exist despite the imprecise recommendation, e.g. duckdb_value_to_string(av) on the array value (already bound and used elsewhere, e.g. test_value_to_string) would render '[1, 2, 3]' and validate contents, or a DB round-trip like the sibling test_list_value_from_column_logical_type (1650+) using an ARRAY column. The defect is real and correctly characterized (too-loose assertion, genuine coverage gap in the array-value path); severity 'low' is appropriate since this is a test-quality gap in a single value-creation helper, not a production code correctness bug, and matches the severity assigned to the directly analogous sibling finding TST-COR-1.

confirmed.title: Only the short (inline) string_t layout is read back; long (>12 char, out-of-line) strings untested
confirmed.description: aux_read_inline_string (267-272) decodes DuckDB string_t as a uint32 length at data_p followed by inline chars at data_p+4, and BLOB reads use the same inline layout (778-782). Every string/blob tested is short: 'hello', 'hello world'[:5], '42', 4-byte blob -- all within the 12-byte inline capacity of string_t. The long-string representation (len > 12, where bytes 4..8 are a prefix and 8..16 hold an out-of-line data pointer) is never produced or read, so any binding/reader assuming inline-only layout would pass.
confirmed.impact: A UDF or bind path that mishandles long (out-of-line) strings would not be detected; the string-reading helper itself is only correct for short strings and is never stressed with a long value.
confirmed.recommendation: Add a bind_varchar / get_varchar round-trip with a >12-character string and a >12-byte blob, reading back via the out-of-line pointer layout (or via duckdb_value/string_at) and asserting equality.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current test/test_ducklib.py and duckdb.h. duckdb_string_t (duckdb.h struct comment, scratchpad copy lines 349-365) inlines VARCHARs up to 12 characters; longer strings store a 4-byte prefix + 8-byte out-of-line pointer instead. aux_read_inline_string (test/test_ducklib.py:267-272) unconditionally reads a uint32 length at data_p then char data at data_p+4, i.e. only the inlined layout, and is used at lines 376 and 761 with 'hello' (5 chars) and 'hello world'[:5]=5 chars respectively. test_bind_blob (line 767-785) applies the identical inline-only decode to a 4-byte blob (lines 778-782). Grepped the whole file for every aux_read_column_data call site (lines 261-902 and others) and for VARCHAR/blob usage (test_create_get_varchar at 1472 uses 'hello duckdb' = exactly 12 chars, still inline boundary, and reads via duckdb_get_varchar which returns a separate malloc'd C string, not the raw string_t vector layout, so it doesn't exercise this code path either). No test in the file ever produces or reads a >12-byte string/blob through the string_t out-of-line pointer layout. Additionally checked numbduck/ducklib.py, duckdb_utils.py, and pybridge.py: none contain any string_t/out-of-line parsing logic themselves (no matches for string_t, inline, prefix[4], is_inlined) -- that decoding logic exists only in this test file's helper functions, so the gap is confined to test coverage of a test-only helper/pattern rather than a bug in shipped library code. This slightly limits real-world blast radius (there's no current numbduck binding that itself mishandles long strings) but does not refute the core claim: the out-of-line string_t layout is genuinely never exercised anywhere in the suite. Severity 'low' is appropriate given no current production code path depends on it, though it does leave string/blob round-trip correctness for long values as an untested assumption for any future UDF work built on this pattern.

confirmed.title: Destroy of value/logical-type/function handles is never verified (no slot-zero or leak assert)
confirmed.description: Handle liveness-after-destroy is asserted only for database/connection/prepared/data_chunk via buf[0]==0 (98, 208, 287). For the ~150 value, logical-type, and scalar/aggregate-function tests, teardown calls aux_destroy_value (1165-1170), duckdb_destroy_logical_type, or duckdb_destroy_scalar_function on a scratch buffer and never re-reads the slot, never asserts alloc==free, and never checks the destroy actually ran. The leak/stats assertions (rtsys alloc==free) exist only in the three bridge/UDAF tests (3386, 3465, 3547) which measure numba NRT allocations, not DuckDB-side allocations.
confirmed.impact: A wrapper that silently no-ops a destroy (or drops the handle without freeing) would leak DuckDB memory and still pass every value/logical-type/function test. The destroy bindings for the largest handle families are effectively unasserted.
confirmed.recommendation: Where DuckDB zeroes the handle on destroy, assert buf[0]==0 after the destroy call (as done for DB/conn). Where it does not, add at least one long-loop create/destroy test with an OS/process RSS or DuckDB-side allocation check to catch leaks.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against test/test_ducklib.py at HEAD. The DB/connection/prepared/data_chunk teardown helpers do re-read the slot after destroy: test_disconnect asserts duckdb_connection[0] == 0 after duckdb_disconnect (line 97), test_duckdb_destroy_data_chunk asserts data_chunk[0] == 0 after duckdb_destroy_data_chunk (line 208), and aux_destroy_prepared's caller test_prepare_and_destroy asserts stmt[0] == 0 after duckdb_destroy_prepare (line 287). By contrast, aux_destroy_value (lines 1165-1170) builds a scratch buf, calls duckdb_destroy_value(buf.ctypes.data), and returns without ever re-reading buf[0]; grepping every call site of aux_destroy_value plus every direct duckdb_destroy_logical_type / duckdb_destroy_scalar_function / duckdb_destroy_aggregate_function call in the file (123 destroy-related lines total) turns up zero post-destroy slot re-checks anywhere in the value/logical-type/function test sections. The only alloc==free leak assertions in the suite (lines 3373-3374, 3388-3389, 3465-3466) use numba's rtsys.get_allocation_stats(), which tracks numba NRT allocations (Python-side MemInfo/structref bridge), not DuckDB's internal heap -- confirmed by their location inside the structref/UDAF bridge tests (aux_alloc_and_export/_release helpers), unrelated to duckdb_destroy_value/logical_type/scalar_function. DuckDB's C API destroy_* functions take a pointer-to-handle and, per the established and consistently-demonstrated pattern for every other handle family in this same suite (db, connection, prepared statement, data chunk), zero the handle after freeing; duckdb_destroy_value/duckdb_destroy_logical_type/duckdb_destroy_scalar_function/duckdb_destroy_aggregate_function follow the identical `void destroy(handle_t *)` C API shape (ducklib.py lines 163-166, 240, 258, 763-784, 1219-1222), so the same slot-zero check would be available and meaningful here too -- it is simply never exercised for value/logical-type/function handles despite there being on the order of ~150 tests in those sections (well over half the 134 total test functions in the file touch these three handle families). The finding accurately characterizes a real, verifiable gap: no test proves destroy actually runs or frees DuckDB-side memory for these handle families, only that create/use worked before destroy was called. Severity 'low' is appropriate: this is purely a test-coverage/verification gap (matches the file's own 'notes' summary conceding no library bug was found), not a functional defect in ducklib.py itself, and the impact (undetected DuckDB-side leak or silent no-op destroy) is real but bounded to test rigor rather than shipped behavior.

confirmed.title: test_column_logical_type executes but never asserts the type is correct
confirmed.description: test_column_logical_type (934-943) fetches the column's logical type pointer, asserts only logical_type_p != 0, then destroys it. It never calls duckdb_get_type_id on the returned logical type to confirm it is DUCKDB_TYPE_INTEGER, unlike test_create_logical_type_integer (1727-1733) and the type-constructor tests which all verify get_type_id. The test thus proves the pointer is non-null but not that duckdb_column_logical_type returns the correct type for column 0.
confirmed.impact: A binding that returned a valid-but-wrong logical type handle for a result column would pass. Weak assertion on a metadata accessor.
confirmed.recommendation: Add assert duckdb_get_type_id(logical_type_p) == DUCKDB_TYPE_INTEGER before destroying.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read test/test_ducklib.py:934-943 directly. test_column_logical_type fetches out_result_p, calls duckdb_column_logical_type(out_result_p, 0), asserts only logical_type_p != 0, then destroys the logical type buffer and closes the DB. It never calls duckdb_get_type_id on the returned pointer to confirm the column's logical type is DUCKDB_TYPE_INTEGER (the known schema of aux_query_1's column 0, 'i'). By contrast, ducklib.duckdb_get_type_id is a real binding used pervasively elsewhere in the same file (test_create_logical_type_integer at 1727-1748, list/array/map/struct/union/enum logical-type tests at 1780-1902) specifically to assert the correct type id after construction. Nothing in ducklib.py or numbox's proxy/call machinery makes the non-null check equivalent to a correctness check -- duckdb_column_logical_type could return a valid-but-wrong logical-type handle (e.g. a caching/aliasing bug, or wrong column index math) and this test would still pass. The gap is real and narrowly scoped (a single metadata-accessor test), matching the claimed severity of low.

confirmed.title: test_create_array_value asserts only non-null; array value contents are never read back
confirmed.description: test_create_array_value (1634-1648) builds a 3-element array value, asserts av != 0, and destroys everything. Unlike the sibling container tests -- list (get_list_size + get_list_child at 1538-1543), map (get_map_size/key/value at 1576-1588), struct (get_struct_child at 1617-1621) -- it never reads back the array's size or child elements, so the created array value's contents are never verified.
confirmed.impact: duckdb_create_array_value could store wrong or no elements and the test would still pass on the non-null check alone.
confirmed.recommendation: Read back the array's length and/or child values (matching the list/map/struct tests) and assert they equal the inputs 1,2,3.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read test/test_ducklib.py:1634-1648 directly. test_create_array_value builds a 3-element INTEGER array value via duckdb_create_array_value, asserts only `av != 0`, then destroys av/v1/v2/v3/int_type -- it never reads back the array's length or element contents. This is a real, precisely-located gap: the sibling container-value tests do verify contents -- test_create_get_list_value (1531-1550) asserts duckdb_get_list_size == 2 and duckdb_get_list_child(...) == 10/20; test_create_get_map_value (1563-1599) asserts duckdb_get_map_size/key/value; test_create_get_struct_value (1602-1631) asserts duckdb_get_struct_child == 42/99. test_create_array_value has no analogous readback, and no other test in the file exercises the contents of a value built by duckdb_create_array_value (verified via grep across the file; the only other array-related tests -- test_create_array_type at 1791, duckdb_array_type_array_size/child_type -- exercise the LOGICAL TYPE constructor, not a create_array_value VALUE). aux_destroy_value (1165-1170) performs no validation either, so nothing in the test indirectly confirms element values. Checked duckdb.h (v1.3.2-era C API, matching the pin duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6): unlike duckdb_get_list_size/duckdb_get_list_child and duckdb_get_struct_child/duckdb_get_map_size/key/value, there is no dedicated duckdb_get_array_size/duckdb_get_array_child getter for a duckdb_value of ARRAY type -- so the reviewer's specific suggested fix (mirror the list/map/struct getter pattern) isn't literally available as a 1:1 API call, but the underlying defect claim (contents never read back) is independently true regardless of which readback mechanism would be used (e.g. duckdb_value_to_string(av) and asserting on the rendered '[1, 2, 3]' text, or a SQL round-trip, both remain viable and are also unused). This mirrors the already-accepted pattern in TST-cover-6 (weak assertion on a create/get pair) and is a pure test-coverage gap, not a library bug -- consistent with the low severity assigned. No evidence found that the gap is covered elsewhere or that verification is otherwise infeasible, so I confirm at the claimed severity.

confirmed.title: test_scalar_function_set_init never verifies the init callback runs; init impl is a no-op
confirmed.description: test_scalar_function_set_init (2376-2420) registers a UDF with duckdb_scalar_function_set_init whose callback (_init_cb -> _init_cb_impl, 2362-2369) is a bare 'pass'. The test only asserts the ordinary add_one result is 43. Nothing observes that the init callback was invoked or mutated any state, so set_init is smoke-tested for acceptance only -- if the binding silently ignored the init pointer, the test would still pass.
confirmed.impact: The v1.5+ set_init binding is exercised for 'does not error' but not for 'the init function actually runs / receives correct info', so a broken init-registration would go undetected.
confirmed.recommendation: Have the init callback write an observable marker (e.g. via extra_info or a state slot) and assert the marker after the query, or otherwise verify the init callback fired.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read test/test_ducklib.py:2362-2369 and :2376-2420 directly. _init_cb_impl (line 2363-2364) is a bare `pass` under @njit, wrapped by the @cfunc _init_cb (2367-2369) which just calls it. test_scalar_function_set_init (def at 2376) registers a scalar function, calls ducklib.duckdb_scalar_function_set_init(func_p, _init_cb.address) (its return value is void, unchecked), then only asserts rc == DuckDBSuccess for duckdb_register_scalar_function and duckdb_query, and asserts the final SELECT with_init(42) result equals 43. Nothing in the test observes whether the init callback pointer was actually stored/invoked by DuckDB -- the add_one scalar function alone produces 43 regardless of whether set_init did anything. Confirmed: if the duckdb_scalar_function_set_init binding (numbduck/ducklib.py:1285-1288, a thin proxy_if_available wrapper around the C API with signature void(intp, intp)) silently failed to pass the pointer through, or the underlying DuckDB engine never invoked the init callback for this code path, this test would still pass. This is a genuine test-coverage gap (weak assertion), not a functional bug in ducklib.py itself, so severity=low is appropriate, matching the reviewer's claim.

confirmed.title: JIT (@njit) tests assert Success only; no in-JIT error/edge branch is covered
confirmed.description: The JIT section (993-1160) only exercises happy paths: jit_open_close (1013) and jit_connect_query_disconnect (1029) assert DuckDBSuccess and non-null pointers; jit_prepare_bind_execute (1061) reads back values but only for a successful prepare/bind/execute. No @njit test drives an error return code (invalid SQL, failed bind, null handle, unbound param) through the wrappers from inside compiled code. Error-code propagation across the JIT boundary -- a core invariant per CLAUDE.md 'Error Handling' -- is only ever tested in Python-called paths.
confirmed.impact: A wrapper that mishandles a DuckDBError return specifically under @njit lowering (e.g. wrong sign/truncation of the state code) would be caught only in Python calls, not in the JIT calls the library exists to enable.
confirmed.recommendation: Add an @njit test that issues an invalid query and/or an out-of-range bind and asserts the returned rc == DuckDBError from within compiled code.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read test/test_ducklib.py:993-1160 (the JIT section) in full. The three @njit driver functions there -- jit_open_close (1013-1020), jit_connect_query_disconnect (1029-1046), and jit_prepare_bind_execute (1061-1131) -- only run valid SQL/valid binds and their corresponding pytest wrappers (1023, 1049, 1134) only assert ducklib.DuckDBSuccess / non-null pointers. No @njit-decorated function in the file drives an invalid-SQL query, an out-of-range bind, or unbound-params execute and returns/observes a DuckDBError from inside compiled code. Every DuckDBError-asserting test in the suite (grep confirms lines 52, 85, 148, 295, 394, 407, 421, 452, 508-515, 542-549, 578-585, 614-621, 2077) is a plain top-level `def test_...` (not @njit), calling ducklib wrappers directly from the Python interpreter. This distinction is architecturally real, not pedantic: per numbox/core/proxy/proxy.py (proxy() at line 40), each ducklib wrapper is itself an @njit-compiled dispatcher (`func_proxy_name`); calling it from plain Python goes through numba's dispatcher boxing/unboxing entry point, whereas calling it from inside another @njit function (as jit_open_close etc. do) is a direct native LLVM call via the `_{func_proxy_name}` intrinsic -- a genuinely different lowering path (this is exactly the calling-convention distinction _stable_cfunc_alias and the proxy intrinsic exist to handle). I confirmed via grep across the whole file (all @njit occurrences, all DuckDBError occurrences) that no other @njit-scoped function anywhere combines an error-producing DuckDB call with an assertion on the resulting error code; the one njit-adjacent error test, test_scalar_function_set_error (2041-2080), only exercises duckdb_scalar_function_set_error (a void callback-side call) from inside @njit, then checks the resulting DuckDBError via a Python-level duckdb_query call, not through a nested-njit rc read. So the finding's premise -- happy-path-only JIT tests, error paths only demonstrated via the interpreter-to-dispatcher boundary -- holds exactly as described. Severity 'low' is appropriate: this is a coverage gap with a plausible but narrow failure mode (a bug specific to error-code propagation across the nested-njit calling convention), not a demonstrated defect, consistent with the reviewer's own 'medium confidence' framing and the low severity given to sibling coverage-gap findings in the same batch.

confirmed.title: find_duckdb_shared_lib regex is not end-anchored, so a sidecar can trip the len==1 invariant and hide a valid lib (or select the wrong file)
confirmed.description: Both discovery regexes use re.match without a trailing '$': `re.match(r"duckdb[\w.-]*\.(so|dll|dylib|pyd)", file_)` (line 98) and `_duckdb[\w.-]*\.(so|dll|dylib|pyd)` (line 104). re.match anchors only at the start, so any name that merely CONTAINS a valid extension as a substring also matches, e.g. `duckdb.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so.debug` or a versioned soname `duckdb....so.1`. The `.` in the character class `[\w.-]` and the un-anchored tail both widen the match. The loader then enforces `len(pkg_libs) == 1` (line 99) / `len(site_libs) == 1` (line 105); a second matching sidecar makes len==2 and the function raises RuntimeError at line 107 even though a perfectly loadable library is present. On Windows the duckdb package can ship both the engine `duckdb.dll` and the binding `duckdb*.pyd` in the same package dir, and both extensions are in the alternation, which independently produces len>1 and picks neither. Conversely, with exactly one over-broad match the wrong file (e.g. a .pyd binding rather than the C-API-exporting .dll) could be returned.
confirmed.impact: Import of ducklib fails with a hard 'could not find unambiguous duckdb shared library' error, or loads a non-C-API file, on layouts that carry a debug/soname sidecar or (Windows) a separate .dll + .pyd — a valid lib is missed even though it exists.
confirmed.recommendation: Anchor the extension at end of string (add '$' or use re.fullmatch), and prefer selecting the actual C-API-exporting object explicitly (e.g. verify with _has_capi_symbols before accepting a candidate) rather than relying solely on a len==1 count over a broad regex.
confirmed.verdictReasoning:
Read numbduck/utils.py at HEAD: line 98 is `pkg_libs = [file_ for file_ in duckdb_dir_files if re.match(r"duckdb[\w.-]*\.(so|dll|dylib|pyd)", file_)]`, gated by `len(pkg_libs) == 1` at line 99; line 104 is the parallel `_duckdb[\w.-]*\.(so|dll|dylib|pyd)` check gated by `len(site_libs) == 1` at line 105; both funnel into `raise RuntimeError(...)` at line 107 if the count isn't exactly 1. Directly tested `re.match(r"duckdb[\w.-]*\.(so|dll|dylib|pyd)", 'duckdb.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so.debug')` and `re.match(..., 'duckdb.so.1.3.2')` -> both return a truthy match, confirming re.match's start-only anchoring lets an unrelated trailing suffix ride along after the required '.so'/'.dll'/'.dylib'/'.pyd' token, exactly as the finding describes. The regex mechanic and all cited line numbers are accurate on the current tree.

However, I checked whether this is more than theoretical by downloading and inspecting the actual PyPI duckdb wheels across the project's supported pin range (duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6): 1.3.2 and 1.5.4 for manylinux, win_amd64, and macosx. In every case exactly one file matches the relevant regex in the relevant directory (duckdb/duckdb.cpython-*.so or duckdb/duckdb.cp312-win_amd64.pyd for 1.3.x; _duckdb.cpython-*.so or _duckdb.cp312-win_amd64.pyd directly in site-packages for 1.4+). None of these real wheels ship a second file (no .so.debug sidecar, no separate engine .dll alongside a .pyd) that would trip len==1 into len==2. So the specific 'Windows ships both duckdb.dll and duckdb*.pyd' scenario in the finding's description does not hold for any officially published wheel in the pinned range (Windows wheels contain only one _duckdb*.pyd/duckdb*.pyd, no .dll at all) -- that part of the impact narrative is not substantiated by real packaging.

Net: the underlying code defect (missing end-anchor on both discovery regexes, real files/lines as cited) is real and mechanically verified, but the practical trigger requires a contrived/foreign sidecar file not produced by any current officially released duckdb wheel, so the risk is latent/defensive rather than actively manifesting. This matches the original reviewer's own 'low' severity and 'low' confidence self-rating, which I confirm as appropriate -- not upgrading, not refuting the underlying claim.

confirmed.title: Legacy-cache os.remove is an unconditional filesystem mutation inside a discovery ('find') function and can crash import
confirmed.description: _find_standalone_libduckdb (a lookup) unconditionally deletes the old unversioned cache: `if os.path.isfile(old_cached): os.remove(old_cached)` (lines 38-40). os.remove is unguarded — a read-only $HOME, root-owned legacy file, or a concurrent process racing the same delete will raise PermissionError/FileNotFoundError, which propagates out of load_duckdb and turns 'import numbduck.ducklib' into a crash on the very macOS-stripped-wheel path this fallback is meant to service.
confirmed.impact: On the macOS fallback path, a non-writable or racing legacy cache file converts a recoverable library-discovery step into an import-time exception.
confirmed.recommendation: Wrap the removal in try/except (swallow/log OSError), or move the one-time migration cleanup out of the read-flavoured discovery function entirely so a failed unlink cannot abort loading.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Code at numbduck/utils.py:38-40 exactly matches the description: `old_cached = os.path.join(_LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_BASE, "libduckdb.dylib"); if os.path.isfile(old_cached): os.remove(old_cached)` with no surrounding try/except. _find_standalone_libduckdb (utils.py:33-47) is called from load_duckdb (utils.py:113-130) at line 119 with no enclosing try/except, and load_duckdb itself is invoked at ducklib.py:12 (`duckdb_lib = load_duckdb()`) at module import time with no try/except anywhere in numbduck/__init__.py or ducklib.py. So any OSError from os.remove (PermissionError on a read-only $HOME or root-owned legacy file, or FileNotFoundError from a TOCTOU race between the os.path.isfile check and os.remove) propagates all the way out and turns `import numbduck.ducklib` into an unhandled crash. This path is only reached when the wheel's C API symbols are missing (_has_capi_symbols false), which CLAUDE.md documents as the real, currently-active macOS duckdb 1.4.1-1.5.2 wheel-stripping scenario, so the fallback code is genuinely exercised in practice, not dead code. Severity is correctly low rather than higher: the legacy unversioned cache file only exists for users who previously ran a pre-versioned-cache release of numbduck (a one-time migration artifact), so os.path.isfile(old_cached) is False and os.remove is never invoked for the overwhelming majority of installs; the failure additionally requires a permission/ownership problem or a concurrent-process race on top of that. No mitigating catch exists anywhere in the call chain, and the recommended fix (try/except OSError around the remove, or moving the cleanup out of the discovery function) is cheap and low-risk, consistent with a low-severity, easy-to-fix robustness gap rather than a high-impact defect.

confirmed.title: macOS fallback leaves a dual DuckDB runtime (symbol-less wheel + standalone) globally loaded with no guard against symbol shadowing
confirmed.description: On the macOS stripped-wheel path load_duckdb first loads the wheel RTLD_GLOBAL at line 115 (and the wheel is already resident from `import duckdb` at line 1), then loads the standalone/downloaded dylib RTLD_GLOBAL at line 121/130. Two independent DuckDB engines are now in-process. Correct today only because the wheel exports none of the duckdb_* C-API symbols (only PyInit__duckdb + duckdb_adbc_init), so RTLD_DEFAULT resolves the JIT's extern duckdb_* refs to the standalone. If a future wheel exported even a partial C API, first-in-load-order symbol resolution would silently bind the JIT to the wheel copy; and any handle created via the Python `duckdb` module (wheel engine) passed into numbduck njit code (standalone engine) is cross-runtime UB. The loader neither re-checks which copy backs the resolved symbols nor documents/guards the constraint.
confirmed.impact: Latent (not active on current wheels): a partial-C-API wheel or user-mixed handles between the Python duckdb module and numbduck would cause wrong-copy binding or crashes, surfacing only at JIT-call time, not at load.
confirmed.recommendation: Document the single-engine constraint; consider asserting the resolved duckdb_open address belongs to the standalone (e.g. via dladdr) when taking the fallback path, and warn if the wheel also exports C-API symbols.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Mechanism and premise both verified against current code. numbduck/utils.py:1 imports duckdb (loads the wheel's shared object); load_duckdb() at line 115 explicitly re-loads the same wheel lib via numbox's load_lib_path(path) -> ctypes.CDLL(path, mode=RTLD_GLOBAL) (numbox/core/bindings/utils.py:178-180); if _has_capi_symbols (probes only `duckdb_open`, utils.py:29-30) is False, the macOS fallback loads the standalone/downloaded dylib at line 121 (or 130), again RTLD_GLOBAL, into the same still-live process -- both objects remain resident (ctypes CDLL is never dlclose'd/GC'd here; nothing in utils.py or ducklib.py releases the wheel handle). numbox's own _call_lib_func intrinsic (numbox/core/bindings/call.py:72) resolves each C symbol at lowering time via `ll.address_of_symbol(func_name)`, and numbox's own CLAUDE.md documents that this is backed by llvm::sys::DynamicLibrary::SearchForAddressOfSymbol, which for process-wide lookups is 'equivalent to dlsym(RTLD_DEFAULT, ...) -- it searches all Mach-O images/ELF objects in load order and returns the first match.' That doc explicitly states RTLD_GLOBAL load order determines which of several same-named-symbol copies wins, and numbox already implements a detect-and-refuse guard for exactly this class of problem for sqlite (pysqlite_bridge.py libraries_coordinated()/extract_connection_ptr), confirming the risk pattern is real and recognized in the sibling codebase, but no analogous guard exists in numbduck/utils.py for duckdb. Today the risk is genuinely inert: verified the macOS wheel exports only PyInit__duckdb + duckdb_adbc_init (per numbduck/CLAUDE.md, citing duckdb-python PR #81's CMakeLists.txt -exported_symbol list), ducklib.py never binds/calls duckdb_adbc_init (grep found zero 'adbc' references in numbduck/ducklib.py), and load_duckdb() returns early at line 116-117 without ever touching the standalone path whenever the wheel DOES satisfy _has_capi_symbols, so a wheel exporting the FULL C API is also safe. The narrow, correctly-identified gap is a wheel that exports partial C API (some duckdb_* symbols) while still missing duckdb_open specifically (the only probe used) -- that wheel would fail the gate, trigger the standalone fallback, and its early-loaded overlapping symbols would silently win at JIT-resolution time over the standalone's copies, per the load-order mechanism above. This is forward-looking but not idle speculation: numbduck/CLAUDE.md's own Project Status section records that duckdb/duckdb-python#404 has a maintainer committing to add C API export before 1.5.3, and the project's pin (duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6) does not exclude such an incremental/partial release. Severity/confidence as originally assigned (low/low) is appropriate: no active defect on any currently shipping wheel, the trigger condition is a specific hypothetical future packaging state, and the recommended fix (document constraint; optional dladdr-based assertion) is proportionate, not a hard blocker.

confirmed.title: Cache dylib path and filename literal duplicated across two functions
confirmed.description: The bare filename literal "libduckdb.dylib" is repeated four times (old_cached :38, cached :41, dest :87, zf.open member :88), and the *cached destination path* `os.path.join(_LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_DIR, "libduckdb.dylib")` is independently reconstructed in two different functions: `_find_standalone_libduckdb` (:41, the path it looks for) and `_download_libduckdb` (:87, the path it writes to). These two must stay byte-for-byte identical or the loader downloads to a location the finder never checks (silent re-download every import), yet nothing in the code ties them together — they are two literal copies of the same join. There is already a module-level constants block (`_LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_BASE`/`_LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_DIR`, :16-21) that this filename and the derived cache-file path clearly belong in.
confirmed.impact: A future edit to the cached filename or layout in one function silently desynchronizes the discover/write contract, causing perpetual re-downloads or a lib that is written but never found. Extra copies also make the migration-cleanup literal at :38 easy to overlook.
confirmed.recommendation: Introduce a `_LIBDUCKDB_DYLIB_NAME = "libduckdb.dylib"` constant and a derived `_LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_FILE = os.path.join(_LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_DIR, _LIBDUCKDB_DYLIB_NAME)` next to the existing constants, and reference those from both functions (and the zip member name).
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current numbduck/utils.py: the literal "libduckdb.dylib" appears exactly at L38 (old_cached), L41 (cached), L87 (dest), L88 (zf.open member), and the cache-file path os.path.join(_LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_DIR, "libduckdb.dylib") is indeed independently re-derived in _find_standalone_libduckdb (L41, the read/find side) and _download_libduckdb (L87, the write side) with no shared constant, even though a constants block exists at L16-21 that is the natural home for such a constant. The description's mechanism, line numbers, and function attributions are all accurate. However, severity is overstated: both duplicate copies currently compute an identical value (same _LIBDUCKDB_CACHE_DIR, same literal), so the loader today correctly finds what it downloads — there is no active bug, race, or user-facing failure, only a latent risk that a future one-sided edit could desynchronize the pair. This is a straightforward DRY/maintainability nit with a trivial, low-risk fix, not a present functional or robustness defect (contrast with the genuinely 'medium' findings in the same batch, e.g. UTL-DES-2/3/5, which describe concrete current failure triggers). Downgrading to low severity; the finding itself (real duplication, correctly characterized) is confirmed.

confirmed.title: Read-flavoured _find_standalone_libduckdb performs an unconditional os.remove side effect
confirmed.description: `_find_standalone_libduckdb` is named and used as a pure discovery function (its result feeds an `if standalone:` at :119-120), but it embeds an unconditional filesystem mutation: it `os.remove`s the legacy unversioned cache `~/.numbduck/lib/libduckdb.dylib` if present (:37-40). Hiding a destructive migration inside a lookup violates least surprise, makes the function non-idempotent to test (a unit test for discovery must now mock/tolerate `os.remove`), and is unguarded — a read-only home directory, a permissions issue, or a concurrent numbduck process racing the same delete makes the 'find' throw where a lookup should simply return a path or None.
confirmed.impact: Reduced testability of the discovery path and a latent crash/race: an environment where the legacy file exists but is not deletable turns a benign library load into an OSError.
confirmed.recommendation: Move the legacy-cache cleanup into its own explicitly-named migration step (called once from load_duckdb, or lazily) wrapped in try/except OSError, and keep `_find_standalone_libduckdb` side-effect free.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against current numbduck/utils.py:33-47. _find_standalone_libduckdb is named/used as a discovery function (feeds `if standalone:` at utils.py:119-120) but unconditionally executes os.remove(old_cached) at line 40 with no try/except guard, on the mainline (non-NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB-override) path. Traced the call chain: numbduck/ducklib.py:12 calls `duckdb_lib = load_duckdb()` at module import time with no surrounding try/except; load_duckdb() (utils.py:113-130) calls _find_standalone_libduckdb() unconditionally on the macOS symbol-less-wheel fallback path (utils.py:119). Thus a permission error or TOCTOU race on the os.remove would surface as a raw unhandled OSError during `import numbduck.ducklib`, exactly as described. No mitigating try/except, idempotency guard, or separation of migration-vs-lookup exists elsewhere in the file. Severity 'low' fits: narrow trigger window (macOS fallback path AND legacy unversioned cache present AND permission/race failure), a design/testability smell rather than a common-path functional bug.

confirmed.title: Download failures (404 / missing zip member) surface as raw urllib/zipfile errors, and version-range comment is rot-prone
confirmed.description: The download assumes the wheel's `duckdb.__version__` string is exactly a DuckDB GitHub release tag that ships an asset literally named `libduckdb-osx-universal.zip` containing a member literally named `libduckdb.dylib` (:52-56, :88). If the wheel version has a pre/post-release suffix, or the asset/member naming ever differs, `urlopen` raises a raw `HTTPError: 404` (:83) or `zf.open` raises `KeyError` (:88) — neither wrapped in a numbduck-branded message pointing back to `brew install duckdb` / NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB. There is also no timeout on `urlopen`, so a hung connection blocks import indefinitely. Separately, the hardcoded comment at :118 ('macOS with 1.5.2 >= duckdb >= 1.4.1') is a documented version-range assumption that will silently rot as the `duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6` pin advances.
confirmed.impact: A version whose release layout differs, or a network hiccup, degrades a recoverable situation into an opaque stack trace or an indefinite hang during import; the stale comment misleads future maintainers about the actual affected version window.
confirmed.recommendation: Wrap the fetch/extract in try/except (HTTPError, URLError, KeyError) re-raising the branded RuntimeError, pass a `timeout=` to `urlopen`, and replace the fixed version-range comment with a reference to the tracking issue / a note that the window is whatever the wheel strips (detected dynamically by `_has_capi_symbols`).
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Verified against numbduck/utils.py on the current tree. (1) `_download_libduckdb` line 83 `with urlopen(url) as resp:` has no `timeout=` argument and no surrounding try/except — a 404 (mismatched release tag/asset name) raises a raw `urllib.error.HTTPError`, and a hung connection blocks indefinitely (default socket timeout is None/blocking). (2) Line 88 `with zf.open("libduckdb.dylib") as src` has no try/except — if the zip's member name ever differs, `zipfile.ZipFile.open` raises a raw `KeyError`. (3) Neither `_download_libduckdb` (lines 50-91) nor its sole caller `load_duckdb` (line 129: `downloaded = _download_libduckdb()`) contains any try/except around the fetch/extract, so both errors would propagate unbranded. Confirmed no wrapping exists anywhere else in the package: `grep -rn except numbduck/` finds only an unrelated `except json.JSONDecodeError` in configurations.py. Because `load_duckdb()` runs at ducklib.py import time (numbduck/ducklib.py:12 `duckdb_lib = load_duckdb()`), any such failure surfaces as a raw exception during `import numbduck.ducklib`, exactly as claimed, with no pointer back to the brew/NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB guidance the surrounding code otherwise provides (see the branded RuntimeError at utils.py:71-77 for the decline path). (4) The version-range comment at line 118 (`# Python wheel missing C API symbols (macOS with 1.5.2 >= duckdb >= 1.4.1)`) is purely descriptive/non-functional — actual gating is done dynamically by `_has_capi_symbols` (line 116), so the comment cannot desync behavior, but it is a real code-quality nitpick since it names a version window narrower than the `duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6` pin and will visibly go stale as the pin advances. All claimed line numbers (83, 88, 118) and mechanics check out; severity 'low' is appropriate since triggering requires an actual DuckDB release-asset layout change or a network fault, both edge cases relative to the more directly reachable issues (e.g. UTL-DES-3's EOFError under non-interactive stdin, correctly rated medium).

confirmed.title: urlopen has no timeout: a hung/slow network path blocks library import indefinitely (availability)
confirmed.description: The download at line 83 (`with urlopen(url) as resp:`) passes no timeout= argument, so it inherits the global default socket timeout, which is None unless the process set one. A stalled TCP connection, a slowloris-style trickle from a malicious/misbehaving endpoint (relevant on the very network path that could also be attacked in UTL-SEC-1), or a captive portal that accepts the connection but never sends data will hang the read forever. Because this runs at import of ducklib (load_duckdb -> _download_libduckdb) on the macOS stripped-wheel path, the entire library import — and any program importing it — wedges with no progress and no way to recover short of SIGINT.
confirmed.impact: A single unresponsive/hostile endpoint on the download path can indefinitely block import of numbduck (and the whole program that imports it) with no error and no automatic recovery.
confirmed.recommendation: Pass an explicit, bounded timeout (e.g. urlopen(url, timeout=30)) and handle the resulting socket.timeout/URLError by raising the same actionable RuntimeError used elsewhere (brew install / set NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB), so the failure is fast and diagnosable instead of a hang.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read numbduck/utils.py:78-91 (_download_libduckdb) on the current tree. Line 83 is exactly `with urlopen(url) as resp:` with no timeout= argument, and no try/except wraps it (the only pre-existing RuntimeError raises are in the consent-gate branch at lines 70-77, unrelated to network I/O). Grepped numbduck/ and numbox/ for `setdefaulttimeout`/`timeout` and found no process-wide socket timeout set anywhere in either codebase, so urlopen falls back to Python's global default socket timeout, which is None (blocking) unless some other code in the process set one -- and nothing here does. This call only executes on the macOS stripped-wheel path (load_duckdb -> _download_libduckdb) after the user has either answered y/yes to the interactive prompt or set NUMBDUCK_LIBDUCKDB_DOWNLOAD=1, so it is reachable exactly as described. A hung TCP handshake, a slow-trickle/hostile endpoint, or a captive portal that accepts the connection but never completes the response will block resp.read() indefinitely with no recovery path short of killing the process (SIGINT), which matches the claimed availability/DoS behavior. The fix (bounded timeout + converting socket.timeout/URLError into the existing actionable RuntimeError) is a straightforward, low-cost correct recommendation. Severity of 'low' is appropriate: the impact (indefinite hang) is real but the trigger requires an already-opted-in download path (explicit user consent or explicit env var) plus an adverse/hostile network condition, so likelihood and blast radius are both narrow compared to the sibling UTL-SEC-1 integrity finding.

confirmed.title: duckdb_vector_get_validity return typed uint64 instead of intp, breaking the all-pointers-are-intp contract
confirmed.description: signatures["duckdb_vector_get_validity"] = uint64(intp) (ducklib.py:237; wrapper ducklib.py:1207-1210). Per duckdb.h the function is `uint64_t *duckdb_vector_get_validity(duckdb_vector vector)` — it returns a POINTER (uint64_t*) to the validity bitmask, not a scalar. numbduck's documented contract is that every pointer is carried as `intp` (CLAUDE.md UDF note 2: '@cfunc signatures must use nb_types.intp (not nb_types.voidptr) because numbduck uses intp for all pointers'; numbox enforces this via _require_intp in meminfo.py). Every other pointer-returning binding follows it — the sibling accessor duckdb_vector_get_data is intp(intp) (ducklib.py:236), and the consumer duckdb_validity_row_is_valid takes the validity pointer as intp (ducklib.py:234, int8(intp, intp), matching duckdb.h `bool duckdb_validity_row_is_valid(uint64_t *validity, idx_t row)`). Only this one pointer return is typed uint64.
confirmed.impact: In @njit code the returned validity pointer has type uint64, which does not unify with the intp the rest of numbduck (and duckdb_validity_row_is_valid) expects. Callers are forced to insert an explicit intp(...) cast, and omitting it is a numba typing error rather than a silent success — this is exactly what test/test_ducklib.py:1117-1118 must do (`duckdb_validity_row_is_valid(intp(v3_validity_p), intp(0))`), whereas the intp-returning get_vector at line 1111 needs no such cast. A uint64 pointer also does not satisfy numbox helpers that require intp (e.g. _require_intp-guarded paths), and pointer arithmetic over the mask becomes unsigned. Bit pattern is preserved on LP64 (both are 64-bit) so no wrong result occurs on the supported platform; the defect is a real, contract-violating type mismatch and ergonomic/compile-safety hazard, not memory corruption.
confirmed.recommendation: Change the signature to intp(intp): `signatures["duckdb_vector_get_validity"] = intp(intp)` so the pointer return matches the intp-for-all-pointers convention and unifies with duckdb_validity_row_is_valid without casts. After the change, the intp(...) wrappers in the tests (e.g. test_ducklib.py:1118) become unnecessary.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Defect is real and correctly characterized. numbduck/ducklib.py:237 has signatures["duckdb_vector_get_validity"] = uint64(intp), wrapped at ducklib.py:1207-1210. duckdb.h confirms the C prototype is `DUCKDB_C_API uint64_t *duckdb_vector_get_validity(duckdb_vector vector)` -- it returns a pointer (uint64_t*), not a scalar count. numbduck/CLAUDE.md:97 documents the project-wide convention that '@cfunc signatures must use nb_types.intp (not nb_types.voidptr) because numbduck uses intp for all pointers', and the sibling pointer-returning accessor duckdb_vector_get_data is correctly typed intp(intp) at ducklib.py:236. duckdb_validity_row_is_valid (ducklib.py:234, int8(intp, intp)) expects its validity-mask argument as intp, matching the C signature `bool duckdb_validity_row_is_valid(uint64_t *validity, idx_t row)`. Empirical confirmation: test/test_ducklib.py:1117-1118, inside the @njit-compiled jit_prepare_bind_execute function, must write `duckdb_validity_row_is_valid(intp(v3_validity_p), intp(0))` -- an explicit intp(...) cast on the validity pointer -- whereas the intp-returning duckdb_vector_get_data results (v0_p/v1_p/v2_p, same file, lines ~1097-1110) are used directly with no such cast. This intp(...) cast is a singular outlier in the test file (only occurrence of an explicit intp() wrap around a proxy return value before feeding it to another proxy call), consistent with numba's fixed-signature njit/cfunc call resolution not silently unifying uint64 and intp (a numba TypingError without the cast), not just a stylistic choice. So the claim holds: this is the only pointer-returning proxy signature typed uint64 instead of intp, it is a genuine contract violation, and it is independently reproduced by the test suite needing a workaround cast. However, the severity is better characterized as low rather than medium: per the finding's own impact analysis, the bit pattern is identical on the supported LP64 platform (uint64 and intp are both 64-bit), no wrong result or memory corruption occurs, and a missing cast fails loudly at numba compile time (TypingError) rather than silently misbehaving -- this is a type-hygiene/convention-consistency defect with an easy, well-contained fix, not a functional-correctness bug. This matches the severity the prior 2026-06-29 review gave to the same/related findings (DCK-sig-COR-2, DCK-wrap-COR-2, and its own XC-numbox-COR-1, all rated 'low' for this exact ducklib.py:236/237 issue).

confirmed.category: cfunc exception handling / NRT refcount leak at the C boundary
confirmed.title: UDAF @cfunc callbacks have no exception guard; a raise inside an impl is swallowed by numba's cfunc boundary, leaking the borrow_structref incref and handing DuckDB a silent zero/void default
confirmed.description: Every DuckDB aggregate callback is a thin @cfunc wrapper that forwards to a module-level @njit impl with no try/except: _irr_state_size_cb (109-111), _irr_init_cb (124-126), _irr_update_cb (165-167), _irr_combine_cb (188-190), _irr_finalize_cb (209-211), _irr_destroy_cb (223-225). Per the codebase's own numba contract (MEMORY reference_numba_cfunc_swallows_exceptions: numba @cfunc returns the zero default and does NOT unwind to C on a Python exception, and NRT refs held across a raising call are leaked), any exception escaping an impl is silently converted to a 0/void return at the DuckDB boundary. Concretely: _irr_update_impl (156-157) and _irr_combine_impl / _irr_finalize_impl hold a live +1 from borrow_structref (numbox meminfo.py:131-140) at the moment they call vector_push / vector_extend, whose growth path allocates via numpy.empty (numbox vector.py:123,137); if that allocation raised, numba tears the frame down without the scope-exit decref, so the borrow's incref leaks (the group's MemInfo never reaches refcount 0, so its structref + the two Float64Vector heap buffers are never freed) AND the partially-updated aggregate is returned to DuckDB as success with no error signalled. _irr_state_size_cb returning the zero default would be catastrophic (0-byte state slot), though its body cannot actually raise. For realistic (non-OOM) inputs no impl raises, so the export(+1)/release(-1) ladder stays balanced -- this is a latent robustness gap, not an active miscount.
confirmed.impact: On an allocation failure (or any future edit that introduces a raising call into an impl), the C boundary silently swallows the error: the borrow_structref +1 leaks the group's MemInfo and its nested vector buffers, the DuckDB aggregate result is silently wrong/partial, and no rc/error is propagated to DuckDB or the caller. The failure is invisible until a downstream NRT alloc!=free check (irr.py:372-377) trips.
confirmed.recommendation: Wrap each impl body in a bare try/except (the documented cure -- do NOT use try/finally, which re-raises on numba 0.65.1) so the frame runs its NRT cleanup on the error path and the callback returns a defined default; for callbacks where a failure must be visible, surface it (e.g. leave the finalize output at math.nan, and prefer duckdb_aggregate/scalar error-signalling APIs over a silent zero). At minimum add a comment at each @cfunc wrapper noting the swallow-on-raise contract so future edits do not introduce an uncaught raising call across a held borrow_structref incref.
confirmed.verdictReasoning: Read every cited line on the current tree; all six @cfunc wrappers in examples/irr.py (109-111, 124-126, 165-167, 188-190, 209-211, 223-225) call their @njit impl with zero try/except, confirmed by direct file read. _irr_update_impl (irr.py:156-158) and _irr_combine_impl (irr.py:178-181) each hold a live borrow_structref incref (numbox/utils/meminfo.py:131-140) across a separate compiled-function call (vector_push / vector_extend, numbox/core/vector/vector.py:120-141) whose growth path allocates via numpy.empty (vector.py:123 and :137) -- exactly the 'held live across a separate call that raises' precondition for numba's documented cfunc-boundary NRT leak. This mechanism is not hearsay: numbox's own sibling UDAF path (numbox/core/bindings/_sqlite_udf_helpers.py, module docstring lines 11-19) explicitly documents that an unguarded numba @cfunc 'SWALLOWS the exception (prints Exception ignored and returns the zero default without unwinding)' and that the in-body try/except is required so 'numba can run the borrowed state's reference-count decrement, which the unwind would otherwise skip -- a per-group meminfo leak' -- and this exact failure mode is empirically exercised by passing tests in numbox/test/core/test_sqlite_udf_helpers.py (test_step_exception_surfaces_error_and_no_leak, test_finalize_exception_surfaces_error_and_no_leak, etc.), which assert alloc==free only for the GUARDED callbacks. numbduck's examples/irr.py uses the identical primitives (borrow_structref, Float64Vector/vector_push/vector_extend from the same numbox modules) but omits the guard numbox itself already established as necessary for this exact pattern. duckdb C API confirmed (ducklib.py) to expose duckdb_scalar_function_set_error but no aggregate-function error-signalling channel, consistent with the finding noting DuckDB aggregates have no sqlite3_result_error analogue. All file:line citations (irr.py cfunc ranges, meminfo.py:131-140, vector.py:123/137, irr.py:372-377 NRT check) verified exact against the current tree. The claim that _irr_state_size_impl's body 'cannot actually raise' is also correct (it is a constant return, numpy.uint64(8)). Severity: low is appropriate -- the leak requires an actual allocation failure (OOM) or a future edit introducing a raising call inside a held borrow; for realistic non-OOM inputs the ladder stays balanced, matching the review's own 'latent robustness gap, not an active miscount' characterization. This is demo/example code (examples/irr.py), not the numbox core library, which further supports low over medium/high, though the gap is real and the fix pattern is cheap (numbox already has the template).

refuted.title: Kernel treats literal-constant argument vectors as flat n-element arrays (out-of-bounds read of args lat2/lon2)
refuted.description: The SQL calls the UDF as hv_jit(lat, lon, 37.7749, -122.4194) (haversine.py:152 via sql_py -> sql_jit at 155). Arguments 3 and 4 are SQL literal constants. In DuckDB, a BoundConstantExpression evaluates to a CONSTANT_VECTOR whose data buffer holds a SINGLE physical value; DuckDB does not flatten scalar-function argument vectors before invoking the C-API callback (the C wrapper reinterpret_casts the input DataChunk and calls the user function directly). The kernel, however, reads every input column identically: v_lat2 = duckdb_data_chunk_get_vector(chunk, 2), d_lat2 = duckdb_vector_get_data(v_lat2), a_lat2 = carray(..., (n,), float64) (lines 92-93, 96-97, 101-102), then indexes a_lat2[i]/a_lon2[i] for i in range(n) (lines 107-109, 112). For a CONSTANT vector the data pointer addresses only one double, so a_lat2[1..n-1] and a_lon2[1..n-1] read past the 8-byte constant buffer (up to ~2047 doubles per 2048-row chunk) -> heap over-read and garbage store coordinates for every row except row 0 of each chunk. This is the classic DuckDB constant-vector gotcha; the kernel performs no duckdb_vector get-type/flatten check. The canonical test (test_udf_benchmark, jit_square(x), test_ducklib.py:2685-2745) only ever passes a single FLAT column argument, so it never exercises constant inputs and would not catch this.
refuted.impact: Out-of-bounds heap reads and incorrect distances for all non-first rows of each chunk, yielding a wrong count(*) in the < 50 km filter. Whether it manifests depends on DuckDB's actual constant-vector delivery for the C-API scalar path across the pinned range duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6; if any version delivers constants un-flattened, the example silently miscomputes (and could crash under ASAN).
refuted.recommendation: Do not assume flat inputs for constant arguments. Either query the vector type and broadcast a constant (read index 0 when the vector is CONSTANT), or bind the store lat/lon as scalars passed outside the chunk (e.g. via extra_info / a captured constant) rather than as SQL literal UDF arguments, or add an explicit flatten step. At minimum, exercise the constant-argument path in a differential test since the current test suite passes only flat columns.
refuted.verdictReasoning: The finding claims DuckDB's C API scalar-function wrapper passes constant-vector arguments (e.g. the SQL literals 37.7749/-122.4194 in hv_jit(lat, lon, 37.7749, -122.4194)) through to the user callback un-flattened, causing haversine.py's carray reads of a_lat2[i]/a_lon2[i] for i in range(n) (lines 101-102, 107-112) to read out of bounds past a 1-element constant buffer. This is refuted by DuckDB's own source: src/main/capi/scalar_function-c.cpp's CAPIScalarFunction (the function actually registered as ScalarFunction::function and invoked by the expression evaluator on every call) executes `auto all_const = input.AllConstant(); input.Flatten();` UNCONDITIONALLY before reinterpret_casting the chunk and invoking the user's duckdb_scalar_function_t callback. DataChunk::Flatten() materializes every vector, including ones that started as CONSTANT_VECTOR from a BoundConstantExpression, into a FLAT_VECTOR with the value broadcast to all n rows -- so by the time the callback runs, lat2/lon2 are already flat n-element arrays. The subsequent `if (all_const && ...) result.SetVectorType(CONSTANT_VECTOR)` only re-collapses the OUTPUT vector for optimization; it does not affect what the callback reads. I verified this Flatten() call is present, in the identical form, in the duckdb/duckdb source at both v1.3.2 and v1.5.1 (the endpoints of numbduck's pin duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6), fetched via `gh api repos/duckdb/duckdb/contents/src/main/capi/scalar_function-c.cpp?ref=<tag>`. So the premise 'DuckDB does not flatten scalar-function argument vectors before invoking the C-API callback' is factually false for the entire supported version range, there is no out-of-bounds read, and haversine.py's kernel (examples/haversine.py:88-113) is correct as written. Severity corrected to none (finding does not survive verification).

refuted.title: Committed __version__ is empty; local unstamped build produces an invalid version
refuted.description: The tracked `numbduck/__init__.py` is literally `__version__ = ""` (no newline). pyproject.toml:29-30 resolves the dynamic version via `attr = "numbduck.__version__"`, so an unstamped build reads the empty string. The build backend is pinned to setuptools~=75.3.0 (pyproject.toml:2), which validates versions against PEP 440; an empty string is not a valid version. Only the CI/release workflows rewrite `__init__.py` before building (numbduck_ci.yml:61-63, release.yml:30-31), so wheels built inside CI are fine, but the documented developer path `pip install -e .` / `python -m build` on a clean checkout has no stamp step and hits the empty version. This is a design gap: the source of truth for local dev is a value that is never itself buildable.
refuted.impact: A fresh-clone `pip install -e .` or `python -m build` (both documented dev commands in CLAUDE.md) can fail with an invalid/empty version, or at best produce degenerate metadata, confusing new contributors. The mechanism silently depends on a CI-only side effect.
refuted.recommendation: Commit a valid placeholder dev version (e.g. `__version__ = "0.0.0.dev0"`) so unstamped local builds succeed with an honest dev marker, while CI/release still overwrite it with the tag-derived version. This keeps the stamp flow intact and removes the clean-checkout failure.
refuted.verdictReasoning: Confirmed the tracked file numbduck/numbduck/__init__.py:1 is `__version__ = ""`, and pyproject.toml:29-30 resolves dynamic version via `attr = "numbduck.__version__"`. But the finding's core mechanism claim -- that setuptools~=75.3.0 rejects the empty string as an invalid PEP 440 version, causing `pip install -e .` / `python -m build` to fail or produce degenerate metadata on a clean checkout -- is factually wrong. Reproduced with a minimal package matching numbduck's pyproject.toml + an empty-string __init__.py, installed with the exact pinned build deps (setuptools~=75.3.0 -> resolved 75.3.4, wheel~=0.45.0, build==1.2.2.post1): both `pip install -e .` and `python -m build --wheel` succeed cleanly and produce a valid, well-formed version string '0.0.0' (visible in dist-info METADATA and the wheel filename), not an error and not a degenerate/invalid version. Root cause: setuptools' vendored distutils has `setuptools/_distutils/dist.py:1174: return self.version or "0.0.0"` -- an empty/falsy version string is silently defaulted to '0.0.0', which setuptools' own test suite comments document as 'Default version given by setuptools' (setuptools/tests/test_config_discovery.py:259). So a fresh clean-checkout `pip install -e .` does NOT fail and does NOT hit an invalid-version error; it just gets a generic placeholder version, which is a much smaller (arguably cosmetic) issue than 'build fails' or 'invalid version'. The recommendation (commit a valid dev placeholder like 0.0.0.dev0) may still be a reasonable minor polish, but the finding as written mischaracterizes the actual failure mode and its severity is not supported -- there is no build/install failure to fix.

refuted.title: numbduck_ci.yml splices github.ref_name into run: shell and into __init__.py on tag builds (script injection)
refuted.description: Same injection class as BLD-SEC-1, in the main CI workflow. Line 56 `echo "VERSION=${{ github.ref_name }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV` (reached only when `github.ref_type == 'tag'`) and line 63 `echo "__version__ = '${{ env.VERSION }}'" > numbduck/__init__.py` splice the tag name into shell script text. A tag name containing shell metacharacters executes arbitrary commands in the CI runner. The `build` job holds only `contents: read` and does not publish (the wheel at line 86 is built but never uploaded), and non-tag pushes use the safe synthetic `0.1.<run_number>` VERSION, so the blast radius is smaller than release.yml — but the sharp edge is identical and should be fixed the same way.
refuted.impact: Arbitrary command execution in a CI runner on a tag push with a crafted tag name; token is read-only and nothing is published, so impact is limited to runner compromise (secret exfil is minimal here since permissions are contents: read).
refuted.recommendation: Apply the same fix as BLD-SEC-1: move `github.ref_name` into the step `env:` and reference the quoted shell variable; do not expand GitHub expressions into `run:` text. Fixing both workflows with one idiom also removes the cosmetic drift between them.
refuted.failure_scenario: A maintainer pushes tag `` v2`id>/tmp/x` ``; at line 56 the backtick command substitution runs during the Determine version step in every matrix job.
refuted.verdictReasoning: The cited code exists exactly as described: numbduck_ci.yml:56 `echo "VERSION=${{ github.ref_name }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV` (inside the `if [ "${{ github.ref_type }}" == "tag" ]` branch at line 55) and line 63 `echo "__version__ = '${{ env.VERSION }}'" > numbduck/__init__.py` are textually present and use the same unsafe direct-interpolation-into-run:-text pattern as release.yml's BLD-SEC-1. However, the finding's failure_scenario -- 'A maintainer pushes tag `v2\`id>/tmp/x\``; at line 56 the backtick command substitution runs during the Determine version step in every matrix job' -- is not achievable on the current tree, because this specific workflow's triggers make the vulnerable branch dead code. numbduck_ci.yml:3-7 declares only `on: push: branches: ["**"]` and `on: pull_request: branches: ["main"]` -- there is no `tags:` or `tags-ignore:` key anywhere in the file. GitHub's documented behavior (docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions, on.push.<branches|tags> section) states verbatim: 'If you define only tags/tags-ignore or only branches/branches-ignore, the workflow won't run for events affecting the undefined Git ref' -- confirmed independently via two separate fetches of GitHub's official docs. Because numbduck_ci.yml defines only a branches filter and no tags filter, pushing a git tag does NOT trigger this workflow at all; the push event is simply not evaluated/dispatched for tag refs. For the workflow's other trigger, pull_request, github.ref_type is always 'branch' (a PR ref is never a tag). Therefore `github.ref_type == "tag"` can never be true for any run of numbduck_ci.yml under its current trigger configuration, the injection sink at line 56/63 is unreachable, and the 'Determine version' step always falls into the safe synthetic-version else-branch (`BUILD_VERSION="0.1.${{ github.run_number }}"`, where run_number is a GitHub-controlled integer, not attacker-influenced). This is a materially different situation from release.yml (BLD-SEC-1), which triggers on `release: types: [published]` -- a release IS associated with a real tag, so `github.ref_type` genuinely is 'tag' there and that sink is live; BLD-SEC-1 remains a valid, reachable finding. The code pattern in numbduck_ci.yml is still a latent anti-pattern (identical to release.yml's, presumably copy-pasted) and would become exploitable if a `tags:` filter were ever added to this workflow's `on.push` block without also fixing the interpolation -- worth a defensive cleanup for consistency with the release.yml fix -- but as characterized, the finding asserts an active, exploitable script-injection vulnerability reachable by 'a maintainer pushing a tag', and that specific attack is not possible given the workflow's actual trigger configuration. The dead-code status is not mentioned or accounted for anywhere in the finding's reasoning about reduced severity (which cites only reduced permissions/no-publish, not unreachability). Downgrading to 'none' (dormant/latent code-quality nit, not an active vulnerability) rather than confirming the claimed 'low' severity live exploit.

refuted.title: create_duckdb_result hard-codes a 48-byte buffer that libduckdb writes through by pointer
refuted.description: create_duckdb_result() returns allocate_buffer(6) = 6 x int64 = 48 bytes (duckdb_utils.py:36-39). This buffer's .ctypes.data is passed as the duckdb_result* out-param to duckdb_query / duckdb_execute_prepared, which memcpy the FULL duckdb_result struct through that pointer. The 48-byte size is pinned only against duckdb.h v1.3.2 (docstring at line 38), where duckdb_result is exactly six 8-byte fields (3x idx_t + 3x pointer). The project pin is duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6, spanning 1.4 and 1.5. There is no runtime size check (e.g. ctypes.sizeof) tying the allocation to the loaded library's actual struct. If any in-range release enlarges duckdb_result, libduckdb writes past the 48-byte numpy buffer -> heap-adjacent out-of-bounds write / corruption, a memory-safety fault rather than a catchable error. This is the memory-safety facet; the version-drift/design facet overlaps DES. Confidence is low because duckdb_result has in practice been stable at 48 bytes across the 1.x line (all real payload sits behind the internal_data pointer), so the risk is latent, not a live bug on 1.3.2.
refuted.impact: Latent heap out-of-bounds write if duckdb_result grows within the >=1.3.2,<1.6 pin; would manifest as silent memory corruption on query/execute, not a clean error.
refuted.recommendation: Derive the result-buffer size from the loaded library instead of hard-coding 6: allocate ceil(sizeof(duckdb_result)/8) int64s using the actual struct size (or assert 48 >= that size at import). At minimum add a startup assertion against the running duckdb version so an enlarged struct fails loudly instead of corrupting the heap.
refuted.verdictReasoning: The claimed defect is conditional: 'IF any duckdb release in [1.3.2, 1.6) enlarges duckdb_result, THEN libduckdb writes past the 48-byte numpy buffer -> heap OOB write.' This premise is empirically false across the entire currently-pinned range, not merely 'stable in practice' as the finding hedges. (1) Source: duckdb.h's duckdb_result struct at v1.3.2 (fetched from github.com/duckdb/duckdb v1.3.2 tag) is byte-for-byte identical to the struct in the current tree's docstring at numbduck/duckdb_utils.py:38 -- three idx_t (8B) + duckdb_column* (8B) + char* (8B) + void* internal_data (8B) = 48B, matching allocate_buffer(6) at duckdb_utils.py:39. (2) Design: all real per-query state lives behind the opaque internal_data pointer; the five 'deprecated_*' fields are a frozen legacy layout kept only for source/binary compatibility with pre-1.0 callers. This is precisely the C-API stability mechanism DuckDB uses to guarantee duckdb_result never needs to grow across releases -- the struct is deliberately inert, not merely 'observed to be stable'. (3) Empirical confirmation: I ran duckdb_open/duckdb_connect/duckdb_query against the actual compiled libduckdb C API (symbols duckdb_query/duckdb_connect/duckdb_open present via nm -D) extracted from the real duckdb 1.4.0 and 1.5.1 Python wheels (both within the >=1.3.2,<1.6 pin), writing the out-param into a 48-byte buffer followed by a 64-byte 0xAB canary region.
